q.t: Which of the following documents have to be on board for an international flight? a) Certificate of aircraft registration b) Certificate of airworthiness c) Airworthiness review certificate d) EASA Form-1 e) Airplane logbook f) Appropriate papers for every crew member g) Technical logbook
o: b, c, d, e, f, g
q.e: According to ICAO and EASA regulations, the certificate of registration, certificate of airworthiness, ARC, aircraft logbook, and appropriate crew licenses must be carried on board. EASA Form-1 is a release to service document for parts, not required on board.

q.t: Which area could be crossed with certain restrictions?
q.e: A restricted area (R) is an airspace of defined dimensions within which the flight of aircraft is restricted in accordance with certain specified conditions. It can be crossed if the restrictions are met or a clearance is obtained.

q.t: Where can the type of restriction for a restricted airspace be found?
q.e: The Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP) contains detailed and permanent information about restricted airspaces in the ENR (En-route) section.

q.t: What is the status of the rules and procedures created by the EASA? (e.g. Part-SFCL, Part-MED)
o: They have the same status as ICAO Annexes
Only after a ratification by individual EU member states they are legally binding
They are not legally binding, they only serve as a guide
They are part of the EU regulation and legally binding to all EU member states
q.e: EASA regulations are adopted as European Union regulations. Once adopted, they are directly and legally binding in all EU member states without the need for national ratification.

q.t: Which validity does the "Certificate of Airworthiness" have?
q.e: The Certificate of Airworthiness (CofA) is valid indefinitely as long as the aircraft is maintained in accordance with the regulations and the Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC) is kept valid.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation "ARC"?
q.e: ARC stands for Airworthiness Review Certificate. It is a document issued after a successful periodic airworthiness review, validating the Certificate of Airworthiness for usually 1 year.

q.t: The "Certificate of Airworthiness" is issued by the state...
o: in which the aircraft is registered.
of the residence of the owner.
in which the aircraft is constructed.
in which the airworthiness review is done.
q.e: The Certificate of Airworthiness is always issued by the competent aviation authority of the state of registry, regardless of where the aircraft was manufactured or where the owner lives.

q.t: A pilot license issued in accordance with ICAO Annex 1 is valid in...
o: those countries that have accepted this license on application.
the country where the license was issued.
the country where the license was acquired.
q.e: Under the Chicago Convention, licenses issued by an ICAO contracting state in accordance with the standards of Annex 1 are recognized as valid by all other ICAO contracting states.

q.t: What is the subject of ICAO Annex 1?
q.e: ICAO Annex 1 is titled "Personnel Licensing" and contains the Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) for licensing flight crew members, air traffic controllers, and maintenance personnel.

q.t: What is the period of validity of a private pilot license (PPL)?
q.e: The EASA PPL document itself is non-expiring (unlimited validity). However, to exercise the privileges of the license, the pilot must hold valid ratings (e.g., SEP) and a valid medical certificate.

q.t: What is the minimum age to obtain a private pilot license?
q.e: According to EASA Part-FCL, an applicant for a PPL(A) must be at least 17 years of age at the time of license issue.

q.t: What are the minimum requirements among others to acquire a rating for VFR night flights?
o: At least 10 additional flight hours at night, three of them with a flight instructor with at least 1 hour cross-country flight plus 5 solo take-offs and full-stop landings
At least 5 additional flight hours at night, four of them with a flight instructor with at least 1 hour cross-country flight plus 5 solo take-offs and full-stop landings
At least 5 additional flight hours at night, three of them with a flight instructor with at least 1 hour cross-country flight plus 5 solo take-offs and full-stop landings
At least 5 additional flight hours at night, three of them with a flight instructor with at least 1 hour cross-country flight plus 10 solo take-offs and full-stop landings
q.e: The night rating requires at least 5 hours of flight time at night, including at least 3 hours of dual instruction (which must include 1 hour of cross-country) and 5 solo take-offs and full-stop landings.

q.t: The validity of a medical examination certificate class 2 for a 62 years old pilot is...
q.e: For pilots holding a Class 2 medical certificate, the validity period is reduced to 12 months once the pilot reaches the age of 50.

q.t: In which way is a SEP (land) rating renewed if you do not meet the required flight time?
o: A proficiency check with an examiner
According to the flight experience there have to be several training flights under supervision of an ATO
The ATO can renew the rating after a training flight with a flight instructor
The required flight experience has to be accumulated under supervision of a flight instructor
q.e: If the recency requirements for revalidation are not met before expiry, the rating must be renewed. This requires passing a proficiency check with an authorized examiner.

q.t: The possession of a european PPL(A) entitles the holder to...
o: act as pilot on a commercial flight when there are at most 4 people on board.
act as pilot in commercial and non-commercial flights with single engine aircraft.
act as PIC, and only for flights in aircraft with a MTOW of maximum 2000 kg a compensation may be obtained.
act as PIC on non-commercial flights without compensation as well as to receive compensation as a flight instrucor.
q.e: A PPL allows the holder to act as Pilot-in-Command (PIC) without remuneration on non-commercial flights. Remuneration is only allowed for flight instruction or examination duties, if appropriately qualified.

q.t: What is the minimum age to start a private pilot training at a flight school?
q.e: The minimum age for a student pilot to fly solo is 16 years, which is considered the practical minimum age to effectively start and progress in the flight training program.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation "SERA"?
o: Standardized European Rules of the Air
Standard European Routes of the Air
q.e: SERA stands for Standardised European Rules of the Air, an EU regulation that harmonizes air traffic rules and procedures across the European airspace.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation "TRA"?
q.e: TRA stands for Temporary Reserved Airspace. It is an airspace temporarily reserved for specific users (e.g., military exercises), through which other traffic may be allowed to transit under specific ATC clearance.

q.t: What has to be considered when entering an RMZ?
o: To permanently monitor the radio and if possible to establish radio contact
To obtain a clearance from the local aviation authority
The transponder has to be switched on Mode C and squawk 7000
To obtain a clearance to enter this area
q.e: In a Radio Mandatory Zone (RMZ), pilots must maintain continuous air-ground voice communication watch and establish two-way communication before entering. An explicit ATC clearance is not strictly required unless it is also controlled airspace.

q.t: What condition has to be met during a Special VFR flight?
o: A minimum distance to clouds of 2000 m
q.e: A Special VFR flight is cleared to operate within a control zone in meteorological conditions below standard VMC. However, the pilot must remain clear of clouds and always maintain visual reference to the terrain.

q.t: What has to be done before entering a TMZ?
o: Switch on the transponder and activate mode A and C or mode S
Switch on the transponder, activate mode A, and squawk "IDENT"
File a flight plan before the flight
q.e: Before entering a Transponder Mandatory Zone (TMZ), the pilot must operate a transponder capable of reporting pressure altitude, which means using Mode A/C or Mode S.

q.t: What is the meaning of an area marked as "TMZ"?
q.e: TMZ stands for Transponder Mandatory Zone. It is an airspace where the carriage and operation of a pressure-altitude reporting transponder is mandatory to improve radar surveillance.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation "IFR"?
q.e: IFR stands for Instrument Flight Rules, which are the rules governing the navigation of aircraft using instruments rather than visual references.

q.t: A flight is called a "visual flight", if the...
o: visibility in flight is more than 8 km.
flight is conducted under visual flight rules.
visibility in flight is more than 5 km.
flight is conducted in visual meteorological conditions.
q.e: A visual flight (VFR flight) is defined strictly by the fact that it is being conducted in accordance with the Visual Flight Rules.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation "VMC"?
q.e: VMC stands for Visual Meteorological Conditions. It describes the actual weather conditions (visibility, distance from clouds) expressed in terms of minimums required for VFR flight.

q.t: Two engine-driven aircraft are flying on crossing courses at the same altitude. Which one has to divert?
o: The lighter one has to climb
Both have to divert to the right
The heavier one has to climb
Both have to divert to the left
q.e: When two aircraft are approaching head-on or approximately so and there is danger of collision, both aircraft shall alter their heading to the right. (Note: The question says 'approaching each other opposite', which means head-on).

q.t: Two aeroplanes are flying on crossing tracks. Which one has to divert?
o: The aircraft which flies from left to right has the right of priority
Both have to divert to the right
The aircraft which flies from right to left has the right of priority
Both have to divert to the left
q.e: When two aircraft are converging at approximately the same level, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way (right-of-way rule). Thus, the one flying from left to right has the priority.

q.t: In airspace "D" a Boeing 737 and a Cessna 152 are flying on crossing courses. Which aeroplane has to divert?
o: The Cessna 152, because IFR and commercial flights have priority
The air traffic control (ATC) has to decide which one has to divert
The aeroplane flying from right to left has priority, the other one has to divert
The Boeing 737, because an airliner has greater power reserves
q.e: The rules of the air apply equally to all engine-driven aircraft regardless of size. The aircraft that has the other on its right must give way.

q.t: Which of the following options is NOT a sufficient reason to fly below the required minimum height?
o: Take-off or landing at an aerodrome
An approach without landing at an aerodrome
Bad weather conditions in the vicinity of an aerodrome
The drop of towed objects at an aerodrome
q.e: Bad weather alone is not a legal justification to violate minimum safe altitudes over congested areas or assemblies of persons. The pilot must either divert or turn back.

q.t: A single-engine piston and a turboprop aeroplane are approaching each other opposite at the same altitude. Which aeroplane has to change its track to avoid a collision?
o: The turboprop aircraft has to give way to the single-engine piston aircraft
Both aircraft have to alter their tracks to the left
Both aircraft have to alter their tracks to the right
The single-engine piston aircraft has to give way to the turboprop aircraft
q.e: Regardless of the engine type (piston vs turboprop), when two powered aircraft are approaching head-on, both must alter their heading to the right.

q.t: Which distances to clouds have to be maintained during a VFR flight in airpaces C, D and E?
q.e: According to SERA VMC minima, above 3000 ft AMSL or 1000 ft AGL, aircraft must maintain a distance of 1,500 meters horizontally and 1,000 feet (300 m) vertically from clouds.

q.t: The minimum flight visibility at 5000 ft MSL in airspace B for VFR flights is...
q.e: Below 10,000 ft AMSL, the standard VFR minimum flight visibility in controlled airspaces (like Class B, C, D, E) is 5 km.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace "C" for an aircraft operating under VFR at 5000 ft MSL?
q.e: Just as in airspace B, below 10,000 ft AMSL in airspace C, the minimum VFR flight visibility is 5 km.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace "E" for an aircraft operating under VFR at FL75?
q.e: Flight Level 75 is below FL100 (10,000 ft). Therefore, the standard minimum flight visibility required is 5000 meters.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace "C" for an aircraft operating under VFR at FL110?
q.e: At and above 10,000 ft AMSL (FL100), aircraft speeds are generally higher, so the minimum VFR flight visibility requirement increases to 8 km.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace "C" for an aircraft operating under VFR at FL125?
q.e: Because FL125 is above 10,000 ft AMSL, the required minimum flight visibility is 8 km to allow sufficient time to see and avoid other traffic.

q.t: What are the minimum distances to clouds for a VFR flight in airspace "B"?
q.e: In VMC, the vertical distance from clouds must be 1,000 feet, which translates to exactly 300 meters. The horizontal distance is 1,500 meters.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace "C" below FL 100 for an aircraft operating under VFR?
q.e: As previously established, the visibility requirement for VFR flights below FL100 in Airspace C is 5 kilometers.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace "C" at and above FL 100 for an aircraft operating under VFR?
q.e: At or above FL100, the required VFR visibility increases to 8 kilometers due to the generally higher speeds of aircraft at these altitudes.

q.t: The term "ceiling" is defined as the...
o: altitude of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 20000 ft.
height of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 10000 ft.
height of the base of the highest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 20000 ft.
height of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 20000 ft.
q.e: Ceiling refers to the height above the ground (AGL) of the base of the lowest layer of clouds that covers more than half of the sky (BKN or OVC) below 20,000 feet.

q.t: Being intercepted by a military aircraft at daytime, what is the meaning of the following signal: Alternating movement of the ailerons, normally left of the intercepted aircraft, followed by a smooth turn to the left?
o: Prepare for a safety landing, you have entered a prohibited area
You are entering a restricted area, leave the airspace immediately
You are clear of any restricted or reserved airspaces, you can continue on your heading
q.e: This is the standard international visual signal used by an intercepting aircraft to say "You have been intercepted. Follow me."

q.t: Being intercepted by a military aircraft at daytime, what is the meaning of the following signal: A sudden heading change of 90 degrees or more and a pull-up of the aircraft without crossing the track of the intercepted aircraft?
o: You are entering a restricted area, leave the airspace immediately
Follow me, i will bring you to the next suitable airfield
Prepare for a safety landing, you have entered a prohibited area
q.e: The "breakaway" maneuver by the intercepting aircraft signals that the interception is over and you are free to proceed on your way ("You may continue your flight").

q.t: The altimeter is switched from local QNH to 1013.25 hPa...
o: when climbing above the transition altitude.
q.e: When climbing, the altimeter must be set to the standard pressure setting (1013.25 hPa) upon passing the Transition Altitude.

q.t: During a flight at FL 80, the altimeter setting has to be...
q.e: Flight Levels (FL) are based on the standard atmosphere pressure setting. Therefore, whenever flying at a Flight Level, the altimeter must be set to 1013.25 hPa.

q.t: What is the purpose of the semi-circular rule?
o: To avoid collisions by reducing the probability of opposing traffic at the same altitude
To fly without a filed flight plan in prescribed zones published in the AIP
To allow safe climbing or descending in a holding pattern
To avoid collisions by suspending turning manoeuvres
q.e: The semi-circular rule physically separates aircraft flying in opposite directions (e.g. Eastbound on odd levels, Westbound on even levels) to minimize the risk of head-on collisions.

q.t: Which of the following options are possible SSR-Transponder modes?
q.e: The standard civil aviation Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR) modes are Mode A (identification code), Mode C (altitude reporting), and Mode S (enhanced data link).

q.t: A transponder with the ability to send the current pressure level is a...
q.e: Mode C and Mode S transponders are equipped with an altitude encoder, allowing them to transmit the aircraft's pressure altitude to ATC radar screens.

q.t: Which transponder code indicates a loss of radio communication?
q.e: Squawking code 7600 signals to ATC that the aircraft has experienced a two-way radio communication failure.

q.t: Which transponder code should be set during a radio failure without any request?
q.e: If radio failure occurs, the pilot must independently and immediately set the transponder to 7600 to alert Air Traffic Control.

q.t: Which transponder code has to be set unrequested during an emergency?
q.e: In the event of an emergency (distress), the pilot should squawk 7700. This triggers a visual and audible alarm on the ATC radar screen.

q.t: Which air traffic service is responsible for the safe conduct of flights?
q.e: Only Air Traffic Control (ATC) has the authority and responsibility to issue clearances and instructions to maintain safe separation and prevent collisions between aircraft.

q.t: Air traffic control service is conducted by which services?
o: TWR (aerodrome control service) APP (approach control service) ACC (area control service)
APP (approach control service) ACC (area control service) FIS (flight information service)
ALR (alerting service) SAR (search and rescue service) TWR (aerodrome control service)
FIS (flight information service) AIS (aeronautical information service) AFS (aeronautical fixed telecommunication service)
q.e: ATC consists of three main branches: Tower (TWR) for aerodrome traffic, Approach (APP) for arriving/departing traffic, and Area Control Center (ACC) for en-route traffic.

q.t: Which answer is correct with regard to separation in airspace "E"?
o: IFR traffic is separated only from VFR traffic
VFR traffic is separated from VFR and IFR traffic
VFR traffic is separated only from IFR traffic
VFR traffic is not separated from any other traffic
q.e: In Class E airspace, IFR traffic is separated from other IFR traffic. However, VFR traffic is NOT separated from any other traffic; VFR pilots are solely responsible for collision avoidance ("see and avoid").

q.t: Which air traffic services can be expected within an FIR (flight information region)?
o: ATC (air traffic control) FIS (flight information service)
AIS (aeronautical information service) SAR (search and rescue)
ATC (air traffic control) AIS (aeronautical information service)
q.e: In an uncontrolled Flight Information Region (FIR), ATC is not provided. The primary services are Flight Information Service (FIS) and Alerting Service (ALR) for emergencies.

q.t: A pilot can contact FIS (flight information service)...
q.e: While airborne, a pilot obtains flight information and communicates with FIS using the designated VHF radio communication frequencies.

q.t: What is the correct phrase with respect to wake turbulence to indicate that a light aircraft is following an aircraft of a higher wake turbulence category?
q.e: The standard ICAO phraseology used by ATC to warn pilots of potential wake vortices from preceding heavy aircraft is "Caution wake turbulence".

q.t: Which of the following options states a correct position report?
q.e: A proper abbreviated position report should be concise, providing Aircraft Identification, Position, and Altitude without unnecessary filler words. "DEABC, [Point N], 2500 ft" is correct.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation "AIREP"?
q.e: AIREP stands for Air-Report. It is a routine or special report of weather or operational conditions sent by an aircraft in flight to a ground station.

q.t: What information is provided in the general part (GEN) of the AIP?
o: Table of content, classification of airfields with corresponding maps, approach charts, taxi charts, restricted and dangerous airspaces
Map icons, list of radio nav aids, time for sunrise and sunset, airport fees, air traffic control fees
Warnings for aviation, ATS airspaces and routes, restricted and dangerous airspaces
Access restrictions for airfields, passenger controls, requirements for pilots, license samples and validity periods
q.e: The GEN (General) section of the AIP contains administrative and explanatory information, tables (like sunrise/sunset), symbols, fees, and general national regulations.

q.t: Which are the different parts of the Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP)?
q.e: The ICAO standard structure divides the AIP into three main parts: GENeral (GEN), EN-Route (ENR), and AeroDromes (AD).

q.t: What information is provided in the part "AD" of the AIP?
o: Warnings for aviation, ATS airspaces and routes, restricted and dangerous airspaces.
Table of content, classification of airfields with corresponding maps, approach charts, taxi charts
Map icons, list of radio nav aids, time for sunrise and sunset, airport fees, air traffic control fees
Access restrictions for airfields, passenger controls, requirements for pilots, license samples and validity periods
q.e: The AD (Aerodromes) section provides detailed information, operational hours, coordinates, and all necessary charts (approach, taxi, parking) for specific certified aerodromes.

q.t: The shown NOTAM is valid until... A1024/13 A) LOWW B) 1305211200 C) 1305211400 E) STOCKERAU VOR STO 113.00 UNSERVICEABLE.
q.e: Item C indicates the end of validity in the format YYMMDDHHMM. Therefore, 1305211400 means Year 2013, Month 05, Day 21 at 14:00 UTC.

q.t: A Pre-Flight Information Bulletin (PIB) is a presentation of current...
o: ICAO information of operational significance prepared after the flight.
AIP information of operational significance prepared prior to flight.
AIC information of operational significance prepared after the flight.
NOTAM information of operational significance prepared prior to flight.
q.e: A PIB is a summary of valid NOTAMs filtered specifically for the pilot's planned route, provided before the flight to ensure awareness of current operational hazards.

q.t: The term "aerodrome elevation" is defined as...
o: the highest point of the landing area.
the lowest point of the landing area.
the highest point of the apron.
the average value of the height of the manoeuvring area.
q.e: Aerodrome elevation is officially defined by ICAO as the elevation of the highest point of the landing area (runway system).

q.t: The term "runway" is defined as a...
o: round area on an aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.
rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.
rectangular area on a land or water aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.
rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of helicopters.
q.e: ICAO defines a runway as a defined rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the term "taxi holding point"?
o: A taxi holding point is an area where the aircraft must stop unless further permission to proceed is given
A taxi holding point is only to be observed for IFR traffic if instrument weather conditions are prevailing
A taxi holding point is the point at which the aircraft must stop unless further permission to proceed is given
A taxi holding point is designed to indicate the beginning of the safety area and may be crossed when a taxi clearance is given
q.e: A holding point is a specific line on the taxiway where an aircraft must hold and not proceed further towards the runway until ATC gives explicit clearance.

q.t: What does the reported runway condition "WET" mean?
o: The surface of the runway is soaked, but there are no significant patches of standing water
A large part of the surface is flooded
The runway is clear of water, ice, and snow
q.e: A "Wet" runway surface appears reflective and soaked, but the water depth is not significant enough to form large standing puddles or risk deep aquaplaning.

q.t: What does the reported runway condition "DAMP" mean?
o: Wet surface, but no significant puddles are visible
Change of colour on the surface due to moisture
The runway is clear of water, ice, and snow
A large part of the surface is flooded
q.e: Damp implies that the surface shows a change of color due to moisture but does not have a shiny appearance like a wet runway. Braking action is generally not severely affected.

q.t: What does "WATER PATCHES" mean regarding the reported runway condition?
o: A large part of the surface is flooded
Patches of standing water are visible
Wet surface, but no significant patches are visible
The runway is clear of water, ice, and snow
q.e: Water patches indicate localized areas of standing water (puddles) on the runway, which can cause localized aquaplaning and loss of braking action.

q.t: How can a wind direction indicator be marked for better visibility?
o: The wind direction indicator may be mounted on top of the control tower.
The wind direction indicator could be made from green materials.
The wind direction indicator could be surrounded by a white circle.
The wind direction indicator could be located on a big black surface.
q.e: To make the windsock easily visible from the air against the grass, it is typically located in the center of a wide white circle painted or laid on the ground.

q.t: What is the meaning of a flashing red light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft in flight?
o: Return for landing, followed by steady green at the appropriate time
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
q.e: A flashing red light directed at an aircraft in the air from the tower's light gun means "Aerodrome unsafe, do not land."

q.t: What is the meaning of a flashing green light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft in flight?
o: Return for landing, followed by steady green at the appropriate time
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
q.e: A flashing green light instructs an airborne aircraft to return to the aerodrome (enter the circuit) and await a steady green light, which will be the clearance to land.

q.t: What is the meaning of a steady green light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft in flight?
o: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Return for landing, followed by steady green at the appropriate time
q.e: A steady continuous green light aimed at an aircraft in flight is the absolute visual clearance to land on the runway.

q.t: What is the meaning of a flashing white light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft on ground?
q.e: A flashing white light instructs an aircraft taxiing on the ground to return to its starting point on the aerodrome (usually the apron).

q.t: What is the meaning of a flashing red light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft on ground?
o: Immediately taxi clear of runway in use
q.e: If a flashing red light is aimed at an aircraft on the ground, it warns of imminent danger and commands the pilot to immediately taxi clear of the landing area or runway in use.

q.t: What is the meaning of a flashing green light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft on ground?
o: Land at this airport and proceed to the apron
q.e: A flashing green light directed at an aircraft on the ground is the visual clearance to safely begin or continue taxiing.

q.t: Of what shape is a landing direction indicator?
q.e: A landing direction indicator is shaped like a large capital "T". Aircraft take off and land parallel to the shaft of the T, flying towards the crossbar.

q.t: What is the purpose of the signal square at an aerodrome?
o: It contains special symbols to indicate the conditions at the aerodrome visually to over-flying aircraft
It is an illuminated area on which search and rescue and fire fighting vehicles are placed
Aircraft taxi to this square to get light signals for taxi and take-off clearance
It is a specially marked area to pick up or drop towing objects
q.e: The signal square is a bordered area on the ground containing large visual symbols (like a cross or a dumbbell) to provide critical information to aircraft without radio communication.

q.t: In which way should a pilot confirm received light signals in flight?
o: Apply some changes of the rudder
q.e: To acknowledge light signals during daytime flight, the pilot should rock the wings (roll the aircraft alternately left and right) to show the tower they understood the message.

q.t: What is the meaning of a steady red light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft on ground?
o: Land at this airport and proceed to apron
q.e: A steady red light directed at an aircraft on the ground is a strict command to "Stop" immediately.

q.t: How are two parallel runways designated?
o: The left runway gets the suffix "L", the right runway "R"
The left runway gets the suffix "L", the right runway remains unchanged
The left runway gets the suffix "-1", the right runway "-2"
The left runway remains unchanged, the right runway designator is increased by 1
q.e: Parallel runways sharing the same magnetic heading are distinguished by adding "L" (Left) and "R" (Right) to their numerical designator (and "C" for Center if there are three).

q.t: According to ICAO Anex 14, which is the colour marking of a runway?
q.e: Runway markings (centerlines, thresholds, touchdown zones) are painted white to distinguish them from taxiway markings, which are yellow.

q.t: What is indicated by a pattern of longitudinal stripes of uniform dimensions disposed symmetrically about the centerline of a runway?
o: At this point the glide path of an ILS hits the runway
Do not touch down before them
Do not touch down behind them
A ground roll could be started from this position
q.e: These longitudinal stripes mark the threshold or a displaced threshold. Touching down before these markings is unsafe because the surface might not be structurally sound for landing impacts.

q.t: Which runway designators are correct for 2 parallel runways?
q.e: As explained earlier, parallel runways use the same magnetic heading number with "L" and "R" suffixes, making "06L" and "06R" the correct format.

q.t: What is a "PAPI" (Precision Approach Path Indicator)?
o: A visual aid that provides guidance information to help a tower controller acquire and maintain the correct approach to an aerodrome or an airport
A visual aid that provides guidance information to help a pilot acquire and maintain the correct glidepath to an aerodrome or an airport
An instrumental aid that provides guidance information to help a pilot acquire and maintain the correct approach to an aerodrome or an airport
A visual aid that provides guidance information to help a pilot acquire and maintain the correct departure track when departing from an aerodrome or an airport
q.e: PAPI consists of a row of light units that change color (red/white) depending on the viewing angle. It helps the pilot maintain the optimal 3-degree vertical descent path during approach.

q.t: An aerodrome beacon (ABN) is a...
o: rotating beacon installed at an airport or aerodrome to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the ground.
rotating beacon installed at the beginning of the final approach to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the air.
rotating beacon installed at an airport or aerodrome to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the air.
fixed beacon installed at an airport or aerodrome to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the air.
q.e: The Aerodrome Beacon (ABN) flashes bright light (often alternating colors like white and green) into the sky to help airborne pilots visually locate the airport from a distance at night.

q.t: Which is the colour of runway edge lights?
q.e: The edge lights defining the lateral limits of the usable runway surface emit a steady white light.

q.t: Which is the colour of runway end lights?
q.e: The lights marking the very end of the usable runway are red, warning pilots that the runway surface is ending.

q.t: What is shown on the printed sign? See figure
q.e: A yellow square sign with a black letter identifies a taxiway. It indicates that the aircraft is currently located on Taxiway A.

q.t: What is shown on the printed sign? See figure
o: 2500 m in the stated direction till reaching the parking area
From this intersection the available runway length is 2500 m in the stated direction
The complete length of the runway in the stated direction is 2500 m
2500 m in the stated direction till reaching the departure point of the runway
q.e: Intersection take-off signs (black numbers on yellow background) inform the pilot how much runway distance is available for the take-off run starting from that specific intersection.

q.t: What is the meaning of this sign at an aerodrome? See figure
o: Landing prohibited for a longer period
After take-off and before landing all turns have to be made to the right
q.e: A double white cross placed in the signal square alerts pilots that glider operations (towing or winch launching) are actively taking place at the aerodrome.

q.t: What is the meaning of the illustrated ground signal as shown in the signal area of an aerodrome? See figure
o: Prohibition on landing for a longer period
After take-off and before landing all turns have to be made to the right
Ground movement restricted to hard surfaces
q.e: A right-angled arrow pointing to the right in the signal square dictates that all traffic circuit turns must be flown to the right (right-hand pattern) instead of the standard left.

q.t: What is the meaning of "DETRESFA"?
q.e: DETRESFA is the standard emergency code word for the Distress phase. It implies that there is reasonable certainty that an aircraft and its occupants are in grave and imminent danger.

q.t: Who provides search and rescue service?
q.e: Search and Rescue (SAR) operations are a collaborative effort utilizing both civilian resources (like fire/police/civil air patrols) and military assets (radar, specialized helicopters).

q.t: How can a pilot confirm a search and rescue signal on ground in flight?
o: Push the rudder in both directions multiple times
Fly in a parabolic flight path multiple times
Deploy and retract the landing flaps multiple times
q.e: To visually acknowledge ground signals from SAR teams, the pilot of the aircraft should rock the wings from side to side.

q.t: With respect to aircraft accident and incident investigation, what are the three categories regarding aircraft occurrences?
o: Event, Serious event, Incident, Serious incident, Accident
q.e: Aviation safety regulations classify abnormal occurrences into three distinct levels of severity: Incidents, Serious incidents (where an accident nearly occurred), and Accidents.

q.t: What is the primary purpose of an aircraft accident investigation?
o: To Determine the guilty party and draw legal consequences
To clarify questions of liability within the meaning of compensation for passengers
To identify the reasons and work out safety recommendations
To work for the public prosecutor and help to follow-up flight accidents
q.e: The sole objective of international accident investigation bodies (like the NTSB or local equivalents) is to find the root causes to prevent future accidents, not to apportion blame or liability.

q.t: The majority of aviation accidents are caused by...
q.e: Statistical data shows that the vast majority (approximately 70-80%) of all aviation accidents and incidents are primarily caused by human error rather than technical failures.

q.t: The "swiss cheese model" can be used to explain the...
o: state of readiness of a pilot.
q.e: James Reason's "Swiss Cheese Model" illustrates how accidents happen when multiple layers of defense fail simultaneously, aligning the "holes" to create an error chain.

q.t: What is the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere at 6000 ft?
q.e: The composition of the atmosphere (approx. 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen) remains constant up to about 70,000 feet. Only the atmospheric pressure and density decrease with altitude.

q.t: What is the percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere?
q.e: Earth's atmosphere consists of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other trace gases like argon and carbon dioxide.

q.t: At which altitude is the atmospheric pressure approximately half the MSL value (1013 hPa)?
q.e: Atmospheric pressure decreases logarithmically. At mean sea level it is around 1013 hPa, and it drops to approximately half that value (around 500 hPa) at 18,000 ft.

q.t: Air consists of oxygen, nitrogen and other gases. What is the approximate percentage of other gases?
q.e: With Nitrogen at 78% and Oxygen at 21%, the remaining 1% is made up of other gases (mostly Argon and Carbon Dioxide).

q.t: Carbon monoxide poisoning can be caused by...
q.e: Smoking tobacco produces carbon monoxide (CO), which binds to hemoglobin much stronger than oxygen, creating a state of "blood hypoxia" even before taking off.

q.t: What does the term "Red-out" mean?
o: Falsified colour perception during sunrise and sunset
q.e: A "Red-out" occurs under negative G-forces (-Gz) when blood is forced into the head and eyes, causing the visual field to redden due to engorged blood vessels.

q.t: Carbon monoxide poisoning can be caused by...
q.e: In piston engine aircraft, cabin heat is often drawn from air passing over the exhaust manifold (heat exchanger). If this manifold cracks, deadly carbon monoxide from the exhaust enters the cabin.

q.t: Which of the following is NOT a symptom of hyperventilaton?
q.e: Cyanosis (blue discoloration of the skin) is a classic symptom of hypoxia (lack of oxygen). Hyperventilation is caused by exhaling too much CO2 due to rapid breathing.

q.t: Which of the following symptoms may indicate hypoxia?
o: Joint pain in knees and feet
Muscle cramps in the upper body area
Blue discolouration of lips and fingernails
Blue marks all over the body
q.e: Cyanosis, which presents as a blue or purplish discoloration of the lips and fingernail beds, is a late and reliable objective sign of severe oxygen deficiency in the blood.

q.t: Which of the human senses is most influenced by hypoxia?
q.e: The retina has a very high demand for oxygen. Therefore, vision (especially night vision and peripheral vision) is the first sense to degrade when experiencing hypoxia.

q.t: From which altitude on does the body usually react to the decreasing atmospheric pressure?
q.e: While significant hypoxic symptoms occur higher up, the human body begins subtle physiological compensations (like slightly increased heart rate) starting around 7,000 feet.

q.t: Which altitude marks the lower limit where the the body is unable to completely compensate the effects of the low atmospheric pressure?
q.e: Above 10,000 to 12,000 feet, the body's compensatory mechanisms (increased breathing and heart rate) are no longer sufficient to maintain adequate oxygenation without supplemental oxygen.

q.t: What is the function of the red blood cells (erythrocytes)?
q.e: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which binds to oxygen in the lungs and transports it to the tissues throughout the body.

q.t: Which of the following is responsible for the blood coagulation?
q.e: Blood platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments responsible for forming clots to stop bleeding (coagulation).

q.t: What is the function of the white blood cells (leucocytes)?
q.e: White blood cells (leukocytes) are the primary component of the immune system, defending the body against infectious diseases and foreign invaders.

q.t: What is the function of the blood platelets (thrombocytes)?
q.e: As stated previously, the primary physiological function of blood platelets is blood coagulation (clotting) to prevent excessive bleeding.

q.t: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for hypoxia?
q.e: Diving prior to flight increases the risk of Decompression Sickness (DCS) due to dissolved nitrogen, but it does not directly reduce the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood like smoking or blood loss do.

q.t: Anemic hypoxia can be caused by...
q.e: Anemic hypoxia occurs when the blood's capacity to carry oxygen is impaired. Carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin 200 times stronger than oxygen, directly causing anemic hypoxia.

q.t: What is an appropriate reaction when a passenger during cruise flight suddenly feels uncomfortable?
o: Adjust cabin temperature and prevent excessive bank
Give additional oxygen and avoid low load factors
Avoid conversation and choose a higher airspeed
Switch on the heater blower and provide thermal blankets
q.e: If a passenger feels airsick (motion sickness), the best immediate action is to provide fresh cool air (adjust temperature), keep them visually focused outside, and fly as smoothly as possible without steep banks.

q.t: What ist the correct term for an involuntary and stereotypical reaction of an organism to the stimulation of a receptor?
q.e: A reflex is an automatic, involuntary physiological response to a stimulus (e.g., blinking when an object approaches the eye).

q.t: What is the correct term for the system which, among others, controls breathing, digestion, and heart frequency?
q.e: The autonomic nervous system controls vital, involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate, digestion, and respiratory rate without conscious effort.

q.t: What is the parallax error?
o: Long-sightedness due to aging especially during night
Wrong interpretation of instruments caused by the angle of vision
A decoding error in communication between pilots
q.e: Parallax error occurs when a pilot reads an analog dial instrument from an angle rather than straight on, causing the needle to appear to point at the wrong value.

q.t: Which characteristic is important when choosing sunglasses used by pilots?
q.e: Pilots must use non-polarised sunglasses because polarized lenses can mask the glare from other aircraft (traffic) and completely black out digital LCD screens in the cockpit.

q.t: Which part of the visual system is responsible for colour vision?
q.e: The cones in the retina are responsible for high-resolution central vision and color perception, functioning best in bright light conditions.

q.t: The connection between middle ear and nose and throat region is called...
q.e: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the nasopharynx, allowing the equalization of air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

q.t: In which situation is it NOT possible to achieve a pressure compensation between the middle ear and the environment?
o: During a light and slow climb
Breathing takes place using the mouth only
q.e: If a pilot flies with a cold or sinus infection, the Eustachian tube becomes swollen and blocked. This traps air in the middle ear, making pressure equalization impossible and causing severe pain.

q.t: Wings level after a longer period of turning can lead to the impression of...
o: steady turning in the same direction as before.
q.e: Due to the inertia of the fluid in the semicircular canals of the inner ear, rolling out into straight flight after a prolonged turn creates a false sensation (illusion) of turning in the opposite direction.

q.t: Which of the following options does NOT stimulate motion sickness (disorientation)?
o: Flying under the influence of alcohol
q.e: Steady, non-accelerated straight and level flight provides stable sensory inputs and does not induce motion sickness or spatial disorientation.

q.t: An acceleration during a straight horizontal flight can lead to the illusion of...
q.e: This is the somatogravic illusion. Rapid forward acceleration pushes the otolith organs backwards, which the brain misinterprets as a pitch-up (climb) attitude, often prompting the pilot to push the nose down dangerously.

q.t: A deceleration during a straight horizontal flight can lead to the illusion of...
q.e: The opposite of the acceleration illusion: sudden deceleration forces the sensory organs forward, tricking the brain into feeling a pitch-down (descent) attitude.

q.t: Which optical illusion might be caused by a runway with an upslope during the approach?
o: The pilot has the feeling that the approach is too fast and reduces the speed below the normal approach speed
The pilot has the feeling that the approach is too high and therefore descents below the regular glide slope
The pilot has the feeling that the approach is too slow and speeds up above the normal approach speed
The pilot has the feeling that the approach is too low and therefore approaches the runway above the regular glide slope
q.e: An upsloping runway creates a visual perspective that makes the pilot feel they are higher than they actually are. In response, they might pitch down and fly below the safe glide path.

q.t: What impression may be caused when approaching a runway with an upslope?
q.e: Note: According to the provided document key, "overshoot" is marked. However, aeromedical theory states an upslope creates the illusion of being too high, typically resulting in a lower approach and a potential undershoot. (The answer follows the exact marking of the source document).

q.t: The occurence of a vertigo is most likely when moving the head...
q.e: Coriolis illusion (severe vertigo) occurs if the pilot makes a sudden head movement in a different geometric plane while the aircraft is in a prolonged coordinated turn.

q.t: A Grey-out is the result of...
q.e: Under positive G-loads (+Gz), blood is forced down toward the legs, reducing oxygen flow to the eyes. This leads to a loss of peripheral vision and color fading, known as a grey-out.

q.t: Visual illusions are mostly caused by...
q.e: The eyes function correctly by sending the visual image to the brain, but illusions occur when the brain misinterprets these visual cues due to lack of references or misleading perspectives.

q.t: The average decrease of blood alcohol level for an adult in one hour is approximately...
q.e: The human body typically metabolizes alcohol at an average rate of about 0.015% BAC per hour (often rounded to 0.01% or 15 mg/100ml in aviation exams).

q.t: Which answer states a risk factor for diabetes?
q.e: Being overweight (obesity) and leading a sedentary lifestyle are the primary risk factors for the development of Type 2 diabetes.

q.t: A risk factor for decompression sickness is...
q.e: Scuba diving forces nitrogen to dissolve into the blood under high pressure. If the person flies shortly after, the lower cabin pressure allows the nitrogen to form dangerous bubbles in the bloodstream (DCS).

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the short-term memory?
o: It can store 10 (±5) items for 30 to 60 seconds
It can store 7 (±2) items for 10 to 20 seconds
It can store 3 (±1) items for 5 to 10 seconds
It can store 5 (±2) items for 1 to 2 minutes
q.e: According to psychological principles (Miller's Law), the working (short-term) memory has a limited capacity of approximately 7 ± 2 chunks of information for about 10 to 20 seconds.

q.t: For what approximate time period can the short-time memory store information?
q.e: If information (like an ATC frequency) is not rehearsed or written down, it will decay and disappear from short-term memory within 10 to 20 seconds.

q.t: What is a latent error?
o: An error which is made by the pilot actively and consciously
An error which only has consequences after landing
An error which remains undetected in the system for a long time
An error which has an immediate effect on the controls
q.e: A latent error is a hidden flaw built into the system (e.g., poor maintenance procedures, confusing manuals) that lies dormant until a specific trigger aligns to cause an accident.

q.t: What does the term "confirmation bias" mean?
o: The feedback loop in a closed communication
The preference to find arguments to proof the own mental model
The bias to confirm each radio call
The critical check of ambiguous situations in flight
q.e: Confirmation bias is the psychological tendency to search for, interpret, and favor information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs or expectations, while ignoring contradictory evidence.

q.t: The ongoing process to monitor the current flight situation is called...
q.e: Situational Awareness (SA) is the continuous perception of the elements in the environment, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their status in the near future.

q.t: Regarding the communication model, how can the use of the same code during radio communication be ensured?
o: By the use of radio phraseology
By using radios certified for aviation use only
By the use of proper headsets
q.e: Using standard ICAO radio phraseology ensures that both the sender and receiver use the same linguistic "code," thereby preventing misunderstandings and ambiguity.

q.t: In what different ways can a risk be handled appropriately?
q.e: The four standard risk management strategies are: Avoid the risk (don't fly), Reduce/Mitigate the risk (take more fuel), Transfer the risk, or Accept the residual risk.

q.t: Under which circumstances is it more likely to accept higher risks?
o: If there is not enough information available
During check flights due to a high level of nervousness
During flight planning when excellent weather is forecast
q.e: Risky shift is a psychological phenomenon where individuals in a group are more likely to make riskier decisions or accept higher risks than they would if they were acting alone.

q.t: What is the meaning of "risky shift"?
o: Crossing of rudder and ailerons on short final
The tendency to accept higher risks in groups
Spontaneous change of landing direction when the runway has an upslope
q.e: As previously mentioned, risky shift describes the tendency for group decisions (or peer pressure) to be riskier than the decisions made by the individuals independently.

q.t: Which dangerous attitudes are often combined?
q.e: Pilots often exhibit a deadly combination of a "Macho" attitude (trying to prove themselves) and "Invulnerability" (the false belief that accidents only happen to other people).

q.t: What is an indication for a macho attitude?
o: Comprehensive risk assessment when faced with unfamiliar situations
Risky flight maneuvers to impress spectators on ground
Quick resignation in complex and critical situations
q.e: A macho attitude is characterized by taking unnecessary risks, showing off, and performing dangerous maneuvers solely to impress others.

q.t: Which factor can lead to human error?
o: To be doubtful if something looks unclear or ambiguous
The bias to see what we expect to see
q.e: Expectation bias leads pilots to see or hear what they anticipate rather than what is actually happening (e.g., reading an altimeter as the cleared altitude rather than the actual altitude).

q.t: What is the best combination of traits with respect to the individual attitude and behaviour for a pilot?
q.e: In terms of Crew Resource Management (CRM), the ideal pilot profile is extroverted (communicates openly and asserts themselves) and stable (remains calm and composed under stress).

q.t: Complacency is a risk due to...
o: the high number of mistakes normally made by humans.
the high error rate of technical systems.
better training options for young pilots.
q.e: When highly reliable automated systems fly the aircraft flawlessly for long periods, pilots can become bored and detached, leading to complacency and a dangerous lack of situational awareness.

q.t: The ideal level of arousal is at which point in the diagram?
q.e: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, optimal performance is achieved at a medium (optimal) level of stress or arousal, which corresponds to the peak of the curve (Point C).

q.t: At which point in the diagram will a pilot find himself to be overstrained?
q.e: At the far right of the curve (Point D), the level of stress or arousal is excessively high. The pilot becomes overstrained, panicked, and performance drops dramatically.

q.t: Which of the following qualities are influenced by stress? 1. Attention 2. Concentration 3. Responsiveness 4. Memory
q.e: High levels of acute stress globally and negatively impair all cognitive functions, including attention, concentration, reaction time (responsiveness), and memory recall.

q.t: Which answer is correct concerning stress?
o: Stress can occur if there seems to be no solution for a given problem
Training and experience have no influence on the occurence of stress
Stress and its different symptoms are irrelevant for flight safety
Everybody reacts to stress in the same manner
q.e: Stress is a biological and psychological response that is strongly triggered when an individual faces a high-demand situation and perceives that they lack the resources or solutions to cope with it.

q.t: What clouds and weather may result from an humid and instable air mass, that is pushed against a chain of mountains by the predominant wind and forced to rise?
o: Thin Altostratus and Cirrostratus clouds with light and steady precipitation.
Overcast low stratus (high fog) with no precipitation.
Smooth, unstructured NS cloud with light drizzle or snow (during winter).
Embedded CB with thunderstorms and showers of hail and/or rain.
q.e: Orographic lifting of unstable, humid air causes rapid vertical cloud development, typically leading to Cumulonimbus (CB) clouds with thunderstorms and showers.

q.t: What type of fog emerges if humid and almost saturated air, is forced to rise upslope of hills or shallow mountains by the prevailling wind?
q.e: Orographic fog (or hill fog) is created when moist air is blown up a slope, cooling adiabatically until it reaches its dew point and condenses.

q.t: What situation is called "over-development" in a weather report?
o: Widespreading of Cumulus clouds below an inversion layer
Vertical development of Cumulus clouds to rain showers
Change from blue thermals to cloudy thermals during the afternoon
Development of a thermal low to a storm depression
q.e: The term "over-development" describes when normally fair-weather Cumulus clouds continue to grow vertically into Cumulus congestus or Cumulonimbus, eventually producing rain showers.

q.t: What is the gas composition of "air"?
o: Oxygen 21%, Water vapour 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
Nitrogen 78%, Oxygen 21%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
Nitrogen 21%, Oxygen 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
q.e: The Earth's atmosphere is composed primarily of Nitrogen (approx. 78%) and Oxygen (approx. 21%), with the remaining 1% consisting of Argon, Carbon Dioxide, and other trace gases.

q.t: Weather phenomena are most common to be found in which atmospheric layer?
q.e: The troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere and contains about 99% of its water vapor, making it the layer where almost all weather phenomena occur.

q.t: What is the mass of a "cube of air" with the edges 1 m long, at MSL according ISA?
q.e: According to the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), the standard density of air at mean sea level is defined as 1.225 kg/m³.

q.t: At what rate does the temperature change with increasing height according to ISA (ICAO Standard Atmosphere) within the troposphere?
q.e: The standard ISA temperature lapse rate in the troposphere is a decrease of 1.98° C (commonly rounded to 2° C) per 1000 feet of altitude.

q.t: What is the mean height of the tropopause according to ISA (ICAO Standard Atmosphere)?
q.e: The standard height of the tropopause in the ISA model is exactly 11,000 meters (which is approximately 36,089 feet).

q.t: The term "tropopause" is defined as...
o: the layer above the troposphere showing an increasing temperature.
the boundary area between the mesosphere and the stratosphere.
the height above which the temperature starts to decrease.
the boundary area between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
q.e: The tropopause is the atmospheric boundary that separates the troposphere (where weather occurs and temperature decreases with altitude) from the stratosphere.

q.t: Temperatures will be given by meteorological aviation services in Europe in which unit?
q.e: In European aviation meteorology (like METARs and TAFs), temperatures and dew points are uniformly reported in Degrees Centigrade (Celsius).

q.t: What is meant by "inversion layer"?
o: An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases with increasing height
A boundary area between two other layers within the atmosphere
An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with increasing height
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with increasing height
q.e: An inversion is a deviation from the normal atmospheric lapse rate, occurring when temperature abnormally increases with an increase in altitude.

q.t: What is meant by "isothermal layer"?
o: An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with increasing height
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with increasing height
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases with increasing height
A boundary area between two other layers within the atmosphere
q.e: Iso means equal and "thermal" means temperature. Thus, an isothermal layer is one where the temperature remains constant regardless of altitude changes.

q.t: The temperature lapse rate with increasing height within the troposphere according ISA is...
q.e: While it is roughly 2°C per 1000 ft in imperial units, the exact metric ISA lapse rate is defined as a decrease of 0.65°C per 100 meters.

q.t: Which process may result in an inversion layer at about 5000 ft (1500 m) height?
o: Intensive sunlight insolation during a warm summer day
Ground cooling by radiation during the night
Widespread descending air within a high pressure area
Advection of cool air in the upper troposphere
q.e: Widespread descending air in an anticyclone undergoes adiabatic compression, which warms the sinking air and often forms a "subsidence inversion" aloft (e.g., around 5000 ft).

q.t: An inversion layer close to the ground can be caused by...
o: thickening of clouds in medium layers.
q.e: During clear, calm nights, the Earth's surface rapidly loses heat through radiation. This cools the air immediately in contact with the ground, creating a radiation inversion.

q.t: What is the ISA standard pressure at FL 180 (5500 m)?
q.e: Atmospheric pressure decreases logarithmically with altitude. At 18,000 feet (approx. 5.5 km), the pressure is roughly half of the sea-level value, which is about 500 hPa.

q.t: The pressure which is measured at a ground station and reduced to mean sea level (MSL) by means of the actual atmospheric conditions is called...
q.e: QFF is the station pressure reduced to mean sea level using the actual temperature and atmospheric conditions, whereas QNH uses the standard ISA temperature lapse rate.

q.t: Which processes result in decreasing air density?
q.e: Air density decreases when air expands. This expansion occurs either when the air is heated (increasing temperature) or when the confining pressure is reduced (decreasing pressure).

q.t: The pressure at MSL in ISA conditions is...
q.e: The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) defines the standard mean sea level (MSL) pressure as exactly 1013.25 hectopascals (hPa).

q.t: The height of the tropopause of the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is at...
q.e: As previously noted in meters, the standard ISA tropopause height is set at 11,000 meters, which translates to approximately 36,000 feet.

q.t: The barometric altimeter indicates height above...
q.e: A barometric altimeter is essentially an aneroid barometer calibrated to display altitude. It indicates the vertical distance above whichever reference pressure level the pilot dials into the subscale.

q.t: The altimeter can be checked on the ground by setting...
o: QFE and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QNE and checking that the indication shows zero on the ground.
QNH and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QFF and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
q.e: Setting the local QNH on the altimeter subscale should result in the instrument displaying the airfield's actual elevation above mean sea level.

q.t: The barometric altimeter with QFE setting indicates...
o: height above the pressure level at airfield elevation.
q.e: QFE is the actual pressure measured at the airfield elevation. When set on the altimeter, the instrument reads zero on the runway and displays height above that specific airfield level while airborne.

q.t: The barometric altimeter with QNH setting indicates...
o: height above the pressure level at airfield elevation.
q.e: QNH is the altimeter setting that causes the instrument to read the aircraft's altitude above Mean Sea Level (MSL) based on the standard ISA atmosphere model.

q.t: Given the following information, what is the true altitude? (rounded to the nearest 50 ft) QNH: 983 hPa, Altitude: FL 85, Outside Air Temperature: ISA - 10°
q.e: Pressure difference is 30 hPa (1013-983), causing a 900 ft drop (8500-900=7600 ft). Cold air (ISA-10) shrinks the air column, causing an additional 4% true altitude loss. 4% of 7600 is approx 300 ft. 7600 - 300 = 7300 ft.

q.t: How can wind speed and wind direction be derived from surface weather charts?
o: By alignment and distance of hypsometric lines
By alignment of lines of warm- and cold fronts.
By alignment and distance of isobaric lines
By annotations from the text part of the chart
q.e: Isobars connect points of equal pressure. Wind blows roughly parallel to isobars (direction), and the closeness of the isobars (pressure gradient) determines the wind speed.

q.t: Which force causes "wind"?
q.e: Wind is physically driven by the atmosphere's attempt to equalize differences in pressure between two locations. This driving force is the pressure gradient force.

q.t: Above the friction layer, with a prevailing pressure gradient, the wind direction is...
o: at an angle of 30° to the isobars towards low pressure.
q.e: In the free atmosphere above surface friction, the Coriolis force balances the pressure gradient force perfectly, resulting in geostrophic wind that flows parallel to the isobars.

q.t: Which of the stated surfaces will reduce the wind speed most due to ground friction?
o: Flat land, deserted land, no vegetation
Flat land, lots of vegetation cover
q.e: Friction slows down wind near the surface. The "rougher" the surface, the higher the friction. Mountainous terrain with forests presents the greatest aerodynamic obstacle.

q.t: The movement of air flowing together is called...
q.e: Convergence is the meteorological term for the condition where air masses horizontally flow together into a region, accumulating mass and forcing air to rise.

q.t: The movement of air flowing apart is called...
q.e: Divergence is the outward horizontal flow of air from a central region. At the surface, this causes air to spread out, allowing air from above to sink (subsidence).

q.t: What weather development will result from convergence at ground level?
q.e: When air converges at the surface, it has nowhere to go but up. As it ascends, it cools adiabatically, which leads to condensation and the formation of clouds.

q.t: When air masses meet each other head on, how is this referred to and what air movements will follow?
o: Convergence resulting in air being lifted
Divergence resulting in air being lifted
q.e: A head-on collision of air masses is convergence. Because the air cannot go into the ground, it is forced upward, resulting in lifting air.

q.t: What are the air masses that Central Europe is mainly influenced by?
o: Polar cold air and tropical warm air
q.e: The weather in Central Europe is predominantly shaped by the battle at the Polar Front, where cold polar air from the north meets warm tropical (subtropical) air from the south.

q.t: With regard to global circulation within the atmosphere, where does polar cold air meets subtropical warm air?
o: At the subtropical high pressure belt
q.e: The Polar Front is the semi-permanent, planetary boundary located around 50°-60° latitude where the cold polar cell and the warmer mid-latitude Ferrel cell (subtropical air) clash.

q.t: Winds blowing uphill are defined as...
q.e: An anabatic wind is a warm wind that blows up a steep incline or mountain side, driven by solar heating of the slope.

q.t: Winds blowing downhill are defined as...
q.e: A katabatic wind is a downslope wind caused by the cooling of air on higher elevations. The cold, dense air flows downhill due to gravity.

q.t: Air descending behind a mountain range is defined as...
q.e: Air that falls down the lee side of a mountain range (such as in Foehn conditions or a cold drop) is kinetically descending, falling under the classification of a katabatic (downward) wind.

q.t: Foehn conditions usually develop with...
o: instability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
instability, high pressure area with calm wind.
stability, high pressure area with calm wind.
stability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
q.e: A classic Foehn wind requires a stable, wide-scale air mass to be forcibly pushed (by a strong pressure gradient) horizontally against and over a mountain barrier.

q.t: What type of turbulence is typically found close to the ground on the lee side during Foehn conditions?
q.e: As the air spills down the lee side of a mountain range like a waterfall, it interacts with the ground to form violent, tumbling, horizontal vortices known as rotors.

q.t: Light turbulence always has to be expected...
o: above cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
below stratiform clouds in medium layers.
below cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
q.e: Cumulus clouds are visible markers of thermal updrafts rising from the heated ground. Flying below their bases means passing through these alternating rising and sinking thermal currents.

q.t: Moderate to severe turbulence has to be expected...
o: with the appearance of extended low stratus clouds (high fog).
below thick cloud layers on the windward side of a mountain range.
on the lee side of a mountain range when rotor clouds are present.
q.e: Rotor clouds indicate the presence of severe mountain wave turbulence and intense, rolling downdrafts on the lee (downwind) side of mountains.

q.t: Which answer contains every state of water found in the atmosphere?
q.e: Water is unique in that it naturally exists in all three states in the atmosphere: vapor (gas), water droplets (liquid), and ice crystals/snow (solid).

q.t: How do dew point and relative humidity change with decreasing temperature?
o: Dew point remains constant, relative humidity decreases
Dew point decreases, relative humidity increases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity increases
Dew point increases, relative humidity decreases
q.e: If the absolute moisture remains the same (constant dew point), cooling the air brings its temperature closer to the dew point, which mathematically increases the relative humidity toward 100%.

q.t: How do spread and relative humidity change with increasing temperature?
o: Spread remains constant, relative humidity decreases
Spread remains constant, relative humidity increases
q.e: As air warms, its capacity to hold moisture increases, meaning the dew point stays low while temperature rises (spread increases). Consequently, the percentage of saturation (relative humidity) drops.

q.t: The "spread" is defined as...
o: relation of actual to maximum possible humidity of air.
maximum amount of water vapour that can be contained in air.
difference between actual temperature and dew point.
difference between dew point and condensation point.
q.e: The temperature-dewpoint spread is simply the numerical difference between the actual air temperature and the current dew point temperature.

q.t: With other factors remaining constant, decreasing temperature results in...
o: decreasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
decreasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
q.e: Cooling the air pushes its temperature down towards the dew point, shrinking the gap (decreasing spread) and increasing its percentage of moisture saturation (increasing relative humidity).

q.t: What process causes latent heat being released into the upper troposphere?
q.e: Latent (hidden) heat absorbed during evaporation at the surface is released back into the atmosphere when the water vapor turns back into liquid drops (condensation) to form clouds.

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate is...
o: proportional to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
higher than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
lower than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
equal to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
q.e: When a saturated parcel rises and condenses, it releases latent heat. This extra heat offsets the cooling process, making the saturated lapse rate slower (lower) than the dry lapse rate.

q.t: The dry adiabatic lapse rate has a value of...
q.e: A rising parcel of dry (unsaturated) air expands and cools mechanically at a strict physical constant rate of exactly 1.0° C for every 100 meters it climbs.

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate should be assumed with a mean value of:
q.e: Because the release of latent heat slows the cooling of the rising air, the saturated adiabatic lapse rate averages around 0.6° C per 100 meters, which is less than the dry rate.

q.t: What weather conditions may be expected during conditionally unstable conditions?
o: Layered clouds up to high levels, prolonged rain or snow
Shallow cumulus clouds with base at medium levels
Sky clear of clouds, sunshine, low winds
Towering cumulus, isolated showers of rain or thunderstorms
q.e: Conditional instability means the air is stable when dry, but if forced up until it saturates, it becomes violently unstable, triggering towering convective clouds (Cumulonimbus) and thunderstorms.

q.t: Which conditions are likely for the formation of advection fog?
o: Cold, humid air moves over a warm ocean
Warm, humid air cools during a cloudy night
Humidity evaporates from warm, humid ground into cold air
Warm, humid air moves over a cold surface
q.e: Advection fog is caused by the horizontal movement (advection) of a warm, moist air mass over a cold surface (like a cold ocean current or frozen land), cooling the air from below to its dew point.

q.t: Clouds are basically distinguished by what types?
q.e: Aviation cloud classification primarily divides clouds into two morphological categories: Cumuliform (heap-like, convective) and Stratiform (layered, flat).

q.t: Clouds in high layers are referred to as...
q.e: The prefix "Cirro-" designates high-level clouds (e.g., Cirrus, Cirrostratus) that form near the tropopause and consist entirely of ice crystals.

q.t: What weather phenomenon designated by "2" has to be expected on the lee side during "Foehn" conditions?
q.e: The graphic typically represents a mountain wave. Standing stationary on the wave crests downwind of the mountain are the lens-shaped rotor-associated clouds known as Altocumulus lenticularis.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show? (MET-002 shows Cumulus)
q.e: The image displays detached, fluffy, cauliflower-shaped clouds with flat bases and vertical growth, which are the textbook visual definition of Cumulus clouds.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show? (MET-004 shows Cirrus)
q.e: The picture features thin, wispy, hair-like streaks of white clouds high in the sky, completely transparent to sunlight, which is the defining characteristic of Cirrus clouds.

q.t: What factor may affect the top of cumulus clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
q.e: A Cumulus cloud grows vertically as long as its rising air is warmer than the environment. An inversion layer acts as a warm "lid" that stops the thermal updraft, halting the cloud's vertical growth.

q.t: What factors may indicate a tendency to fog formation?
q.e: Fog requires high moisture (indicated by a low temperature-dewpoint spread) and a cooling mechanism (decreasing temperature) to push the air past saturation into condensation.

q.t: What condition may prevent the formation of "radiation fog"?
q.e: A thick layer of clouds acts like a thermal blanket, radiating Earth's heat back down. This prevents the surface from cooling rapidly at night, thereby stopping the formation of radiation fog.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "advection fog"?
o: Cold, moist air is being moved across warm ground areas
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Warm, moist air is moved across cold ground areas
q.e: Advection fog forms when wind horizontally pushes a warm, humid air mass over a significantly colder surface, chilling the air from below until it condenses.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "orographic fog" ("hill fog")?
o: Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
Evaporation from warm, moist ground area into very cold air
Warm, moist air is moved across a hill or a mountain range
q.e: Orographic fog forms mechanically when wind forces humid air up the slope of a mountain. As it rises, it expands and cools adiabatically until fog forms on the hillside.

q.t: What factors are required for the formation of precipitation in clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
Calm winds and intensive sunlight insolation
q.e: Raindrops start microscopically small. To grow large enough to fall, they must be held aloft inside the cloud by moderate to strong updrafts so they can collide and merge with other droplets (coalescence).

q.t: The formation of medium to large precipitation particles requires...
q.e: As reinforced in the previous question, large hail and big raindrops require violent, sustained vertical updrafts to keep them suspended in the storm while they accumulate freezing water layers.

q.t: Which type of cloud is associated with prolonged rain?
q.e: Nimbo means rain, and "stratus" means layer. Nimbostratus is a thick, dark, featureless cloud layer that produces steady, continuous, and prolonged precipitation, usually ahead of a warm front.

q.t: Regarding the type of cloud, precipitation is classified as...
q.e: Meteorology distinguishes precipitation based on its source cloud: continuous/intermittent "rain" falls from layered stratiform clouds, while sudden, heavy "showers" fall from convective cumuliform clouds.

q.t: How is an air mass described when moving to Central Europe via the Russian continent during winter?
q.e: Originating far north in Russia makes it "polar" (freezing cold), and traveling over landmasses rather than oceans makes it "continental" (very dry). Thus, it brings dry, bitter cold.

q.t: The character of an air mass is given by what properties?
o: Temperatures at origin and present region
Region of origin and track during movement
q.e: An air mass takes on the temperature and humidity traits of the surface where it stalled (Region of origin), and is further modified by the surfaces it travels over (Track during movement).

q.t: The symbol labeled (1) as shown in the picture is a / an...
q.e: On synoptic charts, a blue line with sharp, pointed triangles (barbs) pointing in the direction of movement represents a cold front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (2) as shown in the picture is a / an...
q.e: A red line with solid half-circles pointing in the direction of movement indicates the advancing edge of a warm air mass, known as a warm front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (3) as shown in the picture is a / an...
q.e: A purple or magenta line with alternating blue triangles and red half-circles indicates an occluded front, formed when a faster cold front overtakes a slower warm front.

q.t: What cloud sequence can typically be observed during the passage of a warm front?
o: In coastal areas during daytime wind from the coast and forming of cumulus clouds, dissipation of clouds during evening and night
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds and warming during summer; formation of extended high fog layers during winter
Squall line with showers of rain and thunderstorms (Cb), gusting wind followed by cumulus clouds with isolated showers of rain
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus clouds, lowering cloud base with rain, nimbostratus
q.e: A warm front approaches slowly on a shallow slope. It is heralded days in advance by high Cirrus, followed by a thickening and lowering overcast layer (Altostratus), culminating in rain-bearing Nimbostratus.

q.t: What clouds and weather can typically be observed during the passage of a cold front?
o: In coastal areas during daytime wind from the coast and forming of cumulus clouds, dissipation of clouds during evening and night
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus clouds, lowering cloud base with rain, nimbostratus
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds and warming during summer; formation of extended high fog layers during winter
Strongly developed cumulus clouds (Cb) with showers of rain and thunderstorms, gusting wind followed by cumulus clouds with isolated showers of rain
q.e: A cold front acts like a wedge, violently forcing warm air upwards. This rapid lift triggers severe convective weather, featuring towering Cumulonimbus (Cb), gust fronts, and heavy showers.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected within the warm sector of a polar front low during summer time?
o: Visibilty less than 1000 m, cloud-covered ground
Good visibility, some isolated high clouds
Moderate visibility, heavy showers and thunderstorms
Moderate to good visibility, scattered clouds
q.e: The warm sector sits between the warm front and the cold front. In summer, it typically provides a warm, relatively stable air mass with fair visibility and scattered, fair-weather cumulus clouds.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected after the passage of a cold front?
o: Scattered cloud layers, visbility more than 5 km, formation of shallow cumulus clouds
Medium visibility with lowering cloud bases, onset of prolonged precipitation
Poor visibility, formation of overcast or ground-covering stratus clouds, snow
Good visiblity, formation of cumulus clouds with showers of rain or snow
q.e: After the violent squalls of a cold front pass, the heavy rain washes the atmosphere clean. The trailing cold polar air provides excellent visibility, punctuated by unstable showery cumulus clouds.

q.t: A boundary between a cold polar air mass and a warm subtropical air mass showing no horizontal displacement is called...
q.e: When two opposing air masses push against each other with equal force, neither makes significant forward progress. The front stalls and is depicted on maps as a stationary front.
