q.t: What is the usual direction of movement of a polar front low?
o: To the northwest during winter, to the southwest during summer
To the northeast during winter, to the southeast during summer
Parallel to the warm front line to the south
Parallel to the the warm-sector isobars
q.e: Meteorological steering mechanisms usually dictate that a depression (low-pressure system) tracks roughly parallel to the isobars found within its own warm sector, driven by the upper-level winds.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed during the passage of a polar front low?
o: Rising pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, rising pressure behind the cold front
Falling pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, falling pressure behind the cold front
Rising pressure in front of the warm front, rising pressure within the warm sector, falling pressure behind the cold front
Falling pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, rising pressure behind the cold front
q.e: As the low approaches, pressure falls (warm front). Inside the warm sector, pressure levels off and remains constant. When the cold front hits, dragging in dense cold air, the pressure rises sharply.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed when a cold front is passing?
q.e: Directly on the boundary of the cold front is a pressure trough. The pressure reaches a brief minimum (decreasing shortly) and then climbs vigorously (increasing) as the heavy cold air mass floods in.

q.t: What change of wind direction can be expected during the passage of a polar front low in Central Europe?
o: Backing wind during passage of the warm front, veering wind during passage of the cold front
Backing wind during passage of the warm front, backing wind during passage of the cold front
Veering wind during passage of the warm front, backing wind during passage of the cold front
Veering wind during passage of the warm front, veering wind during passage of the cold front
q.e: In the Northern Hemisphere, passing fronts shift the wind clockwise (veering). The wind veers from SE to SW when the warm front passes, and veers again sharply from SW to NW with the cold front.

q.t: Extensive high pressure areas can be found throughout the year ...
o: in areeas showing extensive lifting processes.
in mid latitudes along the polar front
in tropical areas, close to the equator.
over oceanic areas at latitues around 30°N/S.
q.e: Due to global atmospheric circulation (Hadley cells), air that rose at the equator cools and sinks steadily around the 30° latitude belts, creating semi-permanent, extensive high-pressure anticyclones (like the Azores High).

q.t: What cloud type can typically be observed across widespread high pressure areas during summer?
q.e: High pressure guarantees descending air (subsidence), which suppresses deep cloud development. The bright summer sun simply creates shallow, harmless, scattered Cumulus (Cu) clouds near the surface.

q.t: What pressure pattern may result from cold-air inflow in high tropospheric layers?
o: Formation of a high in the upper troposphere
Formation of a large ground low
Formation of a low in the upper troposphere
q.e: Cold air is denser and more compact. When cold air pools in the upper atmosphere, it occupies less vertical volume, effectively lowering the pressure levels aloft and forming an upper-level low (cold drop).

q.t: Cold air inflow in high tropospheric layers may result in...
q.e: A pool of cold air aloft over a warm summer surface creates an extremely steep, unstable temperature lapse rate. This violent instability triggers massive non-frontal convective showers and thunderstorms.

q.t: How does inflowing cold air affect the shape and vertical distance between pressure layers?
o: Increasing vertical distance, raise in height (high pressure)
Decreasing vertical distance, raise in height (high pressure)
Increase in vertical distance, lowering in height (low pressure)
Decrease in vertical distance, lowering in height (low pressure)
q.e: Cold air physically shrinks and compresses. Therefore, the physical distance between specific pressure layers decreases, and their absolute altitude lowers, creating a low-pressure trough aloft.

q.t: What weather phenomena have to be expected around an upper-level trough?
o: Calm wind, forming of shallow cumulus clouds
Calm weather, formation of lifted fog layers
Formation of high stratus clouds, ground-covering cloud bases
q.e: An upper-level trough brings cold air aloft, steepening the atmospheric lapse rate. This instability acts as an engine for vigorous updrafts, leading to the development of Cumulonimbus (Cb) clouds and thunderstorms.

q.t: What frontal line divides subtropical air from polar cold air, in particular across Central Europe?
q.e: The Polar Front is the permanent, planetary-scale boundary zone separating the freezing polar air masses to the north from the warm, subtropical air masses to the south.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Changing weather with passing of frontal lines
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
q.e: In summer, the subsidence (sinking air) of an anticyclone suppresses rain and storms. The sun easily burns off moisture, leaving long periods of calm, blue skies with just a few fair-weather Cumulus clouds.

q.t: What weather conditions in Central Europe are typically found in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Large isobar spacing with strong prevailing westerly winds
Small isobar spacing with calm winds, formation of local wind systems
Small isobar spacing with strong prevailing northerly winds
Large isobar spacing with calm winds, formation of local wind systems
q.e: A high-pressure system is characterized by a "flat" pressure field where isobars are spaced far apart. This lack of pressure gradient kills the synoptic wind, allowing only weak local thermal winds to form.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during winter?
o: Changing weather with passing of frontal lines
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
q.e: In winter, the weak sun cannot burn off trapped moisture. The high pressure creates a strong inversion that traps cold, damp, polluted air at the surface, creating weeks of gloomy, widespread high fog and Stratus.

q.t: What wind conditions can be expected in areas showing large distances between isobars?
o: Strong prevailing easterly winds with rapid backing
Strong prevailing westerly winds with rapid veering
Formation of local wind systems with strong prevailing westerly winds
Variable winds, formation of local wind systems
q.e: Widely spaced isobars mean there is virtually no pressure gradient to drive a strong, prevailing wind. Consequently, winds become weak and variable, dominated only by local topographic effects like valley breezes.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected during "Foehn" on the windward side of a mountain range?
o: Dissipating clouds with unusual warming, accompanied by strong, gusty winds
Scattered cumulus clouds with showers and thunderstorms
Calm wind and forming of high stratus clouds (high fog)
Layered clouds, mountains obscured, poor visibility, moderate or heavy rain
q.e: On the windward (upwind) side, the air is forced up the mountain, cooling and condensing completely. This forms a massive, dark "wall" of clouds that obscures the peaks and dumps heavy, continuous rain.

q.t: Which of the stated wind phenomena will increase in speed since its path is narrowed by mountains?
q.e: The Mistral is a fierce, cold wind in southern France. It accelerates to gale force due to the "funnel effect" as it is squeezed through the narrow Rhone Valley between the Alps and the Massif Central.

q.t: What is the name of the the cold, katabatic wind phenomena blowing from northeast into the Adriatic Sea?
q.e: The Bora is a notorious, violent, and freezing katabatic wind that falls in winter from the cold Dinaric Alps plateaus down to the relatively warmer Adriatic coast in Croatia and Italy.

q.t: Which of the following conditions are most favourable for ice accretion?
o: Temperaturs below 0° C, strong wind, sky clear of clouds
Temperatures between +10° C and -30° C, presence of hail (clouds)
Temperatures between -20° C and -40° C, presence of ice crystals (Ci clouds)
Temperatures between 0° C and -12° C, presence of supercooled water droplets (clouds)
q.e: Severe structural icing requires liquid water. Between 0°C and -15°C, clouds are packed with "supercooled" liquid droplets that instantly freeze solid the moment they strike the aircraft's leading edges.

q.t: What temperatures are most dangerous with respect to airframe icing?
q.e: The range just below freezing (0° to -12° C) is critical. Here, large liquid droplets freeze slowly, spreading backward over the wing before solidifying into a heavy, smooth, and dangerous sheet of Clear Ice.

q.t: Which type of ice forms by very small water droplets and ice crystals hitting the front surfaces of an aircraft?
q.e: Rime ice (zrnitá námraza) forms in colder temperatures from tiny, dry droplets that freeze instantly upon impact. It traps air, creating a milky, opaque, and rough coating.

q.t: Which type of ice forms by large, supercooled droplets hitting the front surfaces of an aircraft?
q.e: Clear ice (ledovka) forms from large, heavy, supercooled drops in temperatures just below freezing. They don't freeze instantly, but flow back over the wing, creating a thick, solid, transparent, and extremely heavy ice layer.

q.t: What situation may result in the occurrence of severe wind shear?
o: Flying ahead of a warm front with visible Ci clouds
Cross-country flying below Cu clouds with about 4 octas coverage
During final approach, 30 min after a heavy shower has passed the airfield
When a shower is visible close to the airfield
q.e: Rain shafts falling from a convective cloud drag down massive amounts of cold air. When this downdraft hits the ground, it explodes outward, generating violent microbursts and severe wind shear directly in the approach path.

q.t: What conditions are favourable for the formation of thunderstorms?
o: Calm winds and cold air, overcast cloud cover with St or As.
Clear night over land, cold air and patches of fog
Warm and dry air, strong inversion layer
Warm humid air, conditionally unstable environmental lapse rate
q.e: A thunderstorm acts like a heat engine. It requires high heat (to trigger updrafts), high moisture (fuel for latent heat), and an unstable atmosphere without inversions to allow the cloud to grow to the tropopause.

q.t: What conditions are mandatory for the formation of thermal thunderstorms?
o: Conditionally unstable atmosphere, low temperature and low humidity
Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and low humidity
Conditionally unstable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
q.e: Thermal (air-mass) thunderstorms are classic summer afternoon events. They depend entirely on extreme surface heating (high temp), a "stuffy" atmosphere (high humidity), and a lack of stabilizing inversion layers.

q.t: With regard to thunderstorms, strong up- and downdrafts appear during the...
q.e: In the mature stage of a Cumulonimbus, precipitation begins to fall. The falling rain drags air down with it, creating a violent downdraft cell that exists right alongside the hot, rising updraft cell.

q.t: Which stage of a thunderstorm is dominated by updrafts?
q.e: The first stage of a storm is the Cumulus building stage. It functions purely as a massive vacuum cleaner, sucking hot air upward in a continuous, powerful updraft before any rain has formed to drag it back down.

q.t: What danger is most immenent when an aircraft is hit by lightning?
o: Rapid cabin depressurization and smoke in the cabin
Explosion of electrical equipment in the cockpit
Disturbed radio communication, static noise signals
Surface overheat and damage to exposed aircraft parts
q.e: The aircraft acts as a Faraday cage, shielding the interior. However, at the exact exit and entry points (like wingtips or radomes), the lightning's immense heat melts and structurally damages the aluminum or composite skin.

q.t: Heavy downdrafts and strong wind shear close to the ground can be expected...
o: during cold, clear nights with the formation of radiation fog.
during approach to an airfield at the coast with a strong sea breeze.
during warm summer days with high, flatted Cu clouds.
near the rainfall areas of heavy showers or thunderstorms.
q.e: Whenever you see heavy, dark curtains of rain falling from a cumulonimbus cloud, be aware that thousands of tons of cold water are dragging freezing air down, causing explosive wind shear at the surface.

q.t: What phenomenon is caused by cold air downdrafts with precipitation from a fully developed thunderstorm cloud?
q.e: A gust front (squall line / húlava) is the leading edge of the storm's downdraft. It races ahead of the storm cell along the ground like a plow, creating a sudden, violent, and freezing wall of wind.

q.t: What has to be considered when taking off in a ground inversion?
o: Climb should be performed with the lowest possible speed and maximum power
Due to low temperatures close to the ground, icing has to be expected
During the climb, a sudden increase in speed and climb performance has to be expected
During climb, a sudden decrease in speed and climb performance has to be expected
q.e: In a ground inversion, it is cold at the surface and warm aloft. Climbing into the warm layer means encountering suddenly less dense air. The wings lose lift and the engine loses power, causing a startling sag in performance.

q.t: What danger is most imminent during an approach to an airfield situated in a valley, with strong wind aloft blowing perpendicular to the mountain ridge?
o: Reduced visibilty, maybe loss of sight to the airfield during final approach
Formation of medium to heavy clear ice on all aircraft surfaces
Heavy downdrafts within rainfall areas below thunderstorm clouds
Wind shear during descent, wind direction may change by 180°
q.e: Wind blowing over a mountain ridge curls down into the valley, creating massive, tumbling horizontal rotors. As you descend, the wind might hit you from the front, and seconds later, violently from behind (180° shear).

q.t: What kind of reduction in visibility is not very sensitive to changes in temperature?
q.e: Haze (zákal) is composed of microscopic dry particles like dust, smoke, or pollution suspended in the air. Since it is not made of water droplets, it cannot simply be "burned off" by a rise in morning temperature.

q.t: Information about pressure patterns and frontal situation can be found in which chart?
q.e: A Surface Weather Chart (Synoptic Chart) provides the classic bird's-eye view of the current meteorological situation, displaying high/low pressure centers with closed isobars and colored frontal lines.

q.t: Which weather chart shows the actual air pressure as in MSL along with pressure centers and fronts?
q.e: As established, the Surface Weather Chart (Přízemní synoptická mapa) plots ground station observations (QFF pressure reduced to sea level) to map the isobars and weather fronts across a continent.

q.t: What information can be obtained from satallite images?
o: Temperature and dew point of environmental air
Flight visibility, ground visibility, and ground contact
Overview of cloud covers and front lines
q.e: Meteorological satellites photograph the Earth from space using visible and infrared lenses. They cannot "see" temperature values, but they provide a perfect visual map of vast cloud layers and advancing storm fronts.

q.t: What chart shows areas of precipitation?
q.e: While a satellite looks at the tops of clouds, a weather radar bounces microwave pulses off the actual falling water droplets and hail inside the cloud, providing a live map of active precipitation zones.

q.t: What information is NOT found on Low-Level Significant Weather Charts (LLSWC)?
q.e: A Significant Weather Chart is a hand-drawn or computer-generated forecast predicting dangerous areas (turbulence, freezing zones). It is a static document and cannot display live, moving radar precipitation echoes.

q.t: Measured pressure distribution in MSL and corresponding frontal systems are displayed by the...
q.e: This repeats the definition of the Surface Weather Chart (Synoptic chart). It is the only map dedicated to outlining isobars (pressure distribution) and frontal boundaries.

q.t: In a METAR, "heavy rain" is designated by the identifier...
q.e: In the METAR shorthand code, "RA" signifies Rain. The modifier "+" indicates a heavy intensity. Therefore, an intense downpour is coded as +RA.

q.t: In a METAR, "(moderate) showers of rain" are designated by the identifier...
q.e: SH designates Showers (sudden, convective rain), and "RA" designates Rain. Without any plus or minus sign, it defaults to a moderate intensity. Thus, SHRA means moderate rain showers.

q.t: What information can be found in the ATIS, but not in a METAR?
o: Information about current weather, for example types of precipitation
Information about mean wind speeds, maximum speeds in gusts if applicable
Approach information, such as ground visibility and cloud base
Operational information such as runway in use and transition level
q.e: A METAR is a strictly meteorological telegram. ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) supplements weather data with vital airport logistics, telling pilots which runway to use, closed taxiways, and the transition level.

q.t: Weather and operational information about the destination aerodrome can be obtained during the flight by...
q.e: When approaching a large airport, a pilot tunes a specific radio frequency to listen to the ATIS. It is a continuously looping robotic broadcast providing the latest weather and active runway information.

q.t: SIGMET warnings are issued for...
q.e: SIGMETs are critical warnings about severe en-route weather phenomena (like volcanic ash or severe turbulence) that affect the safety of all aircraft. They are issued for an entire Flight Information Region (FIR).

q.t: An inversion is a layer ...
o: with increasing pressure with increasing height.
with decreasing temperature with increasing height.
with constant temperature with increasing height.
with increasing temperature with increasing height.
q.e: In a standard atmosphere, it gets colder as you go up. An inversion is a meteorological anomaly where this rule is "inverted," and the air gets warmer as you climb higher.

q.t: What can be expected for the prevailling wind with isobars on a surface weather chart showing large distances?
o: Strong pressure gradients resulting in strong prevailling wind
Strong pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
Low pressure gradients resulting in strong prevailling wind
Low pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
q.e: Isobars drawn far apart indicate that the atmospheric pressure changes very slowly over a vast area. This small (low) pressure gradient provides no driving force, resulting in very weak or calm winds.

q.t: What is referred to as mountain wind?
o: Wind blowing uphill from the valley during daytime.
Wind blowing uphill from the valley during the night.
Wind blowing down the mountain side during daytime.
Wind blowing down the mountain side during the night
q.e: A mountain wind is a katabatic process. At night, the high mountain slopes cool down rapidly, chilling the air above them. This heavy, dense air slides down the slope into the valley.

q.t: Under which conditions "back side weather" ("Rückseitenwetter") can be expected?
o: During Foehn at the lee side
After passing of a warm front
After passing of a cold front
q.e: Back side weather (Rückseitenwetter) describes the post-cold-frontal environment. It is characterized by cool, very clear polar air, excellent visibility, and unstable showery Cumulus clouds.

q.t: What wind is reportet as 225/15?
q.e: Aviation wind is reported as Direction/Speed. The direction 225° indicates wind blowing FROM the South-West. The number 15 indicates the wind speed in knots (kt).

q.t: How does air temperatur change in ISA from MSL to approx. 10.000 m height?
q.e: The International Standard Atmosphere assumes a baseline sea-level temperature of +15°C. Subtracting 2°C for every 1000 feet of altitude yields a chilling -50°C near the tropopause at 10,000 meters.

q.t: What weather is likely to be experienced during "Foehn" in the Bavarian area close to the alps?
o: High pressure area overhead Biskaya and low pressure area in Eastern Europe
Cold, humid downhill wind on the lee side of the alps, flat pressure pattern
Nimbostratus cloud in the northern alps, rotor clouds at the windward side, warm and dry wind
Nimbostratus cloud in the southern alps, rotor clouds at the lee side, warm and dry wind
q.e: Bavaria lies north of the Alps. The Foehn wind brings heavy rain (Nimbostratus) on the Italian windward side (south). On the Bavarian lee side (north), the air descends, becoming warm and dry, forming dangerous rotor clouds.

q.t: Mountain side updrafts can be intensified by ...
o: Solar irradiation on the lee side
By warming of upper atmospheric layers
thermal radiation of the windward side during the night
Solar irradiation on the windward side
q.e: An anabatic (upslope) wind is forced mechanically by the slope, but if the sun violently bakes that windward rock face, the massive thermal heating creates a powerful chimney effect, amplifying the updraft significantly.

q.t: In which situations should a pilot use blind transmissions?
o: When a pilot has flown into cloud or fog unintentionally and therefore would like to request navigational assistance from a ground unit
When the traffic situation at an airport allows the transmission of information which does not need to be acknowledged by the ground station
When no radio communication can be established with the appropriate aeronautical station, but when evidence exists that transmissions are received at that ground unit
When a transmission containing important navigational or technical information is to be sent to several stations at the same time
q.e: Blind transmission is used when two-way communication cannot be established, but the pilot has reasons to believe that the ground station is still receiving the transmissions.

q.t: Leaving a control frequency (except when reaching the final parking position)...
o: is not mandatory to be reported.
q.e: Pilots must maintain a continuous air-ground voice communication watch. Leaving the frequency requires explicit ATC clearance to ensure traffic separation and monitoring.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term "abeam"?
q.e: According to ICAO Doc 8400 (ICAO Abbreviations and Codes), the standard abbreviation for the term "abeam" is ABM.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term "visual flight rules"?
q.e: VFR stands for Visual Flight Rules, which dictate the conditions under which a pilot operates an aircraft in weather conditions generally clear enough to allow the pilot to see where the aircraft is going.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term "obstacle"?
q.e: According to ICAO abbreviations, OBST is the internationally recognized code used in NOTAMs and aeronautical charts for "obstacle".

q.t: What does the abbreviation "FIS" stand for?
q.e: FIS stands for Flight Information Service. It provides advice and information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights, such as weather updates and traffic information.

q.t: What does the abbreviaton "FIR" stand for?
q.e: FIR stands for Flight Information Region. It is an airspace of defined dimensions within which flight information service and alerting service are provided.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "H24" stand for?
q.e: H24 is an ICAO abbreviation indicating that a particular service, facility, or operational hour is available continuously, 24 hours a day.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "HX" stand for?
q.e: The abbreviation HX indicates that a facility or service does not have specific opening hours and operates on a non-continuous or unspecified schedule.

q.t: The altimeter has to be set to what value in order to show zero on ground?
q.e: QFE is the barometric pressure at the aerodrome elevation. When set on the altimeter subscale, the instrument will read zero altitude when the aircraft is on the runway.

q.t: Which altitude is displayed on the altimeter when set to a specific QNH?
o: Altitude in relation to the 1013.25 hPa datum
Altitude in relation to the air pressure at the reference airfield
Altitude in relation to mean sea level
Altitude in relation to the highest elevation within 10 km
q.e: QNH is the pressure reduced to mean sea level based on ISA conditions. Setting QNH causes the altimeter to display the aircraft's altitude above mean sea level (AMSL).

q.t: Which altitude is displayed on the altimeter when set to a specific QFE?
o: Altitude in relation to the 1013.25 hPa datum
Altitude in relation to the highest elevation within 10 km
Altitude in relation to mean sea level
Altitude in relation to the air pressure at the reference airfield
q.e: As QFE relates to the actual station pressure, setting it makes the altimeter show the height above that specific reference airfield (AGL relative to the runway).

q.t: What does the abbreviation "QDR" stand for?
q.e: In the Q-code system, QDR represents the magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft. It corresponds to a VOR radial.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "QUJ" stand for?
q.e: QUJ is a Q-code that indicates the true bearing to the station. It is a geographic direction uncorrected for magnetic variation.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "QTE" stand for?
q.e: QTE represents the true bearing from a station to the aircraft, often used by direction-finding stations to provide the aircraft's geographic line of position.

q.t: Which Q-code is used for the magnetic bearing from the station?
q.e: QDR is the code for the magnetic bearing from the ground station to the aircraft.

q.t: Which Q-code is used for the true bearing from the station?
q.e: QTE is the Q-code used by a ground direction-finding station to give the aircraft its true bearing from that station.

q.t: Which Q-code is used for the true bearing to the station?
q.e: QUJ refers to the true (geographic) bearing an aircraft must fly to reach the station, assuming zero wind drift.

q.t: Which of the listed radiotelephony messages has a higher priority than a flight safety message?
q.e: According to the ITU and ICAO priority of communications, direction finding messages have a higher priority than flight safety messages. The order is: Distress, Urgency, Direction finding, Flight safety, Meteorological, Flight regularity.

q.t: What is the correct term for a message used for air traffic control?
q.e: Clearances and instructions given by Air Traffic Control are categorized and classified as flight safety messages.

q.t: Distress messages are messages...
o: concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
sent by a pilot or an aircraft operating agency which have an imminent meaning for aircraft in flight.
concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
concerning the operation or maintenance of facilities which are important for the safety and regularity of flight operations.
q.e: A distress message (MAYDAY) is defined as a condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and requiring immediate assistance.

q.t: Urgency messages are messages...
o: concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
concerning the operation or maintenance of facilities essential for the safety or regularity of aircraft operation.
sent by a pilot or an aircraft operating agency which have an imminent meaning for aircraft in flight.
concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
q.e: An urgency message (PAN PAN) concerns the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of a person on board or in sight, but does not require immediate assistance.

q.t: Regularity messages are messages...
o: concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
concerning the operation or maintenance of facilities essential for the safety or regularity of aircraft operation.
concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
sent by an aircraft operating agency or an aircraft of immediate concern to an aircraft in flight.
q.e: Flight regularity messages deal with the routine operational status of facilities, aerodrome operations, and aircraft maintenance, having the lowest priority.

q.t: Which of the following messages has the highest priority?
q.e: Request QDM is a direction-finding message. According to communication priority rules, direction finding has priority over flight safety messages (like turning instructions or altimeter settings).

q.t: What is the correct way to transmit the call sign HB-YKM?
q.e: Using the ICAO phonetic alphabet, H is Hotel, B is Bravo, Y is Yankee, K is Kilo, and M is Mike.

q.t: What is the correct way to transmit the call sign OE-JVK?
q.e: According to the ICAO phonetic alphabet: O is Oscar, E is Echo, J is Juliett, V is Victor, and K is Kilo.

q.t: An altitude of 4500 ft is transmitted as...
q.e: Altitudes containing thousands and whole hundreds are pronounced by reading the digit for the thousands followed by "thousand" and the digit for the hundreds followed by "hundred".

q.t: A heading of 285 degrees is correctly transmitted as...
q.e: Headings must be transmitted by pronouncing each digit separately: "two eight five".

q.t: A frequency of 119.500 MHz is correctly transmitted as...
o: one one niner tousand decimal five zero.
one one niner decimal five zero.
one one niner decimal five zero zero.
q.e: Frequencies with trailing zeros in a 25 kHz channel spacing are shortened. The decimal point is pronounced as "decimal". Thus, "one one niner decimal five".

q.t: The directional information "12 o'clock" is correctly transmitted as...
q.e: Relative bearing using the clock code is transmitted by pronouncing the whole number followed by "o'clock", making "Twelve o'clock" the correct standard phrase.

q.t: Times are transmitted as...
q.e: All times in aviation communications must be transmitted in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to avoid confusion across different time zones.

q.t: If there is any doubt about ambiguity, a time of 1620 is to be transmitted as...
o: one tousand six hundred two zero.
q.e: To avoid ambiguity, times are transmitted by pronouncing each individual digit separately. Therefore, 1620 is transmitted as "one six two zero".

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase "Roger"?
o: Permission for proposed action is granted
I understand your message and will comply with it
An error has been made in this transmission. The correct version is...
I have received all of your last transmission
q.e: Roger simply means "I have received all of your last transmission". It does not mean "yes" or that permission is granted.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase "Correction"?
o: Permission for proposed action is granted
I have received all of your last transmission
An error has been made in this transmission. The correct version is...
I understand your message and will comply with it
q.e: Correction is used by a speaker to indicate that an error has just been made in the transmission, followed immediately by the correct version.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase "Approved"?
o: I have received all of your last transmission
Permission for proposed action is granted
I understand your message and will comply with it
An error has been made in this transmission. The correct version is...
q.e: Approved means that the permission for the proposed action requested by the pilot has been officially granted by ATC.

q.t: Which phrase does a pilot use when he / she wants to check the readability of his / her transmission?
q.e: How do you read? is the standard ICAO phraseology used to ask the receiving station to report on the readability of the transmission.

q.t: Which phrase is used by a pilot when he wants to fly through controlled airspace?
q.e: Request is the official phraseology used by a pilot to ask for an ATC clearance, permission, or a specific service.

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot if a transmission is to be answered with "yes"?
q.e: Affirm is the standard ICAO radiotelephony word for "Yes". It is used to prevent confusion with the word "No" which might happen with "Yes".

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot if a transmission is to be answered with "no"?
q.e: Negative is the standard phrase used to mean "No" or "Permission not granted" or "That is not correct". It is easily distinguishable in poor radio conditions.

q.t: Which phrase is to be used when a pilot wants the tower to know that he is ready for take-off?
q.e: A pilot shall never use the word "take-off" unless acknowledging a take-off clearance. To signal readiness, the standard phrase is "Ready for departure".

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot to inform the tower about a go-around?
q.e: Going around is the standard phrase to inform ATC that the pilot is aborting the landing and executing a missed approach.

q.t: What is the call sign of the aerodrome control?
q.e: Aerodrome control service, which manages traffic on the active runway and in the immediate vicinity, uses the call sign "Tower".

q.t: What is the call sign of the surface movement control?
q.e: Surface movement control, which is responsible for taxiways and apron areas, is addressed using the call sign suffix "Ground".

q.t: What is the call sign of the flight information service?
q.e: The aeronautical station providing flight information service (FIS) and alerting service to VFR traffic is addressed as "Information".

q.t: What is the correct abbreviation of the call sign D-EAZF?
q.e: An aircraft call sign is abbreviated by using the first character of the registration and the last two characters. D-EAZF becomes DZF.

q.t: In what case is the pilot allowed to abbreviate the call sign of his aircraft?
o: If there is little traffic in the traffic circuit
After passing the first reporting point
After the ground station has used the abbreviation
q.e: A pilot may only abbreviate the aircraft's call sign after the aeronautical ground station has initiated the use of the abbreviated call sign first.

q.t: What is the correct way of using the aircraft call sign at first contact?
o: Using the first two characters only
Using the last two characters only
Using the first three characters only
q.e: During the initial contact with an ATC unit, the pilot must always use the full aircraft call sign to establish clear identification.

q.t: What is the correct way of establishing radio communication between D-EAZF and Dusseldorf Tower?
q.e: Initial contact follows the format: [Name of station being called] followed by [Name of station calling]. Thus, "Dusseldorf Tower D-EAZF".

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction "Call Hamburg Tower on 121.275"?
q.e: To minimize radio clutter, simply reading back the frequency itself "121.275" along with the aircraft call sign is the required standard operating procedure.

q.t: What does a readability of 1 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable but with difficulty
The transmission is readable now and then
q.e: In the radio readability scale from 1 to 5, a readability of 1 means that the transmission is completely unreadable.

q.t: What does a readability of 2 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable but with difficulty
The transmission is readable now and then
q.e: A readability score of 2 indicates that the transmission is "readable now and then", meaning it cuts in and out and is mostly unintelligible.

q.t: What does a readability of 3 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable now and then
The transmission is readable but with difficulty
q.e: A readability score of 3 indicates that the transmission is "readable but with difficulty", usually due to static or a weak signal.

q.t: What does a readability of 5 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable now and then
The transmission is readable but with difficulty
q.e: A readability score of 5 is the highest score and indicates that the transmission is perfectly readable without any distortion.

q.t: Which information from a ground station does not require readback?
q.e: Wind information is provided for situational awareness and does not represent an ATC clearance or a critical instruction that mandates a strict readback.

q.t: Which information from a ground station does not require readback?
q.e: Traffic information is provided by ATC to help pilots see and avoid other aircraft. It is not an instruction or clearance, thus it does not require a readback.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction "DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead until 2500 feet before turning right heading 220 degrees, wind 090 degrees, 5 knots, runway 12, cleared for take-off"?
o: DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, wilco, heading 220 degrees, 090 degrees, 5 knots, cleared for take-off
DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, then turn right heading 220, 090 degrees, 5 knots
DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, then turn right heading 220, 090 degrees, 5 knots, cleared for take-off
DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, then turn right heading 220, runway 12, cleared for take-off
q.e: All parts of a departure clearance, heading, altitude, runway in use, and the take-off clearance itself must be read back. Wind information is omitted.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction "Next report PAH"?
q.e: Wilco (Will Comply) is the correct phrase to acknowledge an instruction indicating that you understand it and will carry it out.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction "Squawk 4321, Call Bremen Radar on 131.325"?
q.e: Transponder codes and frequency changes are critical instructions that must be strictly read back by repeating the numbers.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging "You are now entering airspace Delta"?
q.e: This is a piece of information (not a clearance or an instruction to perform an action). Acknowledging it with "Roger" confirms that the information was received.

q.t: What does a cloud coverage of "FEW" mean in a METAR weather report?
q.e: Cloud coverage is measured in oktas (eighths) of the sky. "FEW" indicates that 1 to 2 oktas of the sky are covered by clouds.

q.t: What does a cloud coverage of "SCT" mean in a METAR weather report?
q.e: SCT stands for Scattered. It represents a cloud coverage of 3 to 4 oktas (eighths) of the sky.

q.t: What does a cloud coverage of "BKN" mean in a METAR weather report?
q.e: BKN stands for Broken. It indicates that the sky is mostly covered, representing 5 to 7 oktas of cloud coverage. This constitutes a meteorological ceiling.

q.t: Given a visibility of 12 km, what is the correct way to transmit this visibility?
q.e: When the visibility is 10 km or more, it is reported and transmitted as "10 kilometers or more" (One-zero kilometers or more).

q.t: In what case is visibility transmitted in meters?
q.e: In aviation weather reports and ATC transmissions, visibility is transmitted in meters when the visibility is less than 5000 meters (5 km).

q.t: In what cases is visibility transmitted in kilometers?
q.e: Visibility is given in kilometers when it is 5 kilometers or greater, to simplify the communication process.

q.t: What information is broadcasted on a VOLMET frequency?
q.e: VOLMET (Meteorological Information for Aircraft in Flight) is a worldwide network of radio stations broadcasting continuous meteorological information such as TAF, SIGMET, and METAR.

q.t: Which navigation facility may be used for broadcasting the ATIS?
q.e: In some configurations, the voice capability of a VOR (VHF Omnidirectional Range) beacon is utilized to broadcast the ATIS continuous loop audio.

q.t: How can you obtain meteorological information concerning airports during a cross-country flight?
q.e: A pilot in flight can tune into a specific VOLMET frequency to listen to a continuous audio broadcast of meteorological reports for various airports in the region.

q.t: Which transponder code indicates a radio failure?
q.e: Setting the transponder to squawk 7600 alerts Air Traffic Control that the aircraft has experienced a two-way radio communication failure.

q.t: What is the correct phrase to begin a blind transmission?
q.e: When unable to establish two-way communication but believing the transmission might be received, the pilot must begin the broadcast with the phrase "Transmitting blind".

q.t: On what frequency shall a blind transmission be made?
o: On a radar frequency of the lower airspace
q.e: A blind transmission should primarily be made on the frequency currently in use, as that is the frequency the ground station is monitoring for that specific sector.

q.t: How often shall a blind transmission be made?
q.e: Standard procedures require a blind transmission to be broadcast twice (Two times) to ensure the highest probability that the ground station receives the message.

q.t: In what situation is it appropriate to set the transponder code 7600?
q.e: Squawk 7600 is internationally designated specifically for aircraft experiencing a loss of radio communication.

q.t: What is the correct course of action when experiencing a radio failure in class D airspace?
o: The flight has to be continued above 5000 feet complying with VFR flight rules or the airspace has to be left by the shortest route
The flight has to be continued above 5000 feet complying with VFR flight rules or the airspace has to be left using a standard routing
The flight has to be continued according to the last clearance complying with VFR flight rules or the airspace has to be left using a standard routing
The flight has to be continued according to the last clearance complying with VFR rules or the airspace has to be left by the shortest route
q.e: In a Class D airspace radio failure, the VFR pilot should maintain visual meteorological conditions and leave the airspace by the shortest route, or follow the last received and acknowledged clearance.

q.t: Under what conditions may class D airspace be entered with a radio failure?
o: There are other aircraft in the aerodrome circuit
It ist the aerodrome of departure
q.e: Entering a Class D airspace requires a clearance. If the radio fails, entry is strictly prohibited unless an explicit approval (clearance) was granted before the failure occurred.

q.t: Which phrase is to be repeated three times before transmitting an urgency message?
q.e: PAN PAN spoken three times is the international urgency signal used to indicate that the aircraft has a very urgent message concerning safety, but is not in immediate distress.

q.t: Urgency messages are defined as...
o: messages concerning urgent spare parts which are needed for a continuation of flight and which need to be ordered in advance.
information concerning the apron personell and which imply an imminent danger to landing aircraft.
messages concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
messages concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
q.e: An urgency message indicates a condition concerning the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of some person on board or within sight, but does not require immediate assistance.

q.t: Distress messages contain...
o: information concerning urgent spare parts which are required for a continuation of flight and which have to be ordered in advance.
information concerning the apron personell and which imply an imminent danger to landing aircraft.
information concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
information concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
q.e: Distress messages (MAYDAY) are utilized specifically when the aircraft is threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and requires immediate assistance.

q.t: What is the correct frequency for an initial distress message?
q.e: The initial distress message should be transmitted on the air-ground frequency currently in use. If no response is received, the pilot should switch to the emergency frequency 121.500 MHz.

q.t: What kind of information should be included in an urgency message?
o: Nature of problem or observation, important information for support, departure aerodrome, information about position, heading and altitude
Intended routing, important information for support, intentions of the pilot, information about position, departure aerodrome, heading and altitude
Intended routing, important information for support, intentions of the pilot, departure aerodrome, destination aerodrome, heading and altitude
Nature of problem or observation, important information for support, intentions of the pilot, information about position, heading and altitude
q.e: An urgency message should clearly state the nature of the problem, the pilot's intentions, the aircraft's current position, flight level/altitude, and heading to allow ATC to provide appropriate support.

q.t: The correct transponder code for emergencies is...
q.e: Squawking 7700 instantly flags the aircraft on ATC radar screens worldwide as an aircraft in a state of emergency or distress.

q.t: Which of the following frequencies is designated for VHF voice communication?
q.e: Aviation VHF voice communication takes place in the frequency band between 118.000 MHz and 136.975 MHz. Thus, 118.75 MHz is correct.

q.t: Which of the following frequencies is designated for VHF voice communication?
q.e: Frequencies between 108.00 MHz and 117.95 MHz are reserved for navigational aids (VOR/ILS). Voice communications start at 118.000 MHz, making 120.50 MHz the only valid option.

q.t: What is the correct designation of the frequency band from 118.000 to 136.975 MHz used for voice communication?
q.e: VHF stands for Very High Frequency, which covers the radio spectrum from 30 MHz to 300 MHz, containing the civilian aviation voice band.

q.t: Which of the following factors affects the reception of VHF transmissions?
q.e: VHF radio waves travel in a straight "line of sight". Therefore, the higher the aircraft's altitude, the further the VHF signal can reach before being blocked by the curvature of the Earth.

q.t: What is the approximate speed of electromagnetic wave propagation?
q.e: Electromagnetic waves, including VHF radio waves, propagate through space at the speed of light, which is approximately 300,000 kilometers per second.

q.t: An ATIS is valid for...
q.e: The Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS) is typically updated at 30-minute intervals (e.g., at the hour and half-hour) or whenever a significant change in weather or operational conditions occurs.

q.t: Compared to trailing edge flaps, leading edge devices like Slots...
o: allow higher speeds at take-off and landing.
reduce the critical angle of attack at a given speed.
produce less drag while allowing a higher angle of attack.
increase the camber and allow a lower angle of attack.
q.e: Leading edge devices like slots re-energize the boundary layer, delaying airflow separation. This allows the wing to reach a much higher critical angle of attack and generate more lift without the massive drag penalty typical for trailing edge flaps.

q.t: Stabilization around the lateral axis during cruise is achieved by the...
q.e: The lateral axis runs from wingtip to wingtip (pitching motion). The horizontal stabilizer provides the necessary restoring aerodynamic moment to keep the aircraft's pitch attitude stable during flight.

q.t: Flying with speeds higher than the never-exceed-speed (vNE) may result in...
o: too high total pressure resulting in an unusable airspeed indicator.
reduced drag with increased control forces.
an increased lift-to-drag ratio and a better glide angle.
flutter and mechanically damaging the wings.
q.e: Vne is the absolute maximum structural speed. Exceeding it can induce aeroelastic flutter, a rapid and violent vibration that can quickly cause the wings or tail to break apart.

q.t: What effects typically result from propeller icing?
q.e: Ice accumulation alters the aerodynamic profile of the propeller blades, increasing their drag and drastically reducing their thrust (efficiency). This leads to a noticeable drop in RPM and overall power output.

q.t: During a straight and steady climb, which force acts addionally, and in the same direction as the drag force, resulting in more power required for climb than for horizontal flight?
o: A component of the thrust along the rearward flightpath.
The vertical component of the weight force.
A component of the weight force along the rearward flight path.
A component of the lift force along the forward flightpath.
q.e: In a climb, the aircraft's pitch is inclined upward. Gravity pulls straight down, meaning a component of the aircraft's weight now acts backwards along the flight path, directly adding to the aerodynamic drag.

q.t: The static pressure of gases work...
o: only in the direction of the total pressure.
only vertical to the flow direction.
q.e: According to fluid mechanics, the static pressure of a gas or fluid in a given point acts equally in all directions, regardless of the flow of the fluid.

q.t: Bernoulli's equation for frictionless, incompressible gases states that...
o: static pressure = total pressure + dynamic pressure.
dynamic pressure = total pressure + static pressure.
total pressure = dynamic pressure - static pressure.
total pressure = dynamic pressure + static pressure.
q.e: Bernoulli's principle states that for an incompressible fluid, the sum of static pressure and dynamic pressure is constant and is equal to the total (stagnation) pressure.

q.t: If surrounded by airflow (v>0), any arbitrarily shaped body produces...
q.e: Any physical body moving through a fluid (or having fluid move around it) will generate aerodynamic resistance, known as drag, due to friction and form displacement.

q.t: All aerodynamic forces can be considered to act on a single point. This point is called...
q.e: The Center of Pressure (CP) is the theoretical point on an aerofoil where the total sum of a pressure field acts, meaning all aerodynamic forces (lift and drag) are considered to originate from this point.

q.t: The center of pressure is the theoretical point of origin of...
o: all aerodynamic forces of the profile.
q.e: As defined in aerodynamics, the center of pressure is the point where the resultant vector of all aerodynamic forces (both lift and drag components) acting on the airfoil intersects the chord line.

q.t: Number 2 in the drawing corresponds to the... (Refer to an airfoil diagram showing the line from leading to trailing edge)
q.e: The chord is the straight geometric distance connecting the leading edge to the trailing edge of an aerofoil profile.

q.t: Number 3 in the drawing corresponds to the... (Refer to an airfoil diagram showing the curved line equidistant from upper and lower surfaces)
q.e: The mean camber line is a curve drawn exactly halfway between the upper and lower surfaces of an airfoil. It shows the curvature (camber) of the wing.

q.t: The angle of attack is the angle between...
o: the chord line and the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane.
the undisturbed airflow and the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane.
the wing and the fuselage of an aeroplane.
the chord line and the oncoming airflow.
q.e: The Angle of Attack (AoA) is strictly defined as the acute angle between the chord line of the aerofoil and the direction of the relative (oncoming) airflow.

q.t: The ratio of span and mean chord length is referred to as...
q.e: Aspect Ratio (AR) is a measure of how long and slender a wing is. It is calculated by dividing the wingspan squared by the wing area, or simply wingspan divided by the mean chord.

q.t: Which point on the aerofoil is represented by the point where laminar flow becomes turbulent?
q.e: The transition point is the exact location on the surface of the aerofoil where the smooth, orderly laminar boundary layer breaks down and turns into a chaotic, turbulent boundary layer.

q.t: Which point on the aerofoil is represented by the point where the airflow leaves the upper surface?
q.e: The separation point is the location where the boundary layer detaches from the surface of the aerofoil, causing turbulent wake and a massive loss of lift (leading to a stall).

q.t: Wing tip vortex development begins during which phase of flight?
o: While setting take-off power during take-off run
When lift is being generated during rotation
While setting flaps to lower position
As soon as the aircraft starts moving
q.e: Vortices are a byproduct of lift. Therefore, they only begin to form when the wings actually start generating lift, which occurs when the pilot pitches the nose up during rotation.

q.t: Which point on the aerofoil is represented by the very front tip where the airflow divides?
q.e: The stagnation point is the spot on the leading edge where the oncoming air stream is brought to a complete halt (velocity is zero) before dividing to flow over and under the wing.

q.t: What pattern can be found at the stagnation point?
o: All aerodynamic forces can be considered as attacking at this single point
The laminar boundary layer changes into a turbulent boundary layer
Streamlines are divided into airflow above and below the profile
The boundary layer starts separating on the upper surface of the profile
q.e: At the stagnation point, the relative wind hits the wing head-on and splits, with part of the air flowing over the upper surface and the rest flowing under the lower surface.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed at a lift-generating wing profile at positive angle of attack?
o: Pressure above remains unchanged, higher pressure is created below the profile
High pressure is created above, lower pressure below the profile
Low pressure is created above, higher pressure below the profile
Pressure below remains unchanged, lower pressure is created above the profile
q.e: According to Bernoulli's principle, the faster-moving air over the curved top surface creates low pressure (suction), while the slower-moving air underneath creates higher pressure, thus generating lift.

q.t: The position of the center of pressure at a positively shaped profile...
o: moves to the trailing edge while the angle of attack becomes smaller.
is located at approximately 25% of the chord, measured from the leading edge.
does not move since it is independent of the angle of attack.
moves to the leading edge while the angle of attack becomes smaller.
q.e: For an asymmetrical (cambered) airfoil, reducing the angle of attack causes the upper surface pressure distribution to shift backward, moving the center of pressure towards the trailing edge.

q.t: In which way does the position of the center of pressure move at a positively shaped profile with increasing angle of attack?
o: It moves forward first, then backward
It moves forward until reaching the critical angle of attack
It moves to the wing tips
It moves backward until reaching the critical angle of attack
q.e: As the angle of attack increases, the peak of the low-pressure area on top of the wing intensifies near the leading edge, pulling the center of pressure forward until the wing stalls.

q.t: Which statement about lift and angle of attack is correct?
o: Increasing the angle of attack results in less lift being generated by the aerofoil
Decreasing the angle of attack results in more drag being generated by the aerofoil
Too large angles of attack can lead to an exponential increase in lift
Increasing the angle of attack too far may result in a loss of lift and an airflow separation
q.e: Lift increases roughly linearly with the angle of attack up to a certain point. If increased beyond this critical angle, the airflow separates from the upper surface, resulting in a stall and abrupt loss of lift.

q.t: Which statement about the airflow around an aerofoil is correct if the angle of attack increases?
o: The center of pressure moves up
The center of pressure moves down
q.e: As the nose of the airfoil is pitched up (increasing the angle of attack), the oncoming air strikes more of the underside, pushing the stagnation point further down along the leading edge.

q.t: Which statement about the airflow around an aerofoil is correct if the angle of attack decreases?
o: The center of pressure moves forward
q.e: Conversely, when pitching down (decreasing angle of attack), the oncoming air hits the airfoil higher on the leading edge, moving the stagnation point upwards.

q.t: The angle (alpha) shown in the figure between the chord line and the direction of airflow is referred to as...
q.e: The angle alpha (α) between the relative wind (direction of airflow) and the chord line of the wing is universally defined in aerodynamics as the angle of attack.

q.t: In order to improve the stall characteristics of an aircraft, the wing is twisted outwards (the angle of incidence varies spanwise). This is known as...
q.e: Geometric washout means the wing is physically twisted so that the wingtip has a lower angle of incidence than the wing root. This ensures the wing root stalls first, maintaining aileron control.

q.t: Which option states a benefit of wing washout?
o: At high angles of attack the effectiveness of the aileron is retained as long as possible
Greater hardness because the wing can withstand more torsion forces
With the washout the form drag reduces at high speeds
Structurally the wing is made more rigid against rotation
q.e: Because the wing root has a higher angle of incidence, it reaches the critical stall angle before the wingtip. This keeps the airflow smooth over the ailerons at the tips, allowing roll control during a stall.

q.t: Which statement concerning the angle of attack is correct?
o: The angle of attack cannot be negative
Increasing the angle of attack results in decreasing lift
A too large angle of attack may result in a loss of lift
The angle of attack is constant throughout the flight
q.e: The angle of attack must be carefully managed. If it exceeds the critical angle, the smooth airflow detaches (boundary layer separation), leading to a stall and a sudden loss of lift.

q.t: When increasing the airflow speed by a factor of 2 while keeping all other parameters constant, how does the parasite drag change approximately?
o: It increases by a factor of 4
It increases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 4
It decreases by a factor of 2
q.e: Aerodynamic forces, including parasite drag, increase with the square of the airspeed (v^2). Therefore, doubling the speed (2x) increases the drag by a factor of four (2^2 = 4).

q.t: The drag coefficient...
o: may range from zero to an infinite positive value.
is proportional to the lift coefficient.
cannot be lower than a non-negative, minimal value.
q.e: Any physical body moving through a fluid will always have some amount of skin friction and form drag. Therefore, the drag coefficient can never be zero; it will always have a minimum positive value.

q.t: Pressure compensation on an wing occurs at the...
q.e: The high pressure from the underside of the wing attempts to escape to the low-pressure area on top. The only place this can happen freely is at the wing tips, resulting in wingtip vortices.

q.t: Which of the following options is likely to produce large induced drag?
q.e: A small aspect ratio means a short, wide wing. Such a wing has a proportionally larger wingtip area compared to its span, causing massive pressure spillage (vortices) and thus generating large induced drag.

q.t: Which parts of an aircraft mainly affect the generation of induced drag?
o: the outer part of the ailerons.
the front part of the fuselage.
the lower part of the gear.
q.e: Induced drag is a direct byproduct of lift, created entirely by the high-pressure air curling up and over the wing tips into the low-pressure area, creating energy-sapping vortices.

q.t: Where is interference drag generated?
q.e: Interference drag occurs when airflows from two adjacent parts of the aircraft collide and mix. The prime example is the 90-degree junction where the wing root meets the fuselage.

q.t: Which curve on the total drag graph represents the induced drag?
o: The curve increasing exponentially with speed
The curve decreasing continuously with speed
The curve representing the sum of all drags
q.e: Induced drag is inversely proportional to the square of airspeed. It is highest at slow speeds (where high angles of attack are needed) and decreases continuously as airspeed increases.

q.t: Pressure drag, interference drag and friction drag belong to the group of the...
q.e: All drag components that do not actively contribute to the generation of lift (unlike induced drag) are collectively classified as parasite (or profile) drag.

q.t: What kind of drag is NOT part of the parasite drag?
q.e: Induced drag is the "price paid for lift." It is caused by wingtip vortices and is completely distinct from the parasite drag category (which covers shape, skin friction, and interference).

q.t: How do induced drag and parasite drag change with increasing airspeed during a horizontal and stable cruise flight?
o: Parasite drag decreases and induced drag decreases
Induced drag decreases and parasite drag increases
Parasite drag decreases and induced drag increases
Induced drag increases and parasite drag increases
q.e: As you fly faster, you need less angle of attack, so wingtip vortices weaken (induced drag decreases). However, you are punching through the air much faster, so air resistance on the airframe grows rapidly (parasite drag increases).

q.t: Which of the listed wing shapes has the lowest induced drag?
q.e: Aerodynamically, an elliptical wing planform (like on the Spitfire) provides the most uniform lift distribution across the span, which minimizes the intensity of wingtip vortices and results in the lowest possible induced drag.

q.t: Which effect does a decreasing airspeed have on the induced drag during a horizontal and stable cruise flight?
o: The induced drag will slightly decrease
The induced drag will remain constant
q.e: To maintain level flight at slower speeds, the pilot must increase the angle of attack. This creates a much larger pressure differential between the upper and lower wing surfaces, vastly strengthening the wingtip vortices and increasing induced drag.

q.t: Which statement about induced drag during the horizontal cruise flight is correct?
o: Induced drag increases with increasing airspeed
Induced drag has a minimum at a certain speed and increases at higher as well as lower speeds
Induced drag decreases with increasing airspeed
Induced drag has a maximum at a certain speed and decreases at higher as well as lower speeds
q.e: As aircraft speed increases, the wing flies at a much shallower (lower) angle of attack. This reduces the pressure spill-over at the wingtips, meaning induced drag continually decreases as speed builds.

q.t: In which mentioned situation is the total drag at its minimum?
o: Parasite drag is twice as much as induced drag
Parasite drag is equal to induced drag
Induced drag is twice as much as parasite drag
Induced drag is smaller than parasite drag
q.e: The total drag curve is U-shaped. The absolute lowest point of this curve (minimum total drag, L/D max) occurs exactly at the speed where the decreasing induced drag curve intersects the increasing parasite drag curve.

q.t: Which kinds of drag contribute to total drag?
o: Form drag, skin-friction drag, interference drag
Induced drag, form drag, skin-friction drag
q.e: In aviation, total aerodynamic drag is broadly summarized as the simple sum of two main components: induced drag (from lift) and parasite drag (from the physical structure moving through air).

q.t: How do lift and drag change when approaching a stall condition?
q.e: At the critical angle of attack, the boundary layer separates from the wing. The organized airflow breaks down into turbulent wake, which drastically destroys the lifting capability (lift decreases) while producing massive aerodynamic resistance (drag increases).

q.t: In case of a stall it is important to...
o: increase the angle of attack and reduce the speed.
decrease the angle of attack and increase the speed.
increase the bank angle and reduce the speed.
increase the angle of attack and increase the speed.
q.e: To recover from a stall, the pilot must physically "un-stall" the wing by pushing the nose down (decreasing angle of attack) to re-attach the airflow, and apply power to regain flying speed.

q.t: During a stall, the lift...
q.e: This is a restatement of the aerodynamic breakdown during a stall. The loss of attached airflow means lift drops rapidly, and the huge turbulent wake creates massive drag.

q.t: The critical angle of attack...
o: increases with backward center of gravity position.
decreases with forward center of gravity position.
q.e: The critical angle of attack is an aerodynamic constant determined solely by the physical shape (profile) of the wing. The wing will always stall at this exact angle, regardless of how heavy the aircraft is or how fast it is flying.

q.t: What leads to a decreased stall speed Vs (IAS)?
q.e: A lighter aircraft requires less total lift to support its weight in flight. Therefore, it can fly at a slower airspeed before it is forced to reach the critical angle of attack, meaning its stall speed is lower.

q.t: The stall warning will be activated just before reaching which speed?
q.e: Stall warning systems (like horns or stick shakers) are calibrated to activate just above the actual stall speed (Vs), usually 5 to 10 knots beforehand, giving the pilot enough warning to lower the nose.

q.t: In motorplanes the stall warning is usually activated by a change of...
q.e: As the angle of attack becomes dangerously high, the stagnation point moves far down under the leading edge. A mechanical stall vane or suction port placed on the leading edge is tripped by this shifting airflow pattern.

q.t: How should the pilot react to an engaged stall warning?
o: Raise the nose to decrease airspeed
q.e: A stall warning means the wing is on the verge of separating airflow. The immediate life-saving reaction is to push the yoke forward (to lower the angle of attack) and apply full throttle to regain airspeed.

q.t: Which statement regarding a spin is correct?
o: During recovery the ailerons should be crossed
During the spin the speed constantly increases
Only very old aeroplanes have a risk of spinning
During recovery the ailerons should be kept neutral
q.e: Using ailerons during a spin recovery can aggravate the situation by increasing the angle of attack on the down-going wing (deepening the stall) or increasing adverse yaw. Ailerons must be strictly neutralized.

q.t: When extending the flaps for landing at constant angle of attack, in which way does the lift coefficient change far before reaching the maximum lift coefficient?
o: It is not possible to define
q.e: Deploying flaps physically changes the shape of the wing, greatly increasing its camber (curvature). This significantly boosts the wing's lift coefficient at any given angle of attack.

q.t: With regard to flaps, which of the following options provides a lift-increasing effect?
q.e: As mentioned, deploying trailing-edge flaps extends them downwards, which effectively "bends" the airfoil and creates a much larger camber. Highly cambered wings generate substantially more lift.

q.t: Which factor can be changed by deploying flaps for landing?
o: The twist effect of the engine
The position of the center of gravity
q.e: Deploying flaps changes the center of pressure and the downwash on the tail. This induces a strong pitching moment (nose up or nose down depending on the aircraft), requiring the pilot to adjust the elevator trim condition.

q.t: What is the principle of a Fowler flap?
o: A flap from the rear bottom side of the wing is folded down
The rear part of the wing is folded down
At high angles of attack a part of the leading edge lifts
A profile-like flap is extended from the trailing edge of the wing
q.e: A Fowler flap slides backwards on tracks before it hinges downwards. This incredibly efficient design not only increases the camber but also physically increases the total surface area of the wing.

q.t: A take-off with flaps in take-off position causes...
o: a shortening of the take-off run.
q.e: Using a small amount of flap (e.g., 10 degrees) increases the wing's lift significantly without adding too much drag. This allows the aircraft to lift off the ground at a slower speed, substantially shortening the ground roll.

q.t: Provided that no other procedure is described in the Aircraft Operating Handbook, after increasing the engine power in a go-around, the flaps may...
o: remain fully extended until reaching the traffic pattern.
be fully retracted without any delay.
not be operated up to the minimum safe altitude.
be retracted to a middle position.
q.e: During a go-around, full landing flaps create massive drag that prevents the aircraft from climbing. You must promptly retract them "one step" (to a middle position) to shed drag, while retaining enough lift to prevent sinking.

q.t: How do lift and drag change when setting flaps to a lower position?
q.e: Any extension of the flaps downwards into the airstream produces a significant boost in lift (due to increased camber), but also exposes a large flat plate area to the wind, drastically increasing aerodynamic drag.

q.t: The laminar boundary layer on the aerofoil is located between...
o: the transition point and the separation point.
the stagnation point and the center of pressure.
the transition point and the center of pressure.
the stagnation point and the transition point.
q.e: The smooth, low-friction laminar flow begins exactly where the air splits at the leading edge (stagnation point) and continues backward until it trips and becomes chaotic at the transition point.

q.t: What types of boundary layers can be found on an aerofoil?
o: Turbulent boundary layer along the complete upper surface with separated airflow
Laminar layer at the leading wing areas, turbulent boundary layer at the trailing areas
Turbulent layer at the leading wing areas, laminar boundary layer at the trailing areas
Laminar boundary layer along the complete upper surface with non-separated airflow
q.e: Airflow always starts out smooth (laminar) at the smooth leading edge. As it travels backwards, friction and pressure gradients inevitably cause it to trip into a rough, swirling layer (turbulent) before it leaves the trailing edge.

q.t: How does a laminar boundary layer differ from a turbulent boundary layer?
o: The laminar boundary layer produces lift, the turbulent boundary layer produces drag
The laminar boundary layer is thinner and provides more skin-friction drag
The turbulent boundary layer is thicker and provides less skin-friction drag
The turbulent boundary layer can follow the airfoil camber at higher angles of attack
q.e: While turbulent flow causes more skin friction, it contains highly energized, swirling air. This energy allows it to stay attached to the steep, curved back of a wing at high angles of attack much longer than weak laminar flow.

q.t: What structural item provides lateral stability to an airplane?
q.e: Lateral stability (rolling stability around the longitudinal axis) is primarily provided by wing dihedral – the slight upward V-shape angle of the wings. If the plane banks, the lower wing generates more lift and rolls it back level.

q.t: Which statement describes a situation of static stability?
o: An aircraft distorted by external impact will maintain the deflected position
An aircraft distorted by external impact can return to its original position by rudder input
An aircraft distorted by external impact will tend to an even more deflected position
An aircraft distorted by external impact will return to the original position
q.e: Positive static stability is the initial, built-in tendency of an aircraft to naturally try and return to its original trimmed state of equilibrium after being disturbed by a gust or bump, without pilot input.

q.t: Which constructive feature is shown in the figure? (A diagram showing an aircraft from the front with upward-angled wings)
q.e: The upward angle of the wings from the fuselage is called dihedral. This specific design feature guarantees that the aircraft will naturally want to roll back to wings-level, ensuring lateral stability.

q.t: Longitudinal stability is referred to as stability around which axis?
q.e: Longitudinal stability refers to the aircraft's tendency to maintain its pitch attitude (nose up/down). Pitching motions occur by rotating around the lateral axis (the imaginary line running from wingtip to wingtip).

q.t: Stability around which axis is mainly influenced by the center of gravity's longitudinal position?
q.e: Moving the center of gravity forward or backward along the fuselage drastically alters how heavy the nose or tail feels. This directly affects the aircraft's pitch stability, which is rotation around the lateral axis.

q.t: What structural item provides directional stability to an airplane?
q.e: Directional stability (yaw stability) prevents the nose from wandering left or right. A large vertical tail (fin) acts like the feathers on an arrow or a weather vane, keeping the nose pointed straight into the relative wind.

q.t: Rotation around the vertical axis is called...
q.e: The vertical axis is an imaginary pole passing straight down through the center of the aircraft. When the aircraft spins around this pole (nose moves left or right), the motion is termed yawing.

q.t: Rotation around the lateral axis is called...
q.e: The lateral axis passes horizontally from wingtip to wingtip. When the aircraft's nose moves up to the sky or down to the ground around this axis, the motion is called pitching.

q.t: The critical angle of attack...
o: decreases with a rear centre of gravity.
increases with a front centre of gravity.
is changed by different aircraft weights.
is not changed by different aircraft weights.
q.e: As stressed before, the critical angle of attack is a fixed aerodynamic property of the wing's shape. Regardless of whether the aircraft is heavy, light, turning, or straight, it will always stall at the exact same angle.

q.t: In straight and level flight with constant performance of the engine, the angle of attack at the wing is...
q.e: If power is constant and you want to climb, you must raise the nose, sacrificing speed. Slower speed requires a higher angle of attack to maintain lift. Thus, in level cruise (faster speed), the angle of attack is smaller than in a climb.

q.t: What is the function of the horizontal tail (among other things)?
o: To stabilise the aeroplane around the longitudinal axis
To initiate a curve around the vertical axis
To stabilise the aeroplane around the vertical axis
To stabilise the aeroplane around the lateral axis
q.e: The horizontal tail surfaces (stabilizer and elevator) act like the tail of a see-saw. They provide the necessary downward or upward aerodynamic force to balance the heavy engine and stabilize the pitch (around the lateral axis).

q.t: The elevator deflection during take-off rotation...
o: is increased for a rear centre of gravity.
is increased for a front centre of gravity.
q.e: A forward center of gravity makes the nose of the aircraft very heavy. To pry that heavy nose off the runway during takeoff rotation, the pilot must apply much more back pressure and elevator deflection than normal.

q.t: The elevator moves an aeroplane around the...
q.e: When you pull or push the yoke, the elevator on the tail moves up or down. This pushes the tail up or down, causing the nose to pitch. Pitching is rotation around the wingtip-to-wingtip lateral axis.

q.t: What has to be considered with regard to the center of gravity position?
o: The center of gravity's position can only be determined during flight.
By moving the elevator trim tab, the center of gravity can be shifted into a correct position.
By moving the aileron trim tab, the center of gravity can be shifted into a correct position.
Only correct loading can assure a correct and safe center of gravity position.
q.e: The center of gravity is determined purely by physical mass. Trim tabs only relieve control pressures; they cannot alter physics. You must correctly load luggage and passengers before flight to keep the CG within safe limits.

q.t: Rudder deflections result in a turn of the aeroplane around the...
q.e: Pushing the rudder pedals swings the vertical rudder left or right, which pushes the tail sideways. This causes the nose of the aircraft to sweep left or right, which is a rotation around the vertical axis.

q.t: Deflecting the rudder to the left causes...
o: pitching of the aircraft to the left.
yawing of the aircraft to the right.
pitching of the aircraft to the right.
yawing of the aircraft to the left.
q.e: When you push the left rudder pedal, the rudder surface deflects to the left. The wind hits it and pushes the tail to the right. The nose, pivoting around the CG, consequently swings (yaws) to the left.

q.t: What is the advantage of differential aileron movement?
o: The ratio of the drag coefficient to lift coefficient is increased
The total lift remains constant during aileron deflection
The drag of the downwards deflected aileron is lowered and the adverse yaw is smaller
q.e: When banking, the downward-deflected aileron creates massive drag, yanking the nose opposite to the turn (adverse yaw). Differential ailerons make the upward-moving aileron travel further, balancing the drag and minimizing the yawing tendency.

q.t: Which design feature can compensate for adverse yaw?
q.e: As explained, differential aileron deflection is a mechanical linkage design that specifically combats the dangerous and annoying effects of adverse yaw during turns.

q.t: Differential aileron deflection is used to...
o: avoid a stall at low angles of attack.
q.e: To reiterate, the sole engineering purpose of a differential aileron linkage is to counteract the unequal drag on the wings during a roll, thus keeping adverse yaw to an absolute minimum.

q.t: The right aileron deflects upwards, the left downwards. How does the aircraft react?
o: Rolling to the left, no yawing
Rolling to the right, yawing to the right
Rolling to the left, yawing to the right
Rolling to the right, yawing to the left
q.e: An upward right aileron kills lift on the right wing (it drops). A downward left aileron increases lift on the left wing (it rises). The plane rolls right. However, the downward left aileron makes huge drag, pulling the nose left (adverse yaw). Thus: roll right, yaw left.

q.t: The aerodynamic rudder balance...
