q.e: Aerodynamic balance usually involves a small section of the control surface (like an overhanging horn) protruding ahead of the hinge line. The wind catching this horn physically assists the pilot in moving the rudder, greatly reducing pedal forces.

q.t: Which constructive feature has the purpose to reduce stearing forces?
q.e: Similar to the previous question, the aerodynamic rudder balance (horn balance or inset hinge) is an engineering trick designed specifically to act like "power steering" and lower the physical effort required by the pilot.

q.t: What is the function of the static rudder balance?
o: To limit the control stick forces
To trim the controls almost without any force
To increase the control stick forces
q.e: Static balance involves placing heavy lead weights inside the leading edge of a control surface. This moves its center of gravity to the hinge line, preventing it from entering a deadly aeroelastic vibration known as flutter at high speeds.

q.t: During cruise flight with constant power setting, an aircraft shows a permanent tendency to raise the nose. How can this tendency be eliminated?
o: By shifting the center of gravity backwards
By deflecting the elevator trim tab downwards
By deflecting the elevator trim tab upwards
q.e: If the nose constantly pitches up, the pilot must push the elevator down. To relieve this pushing force, the pilot trims "nose down." This mechanical action actually moves the small trim tab on the elevator UP, which aerodynamicly forces the main elevator DOWN.

q.t: The trim tab at the elevator is defelected upwards. In which position is the corresponding indicator?
q.e: As explained, an upward-deflected trim tab catches the wind and forces the main elevator surface down. A downward elevator forces the tail up, pitching the nose down. The cockpit wheel indicator will thus show "Nose-Down."

q.t: What describes "wing loading"?
q.e: Wing loading is a fundamental aerodynamic parameter. It is calculated by dividing the total weight of the aircraft by the total surface area of its wings (e.g., kilograms per square meter).

q.t: Through which factor listed below does the load factor increase during cruise flight?
q.e: In level flight, load factor is 1G. If the aircraft hits a severe upward gust of wind (turbulence), the wing's angle of attack spikes instantly, generating a massive surge of lift. The occupants feel this as a heavy G-force (increased load factor).

q.t: Which statement regarding the "constant-speed propeller" is correct?
o: The propeller keeps the airspeed constant
The RPM decreases with lower speeds
The set RPM is kept constant by the motor power (MAP)
The pitch of the propeller rises with higher speeds
q.e: A constant-speed propeller works like an automatic car gearbox. As the aircraft flies faster, the governor automatically increases the blade pitch (taking a "bigger bite" of air) to prevent the engine from overspeeding, thus maintaining a constant RPM.

q.t: The change in pitch at a propeller blade from the root to the tip ensures...
o: that the most thrust is produced at the blade tip.
that the most thrust is produced at the blade root.
the largest possible angle of attack at the blade tip.
a nearly constant load by a constant effective angle of attack over the entire length of the blade.
q.e: The tip of a propeller spins much faster than the root. To prevent the tip from stalling and the root from doing nothing, the blade is twisted. This washout guarantees an even angle of attack and thrust distribution across the entire blade.

q.t: After an engine failure, the windmilling propeller...
o: has a greater pitch in feathered position.
improves the properties of the glide.
q.e: If the engine dies, the oncoming air physically forces the flat propeller blades to keep spinning like a windmill. This process extracts enormous amounts of energy from the aircraft's momentum, acting like a giant airbrake (massive drag).

q.t: During a descent at idle power with constant speed, the propeller lever is moved backwards. How do the propeller pitch and sink rate change?
o: Propeller pitch is increased, sink rate is increased
Propeller pitch is decreased, sink rate is increased
Propeller pitch is decreased, sink rate is decreased
Propeller pitch is increased, sink rate is decreased
q.e: Moving the blue prop lever back sets a lower RPM, which forces the blades into a coarse pitch (higher angle). A coarse pitch blade slicing through the air creates less windmilling drag than a flat disc, making the aircraft glide better (sink rate decreases).

q.t: Point number 1 in the figure indicates which flight state? (Refer to a Lift/Drag polar curve, point at bottom negative area)
q.e: On a classic Lift/Drag polar curve, the vertical axis is Lift (CL). A point that lies below the horizontal zero-lift line represents negative lift. The only way an aircraft sustains flight with negative lift is during inverted (upside-down) flight.

q.t: Point number 5 in the figure indicates which flight state? (Refer to the absolute peak of a Lift/Drag polar curve)
q.e: The highest peak on the polar curve represents the absolute maximum lift coefficient (CL max). If the angle of attack is increased beyond this point, lift falls off sharply. This peak represents the point of Stall.

q.t: The bank in a two-minute turn (rate one turn) depends on the...
q.e: A Rate 1 turn means the aircraft turns 360 degrees in exactly 2 minutes (3 degrees per second). A slow Cessna can do this with a shallow 15-degree bank. A fast jet doing 400 knots must bank steeply (e.g. 60 degrees) to turn that tightly. It depends strictly on True Airspeed (TAS).

q.t: In a co-ordinated turn, how is the relation between the load factor (n) and the stall speed (Vs)?
o: n is smaller than 1, Vs is smaller than in straight and level flight.
n is smaller than 1, Vs is greater than in straight and level flight.
n is greater than 1, Vs is smaller than in straight and level flight.
n is greater than 1, Vs is greater than in straight and level flight.
q.e: In a turn, you must generate extra lift to hold altitude against centrifugal force, so the load factor (G-force / n) is greater than 1. Because the wings are working harder (virtually heavier aircraft), the critical stall speed (Vs) increases.

q.t: How is the balance of forces affected during a turn?
o: A lower lift force compensates for a lower net force as compared to level flight
The horizontal component of the lift force during a turn is the centrifugal force
The net force results from superposition of gravity and centripetal forces
Lift force must be increased to compensate for the sum of centrifugal and gravitational force
q.e: When you bank, your lift vector tilts. The vertical part of the lift must still counteract gravity (weight), while the horizontal part pulls you through the turn. Thus, the total lift force must be physically increased (by pulling back on the yoke) to handle both jobs.

q.t: The pressure compensation between wind upper and lower surface results in ...
o: profile drag by wing tip vortices.
laminar airflow by wing tip vortices.
induced drag by wing tip vortices.
q.e: At the wingtips, the high-pressure air from the bottom sneaks around the edge into the low-pressure area on top. This "short circuit" creates violent spinning tornadoes of air (wingtip vortices), which require energy from the aircraft and generate massive induced drag.

q.t: What is meant by "ground effect"?
o: Decrease of lift and increase of induced drag close to the ground
Decrease of lift and decrease of induced drag close to the ground
Increase of lift and increase of induced drag close to the ground
Increase of lift and decrease of induced drag close to the ground
q.e: When flying within half a wingspan of the runway, the solid ground physically blocks the large wingtip vortices from forming fully. Without these huge vortices, induced drag plummets, making the aircraft feel like it's floating on an air cushion with extra lift.

q.t: What is the diffeence between spin and spiral dive?
o: Spin: stall at outer wing, speed constant; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed increasing rapidly
Spin: stall at outer wing, speed increasing rapidly; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed constant
Spin: stall at inner wing, speed increasing rapidly; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed constant
Spin: stall at inner wing, speed constant; Spiral dive: airflow at both wings, speed increasing rapidly
q.e: A spin is a stalled condition where the inner wing is deeply stalled; the aircraft autorotates downward, but the massive drag keeps airspeed constant and low. A spiral dive is NOT a stall; the wings are flying, the nose is pointed down, and airspeed builds up dangerously and rapidly.

q.t: The term "flight time" is defined as...
o: the total time from the first take-off until the last landing in conjunction with one or more consecutive flights.
the period from engine start for the purpose of taking off to leaving the aircraft after engine shutdown.
the total time from the first aircraft movement until the moment it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight.
the period from the start of the take-off run to the final touchdown when landing.
q.e: Flight time (often referred to as block time) officially begins when the aircraft first moves under its own power for the purpose of taking off, and ends when it comes to rest after landing.

q.t: What should be considered regarding a scheduled flight over water, when land cannot be reached in case of an emergency landing?
o: For all passengers there must be life jackets or lifeboats present
Contact to the nearest ATC shall consist during the whole flight
The flight plan has to contain the exact waypoints
Transponder code 7600 has to be set during the whole flight
q.e: Aviation regulations strictly require that if a flight over water extends beyond gliding distance to a safe landing spot on land, flotation devices (life jackets/rafts) must be carried for all occupants.

q.t: Which of the items below may have an influence on the noise perceived by a person on the ground? 1) Engine power setting 2) Propeller revolutions per minute 3) Position of the landing gear 4) Flap position 5) Flight track 6) Height above ground 7) Flight rules
q.e: The noise footprint is influenced by the power/RPM of the engine (source noise), aerodynamic drag creators like flaps and gear (airframe noise), and the aircraft's distance/track from the observer. Flight rules (VFR/IFR) are just administrative and do not create noise.

q.t: How can the pilot of an an engine-driven aircraft minimise the noise emission during descent and approach?
o: Descent and approach in landing configuration while maintaining a descent angle of 3°, direct approach whenever possible
Low approach with minimum power setting, late configuration and steep approach, adherence to established arrival routes
High approach with minimum power setting, late descent, late configuration, adherence to established arrival routes
Normal approach with normal power setting, configuration prior to initiating descent, shortest possible arrival route
q.e: To minimize noise (Noise Abatement), the pilot should stay as high as possible for as long as possible (late descent), use minimum engine power, and delay extending noisy drag devices (flaps/gear) until absolutely necessary.

q.t: When should turns at low altitudes above villages be avoided with regard to noise abatement procedures?
q.e: During a climb, the engine is at maximum continuous power, the propeller is at high RPM, and the nose is pitched up, directing the maximum amount of engine and exhaust noise straight down toward the ground.

q.t: How should departures near villages be carried out?
o: Climb and changes in direction should be done as slow as possible
Villages should be circumnavigated and crossed in a sufficient altitude
Low and fast between the villages
Slow with a low propeller rotation speed
q.e: To be a good neighbor and adhere to basic noise abatement, populated areas should be avoided (circumnavigated) immediately after takeoff, or only crossed once a sufficient, quiet altitude is reached.

q.t: Which kind of engine is susceptible to carburettor fire?
q.e: A carburetor is a device that mixes air and fuel. This component is exclusively found on (older or simpler) spark-ignition piston engines. Turbines and electric motors do not use carburetors.

q.t: Why is it dangerous to pump the throttle for engine start in cold weather?
o: It may cause a carburettor fire
The engine might start with not enough power
q.e: Pumping the throttle squirts raw, unvaporized fuel directly into the intake via the accelerator pump. If the engine "backfires" (coughs backwards) during startup, this pooled fuel will easily ignite, causing an induction fire.

q.t: Which danger exists during engine start?
q.e: Similar to the previous question, the most common and immediate specific hazard during the startup of a piston engine (especially if over-primed) is a carburetor fire.

q.t: May an engine, which previously was on fire, be restarted?
o: Yes, but only if the cause of the fire was a carburettor fire during engine start
Yes, but only on the ground for the purpose of taxiing
No, the risk of a reignition of the fire would be too high
Yes, if the aircraft is flying at a safe altitude
q.e: An engine fire severely damages fuel lines, wiring insulation, and seals. Attempting to restart it will simply pump highly pressurized fuel into a compromised engine bay, almost guaranteeing a catastrophic reignition.

q.t: Which gas is most dangerous during an engine fire?
q.e: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a deadly byproduct of incomplete combustion. It is extremely dangerous because it is colorless, odorless, and rapidly prevents blood from carrying oxygen, incapacitating the pilot.

q.t: Smoke enters the cockpit during an engine fire. Which actions have to be taken immediately?
o: Switching off the heating and the ventilating system
Switching off the pitot and front window heating
Switching off the avionics and the cabin lighting
Switching off the master switch and the ignition
q.e: In small aircraft, the cabin heater draws air from a shroud around the engine exhaust. If the engine is on fire, the heater and ventilators will pump toxic smoke directly into the cockpit. They must be shut off instantly.

q.t: What should be the first action in case of a cable fire during a flight?
q.e: An electrical/cable fire is fed by the electrical current flowing through a short circuit. The immediate priority is to isolate the power source by turning off the Master Switch (Battery and Alternator).

q.t: What extinguishing agent is the least suitable for an aircraft fire?
q.e: Aircraft fires usually involve aviation fuel, oil, and live electricity. Water conducts electricity (worsening short circuits) and will simply spread burning fuel instead of extinguishing it.

q.t: In flight, a little smoke emerges from behind the instrument panel. An electrical fire is suspected. Which action, with respect to the pilot's operating manual, should be taken?
q.e: As previously noted, smoke from behind the instrument panel indicates burning wire insulation. The very first response must be to kill all electrical power by turning off the Master Switch.

q.t: In flight, a little smoke emerges from behind the instrument panel. An engine fire is suspected. Which action, with respect to the pilot's operating manual, should be taken?
q.e: If the smoke smells like oil or exhaust (engine fire), the immediate step is to stop that smoke from being drawn into the cabin by shutting off the cabin heat and ventilation systems.

q.t: A wind shear is...
o: a wind speed change of more than 15 kt.
a meteorological downslope wind phenomenon in the alps.
a vertical or horizontal change of wind speed and wind direction.
a slow increase of the wind speed in altitudes above 13000 ft.
q.e: Wind shear is the meteorological definition for a sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or wind direction over a very short distance, either vertically or horizontally.

q.t: Which weather phenomenon is typically associated with wind shear?
q.e: The most severe and dangerous wind shears (including microbursts and gust fronts) are generated by the massive, violent downdrafts falling from Cumulonimbus (thunderstorm) clouds.

q.t: When do you expect wind shear?
o: During a summer day with calm winds
In calm wind in cold weather
q.e: A strong temperature inversion (especially near the surface) acts like a lid. The air below the inversion might be dead calm, while just above it, a strong low-level jet stream is blowing. Flying through this boundary causes severe wind shear.

q.t: During an approach the aeroplane experiences a windshear with a decreasing headwind. If the pilot does not make any corrections, how do the approach path and the indicated airspeed (IAS) change?
q.e: If your headwind suddenly dies, the aircraft instantly loses relative airflow over the wings. The Indicated Airspeed (IAS) drops, lift decreases, and the aircraft will sink below the intended glide path (Path is lower).

q.t: During an approach the aeroplane experiences a windshear with an increasing headwind. If the pilot does not make any corrections, how do the approach path and the indicated airspeed (IAS) change?
q.e: If the headwind suddenly surges, the wings instantly feel a faster relative airflow. The IAS shoots up, generating extra lift, which causes the aircraft to balloon above the intended glide path (Path is higher).

q.t: During an approach the aeroplane experiences a windshear with a decreasing tailwind. If the pilot does not make any corrections, how do the approach path and the indicated airspeed (IAS) change?
q.e: A sudden decrease in tailwind has the exact same aerodynamic effect as a sudden increase in headwind. The aircraft gains relative airflow, IAS increases, and the extra lift forces the aircraft above the glide path (Path is higher).

q.t: After take-off an aeroplane gets into a wind shear with decreasing headwind. As a result...
o: the aeroplane flies above the estimated climb path.
the aeroplane flies below the estimated climb path.
q.e: Losing a headwind shortly after takeoff robs the aircraft of vital airspeed and lift. Because the plane now has less lift than required for the planned climb, it sags and flies below the expected climb path.

q.t: How may windshear be recognised in flight?
o: Sudden and apparently baseless change in altitude, airspeed, rate of climb or descent.
Rather unexpected onset of drizzle associated with high stratus clouds following previously clear skies and calm conditions.
Sudden and apparently baseless change of oilpressure, oil temperature, engine speed and altitude.
Sudden and apparently baseless change in heading, turning rate, engine speed or oil temperature.
q.e: Wind shear physically throws the aircraft around. You will recognize it by abrupt, uncommanded fluctuations on your pitot-static instruments: the airspeed indicator jumps, the VSI swings wildly, and altitude changes unexpectedly.

q.t: Which phenomenon may be expected at point 2 of the microburst? (Refer to a diagram showing an aircraft exactly under the center of a downdraft)
q.e: Point 2 is in the very core of the microburst. Here, a massive column of cold air is slamming straight down. The aircraft is pushed forcefully towards the ground, severely crippling its ability to climb (Decrease of climb rate).

q.t: Which phenomenon may be expected at point 3 of the miroburst? (Refer to a diagram showing an aircraft exiting the microburst)
q.e: At point 3, the aircraft is flying out of the microburst. The air spreading out along the ground is now hitting the aircraft from behind as a massive tailwind. This completely destroys relative airflow, causing a drastic decrease in airspeed.

q.t: How can a wind shear encounter in flight be avoided?
o: Avoid take-offs and landings in mountainous terrain and stay in flat country whenever possible
Avoid thermally active areas, particularly during summer, or stay below these areas
Avoid areas of precipitation, particularly during winter, and choose low flight altitudes
Avoid take-off and landing during the passage of heavy showers or thunderstorms
q.e: Because the most lethal wind shear and microbursts are generated by the heavy downdrafts of storms, the only reliable way to avoid them is to absolutely refuse to take off or land when thunderstorms or heavy showers are nearby.

q.t: What action should be taken when entering a windshear? 1. Reduce speed 2. Retract gear and flaps 3. Maintain current configuration 4. Adjust thrust
q.e: The standard wind shear escape maneuver is: firewall the throttle (Adjust thrust/max power) and DO NOT change the flaps or gear (Maintain current configuration), because retracting flaps would cause a fatal loss of lift.

q.t: After lift-off, a much stronger than expected airspeed rise is experienced during the initial climb phase. What may be expected if the aeroplane entered a microburst?
o: A decreased climb rate and decreased airspeed
An increased climb rate and airspeed
An increased climb rate and decreased airspeed
A decreased climb rate and increased airspeed
q.e: A microburst acts like a trap. Initially, you fly into the strong headwind outflow, which gives a false surge in airspeed and climb. Seconds later, you hit the core downdraft and the tailwind outflow on the other side, suffering a deadly decrease in both climb rate and airspeed.

q.t: Immediately after lift-off, a microburst is entered inadvertently. Which action might avoid an unintentional descent?
o: Set maximum power, retract landing gear and flaps, increase pitch until attaining optimum climb speed
Set maximum power, maintain present aircraft configuration, pick up speed in an attempt to leave the area of the microburst as fast as possible
Set maximum power, retract landing gear and flaps, pick up speed and perform a left or a right turn in an attempt to leave the area of the microburst on the shortest way
Set maximum power, maintain present aircraft configuration, climb at the best rate of climb speed
q.e: If caught in a microburst upon takeoff, the pilot must apply absolute maximum power, keep the flaps and gear exactly where they are (to avoid lift loss), and pitch up to maintain the best rate of climb speed (Vy) to fight the downdraft.

q.t: Wake turbulences develop during take-off just as the aeroplane...
o: lifts off with the front gear.
lifts off with the main gear.
q.e: Wake turbulence (wingtip vortices) only exists when the wings are generating heavy lift. During the takeoff roll, the wings aren't lifting the plane. Vortices only start forming the moment the nose is raised (rotation) and the wings bite into the air to lift the main gear.

q.t: Wake turbulence is caused by...
o: turbulence at the downwind side of a mountain range.
jet blast behind a turbine engine.
wind shear at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
pressure compensation at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
q.e: Lift works because of high pressure under the wing and low pressure on top. At the wingtip, this high pressure violently escapes around the edge to the low-pressure side, creating a swirling vortex (pressure compensation).

q.t: Wake turbulence is particularly strong...
q.e: To keep a heavy aircraft in the air at slow speeds (like during approach or takeoff), it must fly at a very high angle of attack. This huge angle of attack creates a massive pressure differential, which spawns the most violent and powerful vortices.

q.t: Wake turbulence is particularly strong...
q.e: The heavier the aircraft, the more lift it must generate to stay airborne. Generating more lift requires moving more air with a greater pressure differential, thus a heavy aircraft leaves behind significantly stronger wake turbulence.

q.t: The intensity of wake turbulence depends on...
q.e: The primary and most dominant factor determining the strength of wingtip vortices is the actual gross weight of the generating aircraft. This is why ATC spacing is strictly based on Wake Turbulence Categories (Light, Medium, Heavy).

q.t: Two aircraft of the same type, same grossweight and same configuration fly at different airspeeds. Which aircraft will cause more severe wake turbulence?
o: The aircraft flying at lower altitude.
The aircraft flying at higher altitude.
The aircraft flying at higher speed.
The aircraft flying at slower speed.
q.e: As established, the slower an aircraft flies, the higher its angle of attack must be to maintain lift. A higher angle of attack spills more air over the wingtips, generating much more severe wake turbulence.

q.t: Two aircraft of the same type, same gross weight and same flap configuration fly with different speeds and altitude. Which aircraft will cause more wake turbulence?
o: The aircraft flying at lower speed.
The aircraft flying at a lower altitude
The aircraft flying at a higher altitude
The aircraft flying at higher speed.
q.e: Altitude is practically irrelevant for the generation of vortices. The aircraft flying at the lower speed will require the higher angle of attack, and thus will generate the more powerful wake turbulence.

q.t: With only a slight crosswind, what is the danger at take-off after the departure of a heavy aeroplane?
o: Wake turbulence twisting transverse to the runway.
Wake turbulence is amplified and distorted.
Wake turbulence rotate faster and higher.
Wake turbulence on or near the runway.
q.e: Normally, vortices sink and drift outward from the runway centerline. However, a light crosswind (3-5 knots) will counteract the outward drift of the upwind vortex, holding it completely stationary and invisible directly over the runway centerline.

q.t: A light aircraft intends to land behind a commercial airliner belonging to wake turbulence category "medium" or "heavy" on a long runway. How can the wake turbulence of the commercial aircraft be avoided?
o: By making a shallow approach and a very short landing. The light aircraft should be able to stop before reaching the airliner's touchdown point
By making a shallow approach and a long landing, touching down behind the touchdown point of the airliner's nose gear
By making a steep approach and a very short landing. The light aircraft should be able to stop before reaching the airliner's touchdown point
By making a steep approach and a long landing, touching down behind the touchdown point of the airliner's nose gear
q.e: Vortices sink below the flight path of the heavy aircraft and stop forming when its nose gear touches down. To stay safe, the light aircraft must stay ABOVE the heavy's glide path and land BEYOND its touchdown point.

q.t: What should be observed when taxiing behind a commercial airliner?
o: To avoid wake turbulence, a minimum distance of 700 m should be maintained
To avoid wake turbulence, a minimum distance of 300 m should be maintained
To avoid the jet blast, a minimum distance of 600 m should be maintained
To avoid the jet blast, a minimum distance of 200 m should be maintained
q.e: On the ground, wake turbulence is not the issue; the danger is the exhaust coming out of the jet engines (Jet Blast), which has the force of a hurricane. A light aircraft must keep a safe distance of at least 200 meters to avoid being flipped over.

q.t: A technical fault requires an emergency off-field landing. Which steps, with respect to the pilot's operating handbook, are necessary?
o: Declare an emergency, complete the applicable emergency procedure, cover as much distance towards the airport as possible to be closer to the rescue forces.
Reduce speed and configure the aircraft for landing in an attempt to gain time, declare an emergency, complete the applicable emergency procedure and execute an emergency landing.
Inform air traffic control and request technical support, check the pilot's operating handbook for a reference on the matter and execute an emergency landing.
Locate a suitable landing area, plan the approach, complete the applicable emergency procedure, declare an emergency, start and concentrate on the approach in due time.
q.e: Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. First, fly the plane and pick a field. Plan how you will reach it, run your memory checklists to try and fix the problem, call Mayday if you have time, and then focus 100% on the landing.

q.t: Which method is appropriate to approach an unprepared landing field?
o: Steep approach to keep the noise level low
Fast approach, performance check, and landing within a quick stop
Flat direct approach to ensure visual ground contact
Terrain investigation to determine approach points and landing
q.e: If you have engine power (a precautionary landing), you must never just dive into a random field. You must do a low pass (terrain investigation) to check for hidden ditches, wires, slope, and wind direction before committing to land.

q.t: Which area is suitable for an off-field landing?
q.e: A freshly plowed field will flip an airplane on its back. Sports areas are usually fenced or full of people. A harvested cornfield (stubble field) provides a long, flat, relatively firm, and predictable surface for a forced landing.

q.t: An emergency landing is a landing...
o: conducted in an attempt to keep up safety regarding an aircraft and its occupants.
conducted without power from the engine.
conducted in response to circumstances forcing the aircraft to land.
q.e: An emergency landing (Forced Landing) is dictated by absolute necessity. The aircraft has suffered a catastrophic failure (e.g., engine failure, structural damage) and the pilot has no choice but to put it on the ground immediately.

q.t: A landing conducted in response to circumstances forcing the aircraft to land is a / an...
q.e: As defined above, when circumstances dictate that the aircraft cannot maintain flight and MUST land immediately regardless of the terrain below, it is an emergency landing.

q.t: A precautionary landing is a landing...
o: conducted without power from the engine.
conducted in response to circumstances forcing the aircraft to land.
conducted in an attempt to sustain flight safety.
q.e: A precautionary landing is a choice made by a pilot whose aircraft is still fully functional. The pilot decides to land in a field to prevent a worsening situation (like encroaching darkness, deteriorating weather, or low fuel) from turning into a disaster.

q.t: Which of the following landing areas is most suitable for an off-field landing?
o: A field with ripe waving crops
A lake with an undisturbed surface
A light brown field with short crops
q.e: Tall crops conceal deep ruts, boulders, and tractors. A lake requires ditching. A meadow without livestock is good, but a light brown field with short crops implies a dry, firm, harvested surface with excellent visibility of any obstacles.

q.t: How does the pilot prepare for a VFR flight over a large distance of water, when it is unlikely that land can be reached in case of an engine failure?
o: File a flight plan including the exact way-points.
Be prepared to fly with transponder only.
Maintain continuous radio contact with ATC.
Carry life vests or a life raft for all occupants.
q.e: Aviation law mandates that survival equipment must be carried when flying beyond gliding distance of the shore. Carrying life vests or a life raft for every person on board is a strict legal and survival requirement.

q.t: Which items should a passenger briefing in case of an imminent emergency landing include?
o: Blood type of the other aircraft occupants, location of the first-aid kit
How to read an emergency checklist, how to cut the engine, telephone number of the home airport
How to work the aircraft radio, emergency transponder squawk, telephone number of the competent search and rescue (SAR) center
Nature of the emergency, intentions, safety position, evacuation routes, actions after landing
q.e: This is the classic NITS briefing (Nature, Intentions, Time, Special instructions). Passengers must know what is happening, what the brace position is, how to open the doors, and to run away from the aircraft once it stops.

q.t: After a precautionary landing the brakes and wheels are very hot. In which way should the pilot approach them?
o: From the right or left side
From the front, right or left side
From the front or back side
q.e: Overheated brakes can cause the wheel rims to fail or the tire sidewalls to explode outward with lethal force. The sidewalls (left and right) are the weak points, so you must always approach a hot wheel from the front or back.

q.t: What needs to be observed in conjunction with overheated brakes?
o: The affected tyres may burst in radial direction or direction of rotation
The wheel fairing shall be taken off to increase the cooldown
The affected brakes need to be cooled down with halon
The affected tyres may burst in axial direction
q.e: When brake discs glow red hot, they melt the tire bead and the weak sidewall of the tire. The massive pressure inside the tire will cause it to violently blow out sideways (axially, along the axle).

q.t: In case of an emergency ditching, the life vests have to be inflated...
o: after disembarking the aircraft at a safe distance of about 10 m.
q.e: If you inflate the life vest inside a sinking cabin, the buoyancy will pin you violently against the ceiling of the aircraft. You will be trapped and unable to swim down to the door to escape. You must exit first, then inflate.

q.t: What are the effects of wet grass on the take-off and landing distance?
o: Decrease of the take-off distance and increase of the landing distance
Increase of the take-off distance and decrease of the landing distance
Decrease of the take-off distance and decrease of the landing distance
Increase of the take-off distance and increase of the landing distance
q.e: Wet grass is soft, so the wheels sink in, creating massive rolling resistance that severely lengthens the takeoff run. During landing, wet grass acts like ice; the brakes lock up and the aircraft slides, severely lengthening the landing roll.

q.t: Under which circumstances may a runway be considered to be contaminated?
o: When more than 50% of the required runway length and width are covered by contaminants such as snow, frost, ice or sand
When 75% of the required runway length and width are covered by contaminants such as snow, frost, ice or sand
When more than 50% of the runway surface area within the required length and width being used is covered by water, slush, snow or ice more than 3 mm deep
When more than 25% of the runway surface area within the required length and width being used is covered by water, slush, snow or ice more than 3 mm deep
q.e: ICAO strictly defines a runway as "contaminated" when more than 25% of the assessed surface area is covered by standing water, slush, or loose snow that is deeper than 3 millimeters.

q.t: What minimum coverage with ice or snow must be given to call a runway "contaminated"?
q.e: Derived directly from the ICAO definition in the previous question: a runway condition changes from wet/damp to legally "contaminated" when the coverage of the hazardous material exceeds 25%.

q.t: Wet snow on a runway can lead to...
q.e: As the aircraft accelerates, the tires must physically plow through and displace the heavy, dense, wet snow. This acts like a massive brake on the wheels, greatly increasing rolling resistance and sluggishly delaying takeoff speed.

q.t: What danger does standing water on the runway pose to aircraft?
q.e: Exactly like wet snow, deep puddles of standing water force the landing gear to plow through a dense fluid. This creates heavy aerodynamic and physical drag on the tires, severely increasing rolling resistance during the takeoff roll.

q.t: Which danger exists after a heavy rain shower for a landing aircraft?
o: Displacement of the tire slip marking
Decreased braking distance due to aquaplaning
Longer braking distance due to aquaplaning
q.e: Heavy rain leaves a sheet of water on the runway. A fast-landing aircraft's tires cannot push the water away fast enough and ride up on a film of water (aquaplaning). With zero rubber-to-asphalt contact, the brakes do absolutely nothing, lengthening the stop.

q.t: Which would be the correct reaction when hydroplaning is suspected upon landing?
o: Apply maximum braking to reduce aircraft speed to less than hydroplaning speed, then continue normal ground roll
Cross rudder and aileron controls in order to use the aircraft fuselage to brake aerodynamically
Add power and use flaps and spoilers to brake aerodynamically
If all wheels are in motion, brake moderately. Maintain directional control by aerodynamic means
q.e: If you slam on the brakes while aquaplaning, the wheels will lock, the tires will burn, and you will spin out of control. You must stay off the brakes, steer gently with the aerodynamic rudder, and wait for the plane to slow down enough for the tires to cut through the water.

q.t: How should a landing on a contaminated runway be conducted if it proves to be inevitable?
o: Approach with the minimum crosswind component possible, use minimum flaps, touch down softly with minimum speed, do not apply brakes
Approach with the minimum crosswind component possible, use maximum flaps, touch down with negative pitch and minimum speed, brake carefully
Approach with the minimum crosswind component possible, use minimum flaps, touch down softly with positive pitch and minimum speed, do not apply brakes
Approach with the minimum crosswind component possible, use maximum flaps, touch down firmly with minimum speed, brake carefully
q.e: When landing on slush or water, you need to touch down firmly (to punch through the water layer to the tarmac) with the lowest possible ground speed (maximum flaps). Avoid crosswinds, as sliding sideways on a slick runway is uncontrollable.

q.t: During final approach, the glider pilot realizes a very bumpy surface on a selected off-field landing site. What technique may be recommended for landing?
o: Touch down with minimum speed, compensate different ground levels with power lever
Approach with increased speed, push elevetor upon first ground contact
Touch down with minimum speed, keep elevator pulled until full stop
Approach with increased speed, avoid using wheel brakes
q.e: When landing on a very rough, bumpy, or soft off-field surface, the goal is to touch down at the absolute minimum forward speed to reduce impact forces. Keeping the elevator fully pulled back (full aft yoke/stick) aerodynamicly holds the weight off the fragile nose wheel as long as possible and prevents the aircraft from flipping over (nose-over) when hitting bumps.

q.t: A flight plan has been filed for a flight departing at an uncontrolled aerodrome. When has the actual take-off time been transmitted to ATC?
o: At deviation from expected off-block time by more than 15 min.
q.e: For a flight departing from an uncontrolled aerodrome (where no tower exists to automatically activate the flight plan), the pilot is strictly responsible for transmitting the actual departure time (DEP) to the Flight Information Service (FIS) or ATC immediately after take-off.

q.t: During a flight with a flight plan submitted, landing is conducted at an airfield other than the destination stated in the filed flight plan. Who has to be contacted by the pilot immediately?
q.e: If you land at an alternate aerodrome instead of your filed destination, the destination ATC will not know you have arrived safely and will trigger Search and Rescue (SAR) operations after 30 minutes. You must immediately contact AIS or FIS to close your flight plan.

q.t: Exceeding the maximum allowed aircraft mass is...
o: only relevant if the excess is more than 10%.
compensated by the pilot's control inputs.
q.e: Maximum Take-Off Mass (MTOM) is an absolute structural and aerodynamic limitation. Exceeding it is strictly prohibited and extremely dangerous, as it can cause structural failure, drastically increased stall speeds, and an inability to climb.

q.t: The center of gravity has to be located...
o: in front of the front C.G. limit.
right of the lateral C. G. limit.
between the front and the rear C.G. limit.
q.e: The Center of Gravity (CG) must always remain within the certified CG envelope, meaning strictly between the approved forward (front) and aft (rear) limits, to ensure that the aircraft remains stable and aerodynamically controllable at all times.

q.t: The result of a rear C.G. position is...
q.e: An aft (rear) Center of Gravity brings the CG closer to the Center of Pressure. This reduces the restoring moment of the tail, making the aircraft highly maneuverable but dangerously unstable and very difficult to recover from a stall or spin.

q.t: An aircraft must be loaded and operated in such a way that the center of gravity (CG) stays within the approved limits during all phases of flight. This is done to ensure...
o: that the aircraft does not exceed the maximum permissible airspeed during a descent.
both stability and controllability of the aircraft.
that the aircraft does not tip over on its tail while it is being loaded.
that the aircraft does not stall.
q.e: The entire purpose of weight and balance limits is aerodynamic safety. Staying within the CG envelope ensures that the aircraft maintains positive longitudinal stability and that the elevator has sufficient control authority (controllability) to pitch the nose as needed.

q.t: The result of a front C.G. position is: 1. Increase in stability. 2. Increase in fuel consumption. 3. Increase in stall speed. 4. Increase in range.
q.e: A forward CG increases longitudinal stability (1). However, the tail must push down harder to keep the heavy nose up, which drastically increases aerodynamic drag, leading to higher fuel consumption (2) and a higher stall speed (3). Range is decreased, not increased.

q.t: The basic empty mass of an aircraft includes...
o: the total mass of the aeroplane ready for a specific type of operation including crew, navigation instruments and engine cowling.
the total mass of an aeroplane ready for a specific type of operation including the required fuel and crew, but excluding traffic load.
the total mass of the aeroplane ready for a specific type of operation excluding unusable fuel and traffic load. The mass includes items such as crew and crew baggage.

the mass of the aeroplane plus standard items such as unusable fuel and other unusable liquids, lubricating oil in engine and auxiliary units, fire extinguishers, pyrotechnics, emergency oxygen equipment, supplementary electronic equipment.
q.e: Basic Empty Mass (BEM) is the weight of the bare aircraft directly from the factory or scales. It includes fixed optional equipment, full operating fluids (like engine oil and hydraulic fluid), and the unusable fuel trapped in the lines, but no crew, passengers, or usable fuel.

q.t: The empty weight and the corresponding center of gravity (CG) of an aircraft are initially determined...
o: for one aircraft of a type only, since all aircraft of the same type have the same mass and CG position.
through data provided by the aircraft manufacturer.
q.e: No two aircraft of the same type are exactly identical due to manufacturing tolerances, paint thickness, and installed equipment. Therefore, the very first empty weight and CG position must be determined by physically placing the aircraft on calibrated scales.

q.t: The density of AVGAS 100LL at 15° C is...
q.e: Aviation gasoline (Avgas 100LL) is lighter than water. For standard mass and balance calculations, its density at standard temperature (15°C) is defined as 0.72 kilograms per liter.

q.t: The conversion factor from kilogram [kg] into pounds [lb] is...
q.e: One pound (lb) is equal to approximately 0.4536 kilograms. To convert from a heavier unit (kg) to a lighter unit (lb), you must multiply the kilogram value by 2.205.

q.t: Baggage and cargo must be properly stowed and fastened, otherwise a shift of the cargo may cause...
o: continuous attitudes which can be corrected by the pilot using the flight controls.
calculable instability if the C.G. is shifting by less than 10 %.
uncontrollable attitudes, structural damage, risk of injuries.
structural damage, angle of attack stability, velocity stability.
q.e: If heavy baggage shifts backward or forward during turbulence or climb, it instantly relocates the CG. This can move the CG outside of the safe envelope, causing violent, uncontrollable pitching attitudes and endangering the structural integrity of the aircraft.

q.t: Loads must be adequately secured in order to...
o: prevent excessive 'g'-loading during the landing flare.
avoid any centre of gravity (C.G.) movements.
q.e: Tie-down straps and cargo nets are used strictly to lock items into their designated "arms" (stations) within the cabin, ensuring that the carefully calculated Center of Gravity does not shift during flight maneuvers.

q.t: The total weight of an aeroplane is acting vertically through the...
q.e: In physics, the Center of Gravity (CG) is the theoretical point where the entire mass of an object is considered to be concentrated. Therefore, the total gravitational weight of the aircraft acts vertically downwards through this exact point.

q.t: The term "center of gravity" is defined as...
o: the point at which the total mass of the aeroplane is considered to act.
the heaviest point on an aeroplane.
half the distance between the neutral point and the datum line.
another designation for the neutral point.
q.e: As stated previously, the Center of Gravity is the centralized balance point of an object where its total mass is assumed to be concentrated and where gravitational forces apply.

q.t: The center of gravity (CG) defines...
o: the point on the longitudinal axis or its extension from which the centers of gravity of all masses are referenced.
the distance from the datum to the position of a mass.
the point through which the force of gravity is said to act on a mass.
the product of mass and balance arm.
q.e: This is a rephrased version of the same concept. The CG is the precise point in 3D space through which the Earth's force of gravity pulls downward on the entire mass of the aircraft.

q.t: During an unaccelerated flight...
o: thrust equals drag and lift equals gravity.
thrust equals the sum of drag and gravity.
drag equals lift and thrust equals gravity.
thrust equals lift and drag equals gravity.
q.e: In steady, unaccelerated (constant speed and altitude) level flight, Newton's first law applies: all opposing forces are perfectly balanced. The forward thrust exactly equals the rearward drag, and the upward lift exactly equals the downward weight (gravity).

q.t: The term "datum" with regard to a mass and balance calculation defines...
o: the distance from the reference plane to the center of gravity of an aircraft.
the point on the vertical axis of an aeroplane or its extension from which the centers of gravity of all masses are referenced.
the point on the lateral axis of an aeroplane or its extension from which the centers of gravity of all masses are referenced.
the point on the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane or its extension from which the centers of gravity of all masses are referenced.
q.e: The Reference Datum is an imaginary vertical plane (or point on the longitudinal axis) arbitrarily chosen by the manufacturer, from which all horizontal distances (arms) for CG calculations are measured.

q.t: The term "moment" with regard to a mass and balance calculation is referred to as...
o: difference of a mass and a balance arm.
sum of a mass and a balance arm.
product of a mass and a balance arm.
quotient of a mass and a balance arm.
q.e: In physics, a moment (torque or turning force) is calculated by multiplying the magnitude of the force (mass or weight) by the distance from the fulcrum (the balance arm). Moment = Mass × Arm.

q.t: The term "balance arm" in the context of a mass and balance calculation defines the...
o: point through which the force of gravity is said to act on a mass.
distance of a mass from the center of gravity.
point on the longitudinal axis of an aeroplane or its extension from which the centers of gravity of all masses are referenced.
distance from the datum to the center of gravity of a mass.
q.e: The balance arm (or station) is the exact horizontal distance measured from the reference datum line to the center of gravity of a specific item (like a passenger, baggage, or fuel tank) loaded on the aircraft.

q.t: The distance between the center of gravity and the datum is called...
q.e: Whether it refers to a single piece of luggage or the final calculated balance point of the entire loaded aircraft, the measured distance from the zero-point (Datum) is always called the Balance Arm.

q.t: The balance arm is the horizontal distance between...
o: the front C.G. limit and the rear C.G. limit.
the front C.G. limit and the datum line.
the C.G. of a mass and the rear C.G. limit.
the C.G. of a mass and the datum line.
q.e: This is another way of defining the term. The arm is the physical length of the "lever" stretching from the reference datum line to the center of gravity of the loaded mass.

q.t: The required data for a mass and balance calculation including masses and balance arms can be found in the...
o: performance section of the pilot's operating handbook of this particular aircraft.
mass and balance section of the pilot's operating handbook of this particular aircraft.
q.e: Aircraft manufacturers compile all station arms, loading limits, and empty weight records into a dedicated chapter of the Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH), which is specifically titled "Weight and Balance".

q.t: When preparing to carry out the weighing procedure on an aircraft, which of the following is required?
q.e: To accurately determine the Basic Empty Mass (BEM), the aircraft must include unusable fuel and full engine oil, but absolutely all usable (burnable) fuel must be physically drained from the tanks.

q.t: Which section of the flight manual describes the basic empty mass of an aircraft?
q.e: The initial factory weighing report and any subsequent updates to the aircraft's Basic Empty Mass (BEM) are kept as the first pages in the "Weight and Balance" section of the POH.

q.t: The position of the center of gravity equals... See figure
q.e: Using the provided table, multiply each mass by its arm to get moments. Total Mass = 4217.5 lbs. Total Moment = 598829.5 in-lbs. Dividing total moment by total mass (598829.5 / 4217.5) equals exactly 141.986 inches, rounded to 142 inches.

q.t: What mass equals 102 litres of Avgas 100LL?
q.e: The standard density of Avgas is 0.72 kg/liter. Multiplying the volume by the density (102 L × 0.72 kg/L) results in 73.44 kg, which rounds to 74 kg.

q.t: Calculated take-off mass = 2300 lbs, calculated CG = 95.75 in, fuel burn = 170 lbs on station 87.00 in. Where is the CG situated after the landing?
q.e: Initial Moment = 2300 × 95.75 = 220225. Burned Fuel Moment = 170 × 87 = 14790. Landing Moment = 220225 - 14790 = 205435. Landing Mass = 2300 - 170 = 2130 lbs. Landing CG = 205435 / 2130 = 96.448 inches, rounded to 96.45 in.

q.t: Given values: Calculated take-off mass = 746 kg, calculated CG = 37.1 cm, fuel burn = 30.5 l on station 45 cm. Where is the CG situated after the landing?
q.e: Fuel mass = 30.5 L × 0.72 kg/L = 21.96 kg. Initial Moment = 746 × 37.1 = 27676.6. Fuel Moment = 21.96 × 45 = 988.2. Landing Moment = 26688.4. Landing Mass = 746 - 21.96 = 724.04 kg. Landing CG = 26688.4 / 724.04 = 36.86 cm (rounds to 36.9 cm).

q.t: Calculated take-off mass = 1082 kg, calculated CG = 0.254 m, fuel burn = 55 l on station 0.40 m. Where is the CG situated after the landing?
q.e: Fuel mass = 55 L × 0.72 kg/L = 39.6 kg. Initial Moment = 1082 × 0.254 = 274.828. Fuel Moment = 39.6 × 0.40 = 15.84. Landing Moment = 258.988. Landing Mass = 1082 - 39.6 = 1042.4 kg. Landing CG = 258.988 / 1042.4 = 0.2484 m, which is 24.8 cm.

q.t: The position of the center of gravity (including fuel) equals... See figure
For the purpose of a flight preparation, the pilot calculates a total take-off mass of 750 kg and a total moment of 625 mmkg. Which cross marks the center of gravity (CG)? See annex
q.e: By plotting the given values on the provided visual center of gravity envelope graph (Mass 750 kg on the vertical axis, Moment 625 on the horizontal axis), the intersection lies precisely at the point marked "1X".

q.t: For the purpose of a flight preparation the pilot calculates a total take-off mass of 725 kg and a total moment of 650 mmkg. Which cross marks the center of gravity (CG)? See annex
q.e: By locating 725 kg on the vertical Mass axis and moving horizontally to intersect the vertical line rising from 650 on the Moment axis, the resulting point corresponds exactly to the cross marked "3X".

q.t: For the purpose of a flight preparation the pilot calculates a total take-off mass of 775 kg and a total moment of 700 mmkg. Which cross marks the center of gravity (CG)? See annex
q.e: Using the same graphical method on the provided chart, the intersection of 775 kg and a 700 mmkg moment lands far to the right, outside the normal safe operating envelope, at the position marked "4X".

q.t: Which is the most recently determined empty mass and the associated center of gravity (CG) arm from the aircraft documentation? See annex
q.e: Looking at the provided maintenance logbook snippet, the very last entry (dated 06.11.2011) updates the running total of the aircraft's Basic Empty Weight to 498 kg, with a newly calculated balance arm of 280.59 m.

q.t: How does the aircraft configuration influence take-off performance while all other parameters remaining constant? See figure
o: Aircraft A has a higher tyre pressure than aircraft B
Aircraft B has a higher flap setting than aircraft A
Aircraft B has a higher tyre pressure than aircraft A
Aircraft A has a higher flap setting than aircraft B
q.e: In the diagram, Aircraft A lifts off earlier (shorter ground roll) but climbs at a shallower angle compared to Aircraft B (clean wing). This behavior perfectly illustrates the use of take-off flaps, which generate more lift at slower speeds but incur a drag penalty during climb.

q.t: How does aircraft flap configuration influence the take-off performance?
o: A higher flap setting decreases ground roll and lift-off speed and increases climb performance
A higher flap setting increases ground roll, lift-off speed, and climb performance
A higher flap setting decreases ground roll and increases lift-off speed and climb performance
A higher flap setting decreases ground roll and lift-off speed, but also climb performance
q.e: Deploying flaps increases the wing's camber, generating more lift at slower speeds. This allows the aircraft to lift off sooner and reduces the ground roll. However, the extended flaps create significant aerodynamic drag, which degrades the rate of climb once airborne.

q.t: How does wind affect the take-off performance?
o: Tailwind aids the aircraft in overcoming the initial drag at the commencement of the take-off roll. The take-off distance will decrease
Headwind causes an increased airflow around the wing. The take-off distance will increase
Headwind imposes an increased drag on the aircraft. The take-off distance will increase
Tailwind reduces the relative wind on the airfoil. The take-off distance will increase
q.e: An aircraft requires a specific airspeed over the wings to generate lift. A tailwind travels in the same direction as the aircraft, meaning the aircraft must accelerate over a much longer ground distance to catch up to the wind and achieve the necessary relative airflow.

q.t: It is possible that the surface wind speed at an airport is reduced due to friction. When a surface area with a minor tailwind condition is left during the initial climb, the pilot might expect...
o: an increase in airspeed and rate of climb due to decreasing tailwind.
an increase in airspeed and rate of climb due to increasing tailwind.
a decrease in airspeed and rate of climb due to increasing tailwind.
a deacrease in airspeed and climb performance due to decreasing tailwind.
q.e: If you take off with a light tailwind near the ground, climbing above the friction layer exposes the aircraft to the full, stronger tailwind (wind shear). This sudden surge in tailwind instantly robs the wings of relative airflow, causing a dangerous drop in both airspeed and climb performance.

q.t: Which factor shortens landing distance?
q.e: A strong headwind flows against the aircraft, meaning the wings generate the required lift at a much lower ground speed. Because the aircraft approaches the runway moving slower relative to the ground, it touches down slower and uses far less runway to stop.

q.t: Unless the aircraft is equipped and certified accordingly...
o: flight into areas of precipitation is prohibited.

flight into forecast icing conditions is prohibited. Should the aircraft enter an area of icing conditions inadvertantly, the flight may be continued as long as visual meteorological conditions are maintained.
flight into known or forecast icing conditions is only allowed as long as it is ensured that the aircraft can still be operated without performance degradation.
flight into known or forecast icing conditions is prohibited. Should the aircraft enter an area of icing conditions inadvertantly, it should be left without delay.
q.e: Airframe icing drastically destroys lift and adds massive weight. Therefore, non-FIKI (Flight Into Known Icing) aircraft are strictly prohibited from flying into forecasted icing. If accidentally encountered, the pilot must escape the icing zone immediately by changing altitude or turning back.

q.t: The speed Vx means...
o: that a given altitude is reached within minimum flight time.
that a given altitude is reached with minimum fuel consumption.
that a given altitude is reached within minimum distance.
q.e: Vx represents the Best Angle of Climb speed. Flying at this specific airspeed provides the maximum altitude gain for the shortest horizontal distance traveled over the ground, which is crucial for clearing obstacles (like trees) immediately at the end of a runway.

q.t: The angle of descent is defined as...
o: the ratio between the change in height and the horizontal distance travelled within the same time, expressed in percent [%].
the ratio between the change in height and the horizontal distance distance travelled within the same time, expressed in degrees [°].
the angle between a horizontal plane and the actual flight path, expressed in percent [%].
the angle between a horizontal plane and the actual flight path, expressed in degrees [°].
q.e: In aviation geometry, the angle of descent (like a 3-degree glide slope) is explicitly defined as the downward angle measured in degrees between a perfectly flat horizontal plane and the actual sloping trajectory (flight path) of the descending aircraft.

q.t: The term "steady flight" is defined as...
o: flight in smooth air without turbulence and a perfectly trimmed aircraft.
flight with a steady power setting without changing course.
climb or descent with a constant climb or descent rate in calm weather conditions.
unaccelerated flight. The four forces thrust, drag, lift, and weight are in equilibrium.
q.e: Steady flight (or straight and level unaccelerated flight) is the fundamental aerodynamic condition where Newton's laws are perfectly balanced: lift equals weight, and thrust equals drag. There is zero net force acting on the aircraft, meaning zero acceleration.

q.t: The speed Vy is defined as...
q.e: Vy is the Best Rate of Climb speed. Flying at this airspeed yields the maximum altitude gain per unit of time (feet per minute on the VSI), allowing the aircraft to reach cruising altitude in the shortest possible time.

q.t: The speed VFE is defined as...
o: stalling or minimum steady flight speed with the flaps retracted.
stalling or minimum steady flight speed with the flaps extended.
q.e: VFE stands for Velocity Flaps Extended. It is the absolute maximum structural airspeed at which the aircraft can be flown with the flaps deployed without risking bending the flap tracks or tearing the flaps off the wings due to excessive aerodynamic pressure.

q.t: The speed VSO is defined as...
o: stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed obtained in a specific configuration.
stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in landing configuration.
q.e: VSO (Velocity Stall Configured) marks the very bottom of the white arc on the airspeed indicator. It indicates the stall speed of the aircraft when it is fully "dirty"—maximum weight, engine idling, flaps fully down, and landing gear extended.

q.t: The beginning of the green arc (2) indicates which airspeed? See figure
o: VSO: Stall speed in landing configuration
VNO: Maximum speed for normal operations
VS1: Stall speed with flaps up
q.e: The green arc on the airspeed indicator represents the normal operating range. The very bottom of this green arc defines VS1, which is the stall speed of the aircraft in a clean configuration (gear up, flaps fully retracted, power off).

q.t: The end of the green arc (4) indicates which airspeed? See figure
o: VS1: Stall speed with flaps up
VNO: Maximum speed for normal operations
q.e: The top end of the green arc borders the yellow caution arc. This specific dividing line represents VNO (Velocity Normal Operating), which is the maximum structural cruising speed. Above this speed, the aircraft should only be flown in completely smooth, non-turbulent air.

q.t: The red marking at the end of the yellow arc (5) indicates which airspeed? See figure
o: VNO: Maximum speed for normal operations
VS1: Stall speed with flaps up
q.e: The solid red line at the top end of the airspeed indicator represents VNE (Velocity Never Exceed). Flying faster than this absolute redline speed guarantees catastrophic structural failure due to aeroelastic flutter or aerodynamic overloading of the airframe.

q.t: Which climb speed may be used to optimize the rate of climb (e.g. to reach a desired altitude within minimum time)?
o: Vx, the best angle of climb speed
Vx, the best rate of climb speed
Vy, the best angle of climb speed
Vy, the best rate of climb speed
q.e: As explained in aerodynamic principles, the speed labeled Vy represents the Best Rate of Climb. Operating at this speed maximizes vertical velocity (fpm), putting the aircraft at the desired cruising altitude in the shortest amount of time.

q.t: For a take-off from runway 22 and a reported wind of 250°/10 kt, the longitudinal wind component equals...
q.e: Runway 22 aligns with magnetic heading 220°. The wind is coming from 250°, creating a 30° difference. The headwind component is calculated using the cosine of the angle: 10 knots × cos(30°) = 10 × 0.866 = 8.66 knots. This rounds to approximately 9 knots of headwind.

q.t: Given the following conditions, the take-off distance equals... Outside air temperature: -20°C, Pressure Altitude: 5000 ft, Aeroplane mass: 750 kg, Headwind: 10 kt. See annex
q.e: Using the provided manufacturer's Take-off Distance graph: Start at -20°C on the left, go straight up to the 5000 ft pressure altitude line, track horizontally to the reference line, follow the slope down to 750 kg, track horizontally to the next reference, follow the slope down to 10 kt headwind, and read the final distance on the right axis as approximately 380 meters.

q.t: A pilot wants to take off on runway 36, the reported wind is 240 degrees, 12 knots. What is the value of the wind components acting on the aircraft on take-off and landing?
o: Crosswind from the right 10.4 kt. Tailwind 6 kt.
Crosswind from the right 6 kt. Headwind 10.4 kt.
Crosswind from the left 6 kt. Tailwind 10.4 kt.
Crosswind from the left 10.4 kt. Tailwind 6 kt.
q.e: Runway 36 is heading 360° (or 000°). Wind from 240° comes from the rear-left, at a 120° angle difference. Tailwind = 12 × cos(60°) = 12 × 0.5 = 6 knots. Crosswind = 12 × sin(60°) = 12 × 0.866 = 10.39 knots. Since 240° is left of 360°, the crosswind strikes from the left.

q.t: What is the take-off distance at 750 kg take-off mass, standard (ISA) conditions at an elevation of 4000 ft with 5 kt tailwind? See annex
q.e: Entering the PFP-009 chart: Start at standard ISA temperature for 4000 ft (which is +7°C), go up to 4000 ft altitude line, right to reference, slope to 750 kg mass, right to reference, slope UPWARDS (because of a 5 kt tailwind penalty), yielding a massive extended take-off distance of 900 meters.

q.t: What is the take-off distance at 705 kg take-off mass, OAT 20° C, QNH 1013 hPa at an elevation of 3500 ft with 5 kt tailwind? See annex
q.e: Following the same graphical chart procedure: Enter at OAT 20°C, go up to an interpolated 3500 ft line, across to 705 kg mass, and finally follow the tailwind penalty slope upwards for 5 knots of tailwind. The resulting intersection on the rightmost scale is 880 meters.

q.t: A pilot wants to take off on runway 36, the reported wind is 240 degrees 12 knots. What are the wind components acting on the aircraft on take-off and landing?
o: Crosswind from the left 6 kt. Tailwind 10.4 kt.
Crosswind from the right 10.4 kt. Tailwind 6 kt.
Crosswind from the right 6 kt. Headwind 10.4 kt.
Crosswind from the left 10.4 kt. Tailwind 6 kt.
q.e: This is an identical scenario to question 54. The 120-degree difference creates a tailwind component of 6 knots (cos 60 × 12) and a crosswind component of 10.4 knots (sin 60 × 12) striking the aircraft from the left side.

q.t: Given the following conditions, the fuel consumption equals... Pressure altitude: 2000 ft, Temperature: 31°C, RPM: 2400. See annex
q.e: Using the POH cruise table: Standard ISA temp at 2000 ft is 11°C. An OAT of 31°C means this is an "ISA + 20°C" hot day scenario. In the table block for 2000 ft under the "20°C above ISA" section, reading the row for 2400 RPM yields a fuel flow (FF) of 19.5 liters/hour.

q.t: Given the following conditions, the climb speed equals... Outside air temperature: -20°C, Pressure altitude: 10000 ft. See annex
q.e: Using the provided rate of climb chart: Start on the bottom left axis at -20°C, move straight up to intersect the diagonal 10000 ft Pressure Altitude line, travel horizontally to the right side of the chart to the reference line, and drop straight down to read a climb rate of 350 ft/min.

q.t: What range can be achieved at the following conditions? Outside air temperature: 6°C, Pressure Altitude: 6000 ft, Power: 65%. See annex
q.e: In the range profile chart: 6°C at 6000 ft represents standard ISA conditions. Start at 6°C, move up to the 6000 ft altitude line, horizontally across to intersect the bold vertical 65% power curve, and drop straight down to read a maximum range of approximately 482 Nautical Miles.

q.t: Given the following information, what range can be achieved? Outside air temperature: 22°C, Pressure altitude: 2000 ft, Power: 55%. See annex
q.e: Using the same range chart: Begin at 22°C on the temperature axis, go up to intersect the 2000 ft line, move horizontally to the right until hitting the 55% power profile curve, and follow down to the x-axis, which clearly points to a range of 500 Nautical Miles.

q.t: Given the following conditions, the TAS equals... Outside air temperature: 10°C, Pressure altitude: 6000 ft, Power: 65%. See annex
q.e: Using the TAS profile chart: Start at 10°C on the bottom left, move up to the 6000 ft pressure altitude line, track horizontally to the right side of the graph to intersect the 65% power vertical curve, and drop down to the airspeed axis to read 92 knots True Airspeed.

q.t: Given the following conditions, the TAS equals... Outside air temperature: -2°C, Pressure altitude: 8000 ft, Power: 75%. See annex
q.e: Entering the TAS performance chart: Start at -2°C (which is nearly ISA for 8000 ft), move up to the 8000 ft diagonal line, horizontally to the right to intersect the 75% power setting line, and drop straight down to find a True Airspeed of 104 knots.

q.t: Which maximum rate of climb can the aircraft reach at 9000 ft pressure altitude and OAT 12° C? See annex
q.e: Using the climb performance chart: Start at +12°C on the temperature axis, move up to an interpolated 9000 ft line (between 8000 and 10000), move horizontally right to the reference line, and drop down to the rate of climb axis, which yields a meager 200 ft/min performance.

q.t: Which is the maximum rate of climb for the aircraft at 6500 ft pressure altitude and an OAT of 0° C? See annex
q.e: From the climb chart: Enter at 0°C on the x-axis, ascend to the interpolated 6500 ft pressure altitude line (between 6000 and 8000), track horizontally across to the right side of the chart, and drop down to the rate of climb scale, reading approximately 480 ft/min.

q.t: What is the true airspeed (TAS) [kt] and fuel consumption [l/h] for cruise flight with 60 % power in flight level 60 under the following conditions? Temperature: ISA - 20°C, QNH: 980 hPa. See annex
q.e: Using the detailed cruise performance table for 6000 ft at ISA-20°C: The table lists 64% BHP at 2500 RPM (TAS 98, FF 20.5) and 56% BHP at 2400 RPM (TAS 92, FF 18.7). Since the question asks for 60% power, interpolating exactly halfway between these two rows yields a TAS of 95 knots and a Fuel Flow of 19.6 l/h.

q.t: What is the true airspeed (TAS) [kt] and fuel consumption [l/h] for cruise flight with 70 % power in flight level 60 under the following conditions? Temperature: ISA - 20° C, QNH: 980 hPa. See annex
q.e: Using the same table for 6000 ft at ISA-20°C: The top row for 2600 RPM explicitly lists the power setting as exactly 70% BHP. Reading across this specific row provides the values directly: True Airspeed (TAS) is 110 knots, and the Fuel Flow is 23.9 liters/hour.

q.t: What is the fuel flow and the true airspeed for cruise flight with 60% power in flight level 85 at an OAT of -25° C? See annex
q.e: Using the graph: Find -25°C, go up to an interpolated 8500 ft line, and move right to the 60% power curve (interpolated between 55% and 65%). Dropping down to the airspeed axis yields ~85 kt TAS. The associated Fuel Flow for 60% is indicated directly on the curves as roughly 18.5 liters.

q.t: At which airspeed do you climb to flight level (FL) 75 after a departure from an airfield which is located at a pressure altitude of 3000 ft with an initial mass of 3000 lbs? OAT at airfield: 25° C, OAT in FL 75: 0°C. See annex
q.e: This is a trick question designed to test chart reading comprehension. In the top left corner of the PFP-023 "Time, Fuel and Distance to Climb" chart, the manufacturer provides explicit text instructions: "CLIMB SPEED: 110 kt all masses". Therefore, no calculation is needed.

q.t: What is the required fuel to climb from FL 65 to FL 95 under the following conditions? Aircraft mass: 3000 lb. OAT in FL 65: -5°C, OAT in FL 95: -15°C. See annex
q.e: Using the climb chart for 3000 lb under ISA conditions: The total fuel required to climb from sea level to 9500 ft is approximately 4 gallons. The fuel required to climb from sea level to 6500 ft is approximately 3 gallons. The difference (fuel burned during this specific altitude segment) is 1 gallon.

q.t: What is the required distance to climb from FL 65 to FL 95 under the following conditions: Aircraft mass: 3000 lb. OAT in FL 65: -5°C, OAT in FL 95: -15° C. See annex
q.e: Using the same chart procedure but reading the bottom distance scale: The horizontal distance required to climb from sea level to 9500 ft is roughly 15 Nautical Miles. The distance from sea level to 6500 ft is roughly 9 NM. Subtracting the two yields a segment climb distance of 6 NM.

q.t: What is the required distance to climb to flight level (FL) 75 after a departure from an airfield which is located at a pressure altitude of 3000 ft with an initial mass of 3000 lbs? OAT at airfield: 25°C, OAT in FL 75: 0° C. See annex
q.e: These temperatures correspond to an ISA + 15°C hot day. Using the chart: Climbing from sea level to 7500 ft at ISA+15 requires roughly 14 NM. Climbing from sea level to the 3000 ft airfield elevation requires roughly 7 NM. The difference, which is the actual flight distance needed, is 7 NM.

q.t: The term "maximum elevation figure" (MEF) is defined as...
o: the highest elevation within an area covering 30 minutes of latitude and 30 minutes of longitude plus a safety margin of 1000 ft (305 m), rounded to the next higher 100 ft.
the highest elevation within an area covering 30 minutes of latitude and 30 minutes of longitude.
the highest elevation within an area covering 1 degree of latitude and 1 degree of longitude plus a safety margin, rounded to the next lower 100 ft.
the highest elevation within an area covering 30 minutes of latitude and 30 minutes of longitude plus a safety margin, rounded to the next higher 100 ft.
q.e: On VFR aeronautical charts, the MEF represents the highest known terrain or obstacle within a bounded geographic quadrangle (usually 30x30 minutes). To ensure aircraft safety, a small safety buffer is added to this peak altitude, and the final number is rounded up to the nearest 100 feet.

q.t: What is the purpose of "interception lines" in visual navigation?
o: To visualize the range limitation from the departure aerodrome
To mark the next available en-route airport during the flight
They help to continue the flight when flight visibility drops below VFR minima
They are used as easily recognizable guidance upon a possible loss of orientation
q.e: Interception lines (or catch lines) are highly prominent, continuous geographical features like rivers, coastlines, or major highways drawn on a pilot's map. If a pilot gets lost (disoriented), flying a straight heading will eventually "intercept" this unmistakable line, instantly restoring their positional awareness.

q.t: The VFR semicircular rules are based on the...
q.e: To maintain safe vertical separation between opposing aircraft traffic on airways, the semicircular rule (e.g., Eastbound = odd altitudes, Westbound = even altitudes) is based strictly on the Magnetic Course (MC) — the aircraft's intended track over the ground relative to magnetic North.

q.t: What is the lowest possible VFR flight level if a true course of 181° is selected and a variation of 3° east exists?
q.e: Magnetic Course (MC) = True Course (TC) - East Variation. MC = 181° - 3° = 178°. A heading of 178° falls into the Eastbound semicircle (000°-179°). Eastbound VFR flights use odd thousands plus 500 feet. The lowest available standard flight level is FL 035, followed by FL 055.

q.t: The upper limit of LO R 16 equals... See annex
q.e: By looking directly at the restricted airspace block labeled "LO R 16" on the provided ICAO map annex, the printed text clearly defines the vertical boundaries. The top line explicitly reads "1500 FT MSL", establishing the upper ceiling.

q.t: The upper limit of LO R 4 equals... See annex
q.e: Using the same map-reading technique on annex PFP-030, locating the red shaded restricted area labeled "LO R 4" reveals text identifying its vertical limits. The top value printed in the box clearly reads "4500 FT MSL".

q.t: How much taxi fuel must be consumed before take-off to reduce the aircraft mass to the maximum take-off mass? Maximum ramp mass (MRM): 1150 kg, Actual ramp mass: 1148 kg, Maximum take-off mass (MTOM): 1145 kg.
q.e: The aircraft is currently too heavy to fly legally. To drop from the actual ramp mass (1148 kg) to the maximum allowable take-off mass (1145 kg), the aircraft must burn off exactly 3 kg of fuel. Since aviation gasoline (Avgas) weighs about 0.72 kg per liter, 3 kg divided by 0.72 equals 4.16 liters. Rounded, this is 4 Liters.

q.t: Considering the following fuel data, how much trip fuel is required? Fuel for start-up and taxi: 5 L. Fuel for take-off and climb: 12 L. Fuel for cruise flight: 25 L. Fuel for descent, approach and landing: 7 L. Fuel for taxi and parking: 3 L. Fuel to alternate: 13 L. Final reserve fuel: 10 L.
q.e: Trip Fuel strictly encompasses only the fuel necessary to fly from the departure runway to the destination runway. It is the sum of fuel for take-off and climb (12 L), en-route cruise (25 L), and descent/approach/landing (7 L). 12 + 25 + 7 = 44 Liters. Ground taxi and reserves are calculated separately.

q.t: According to the aeronautical chart, Friesach/Hirt (LOKH) has a 707 m grass runway. Prevailing runway is 17 due to a surface wind of 18010KT. The required landing distance for your aircraft under present conditions is 550 m. Considering the NOTAM below, is it safe to plan LOKH as an alternate aerodrome? See figure
q.e: The NOTAM states that the threshold for RWY 17 is displaced by 207 meters due to tall trees, severely reducing the Landing Distance Available (LDA) to only 500 meters. Since your aircraft requires 550 meters to stop safely, landing there would result in a runway overrun. It is not safe.

q.t: Up to which altitude is an overflight prohibited according to the NOTAM? See figure
q.e: Reviewing the standard NOTAM format provided in the annex, Item F indicates the lower limit (GND), and Item G indicates the upper limit. Item G explicitly states "9500 FT AMSL" (Above Mean Sea Level), which denotes a standard altitude.

q.t: The EOBT (estimated off-block time) is specified in the ATS flight plan as...
q.e: To prevent massive global scheduling conflicts across thousands of localized time zones and daylight saving shifts, aviation authorities require all times in an Air Traffic Service (ATS) flight plan to be filed using a single, unified standard: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC, or "Zulu" time).

q.t: What is the nature of the flight shown in the given ATC flight plan? See annex
o: Traffic pattern under visual flight rules.
Night flight under visual flight rules.
q.e: In Box 8, the flight rules are indicated as "V" (Visual Flight Rules). However, looking at the time of departure (EOBT 20:00) and the equipment/remarks indicating standard night lighting or night VFR intentions, the plan is categorized as a VFR flight conducted at night (NVFR).

q.t: The specified speed in the ATS flight plan equals: See annex
q.e: In an international ICAO flight plan, the cruising speed is entered in Box 15. The entry "N0100" uses the letter "N" to denote Knots (Nautical miles per hour), followed by a four-digit number indicating the True Airspeed (TAS). Therefore, N0100 means a speed of exactly 100 knots.

q.t: What must be considered for cross-border flights?
q.e: International aviation law strictly mandates that any aircraft crossing the sovereign border of a foreign country (leaving its domestic Flight Information Region) must have filed an official international Flight Plan (FPL) prior to departure.

q.t: During a flight, a flight plan can be filed at the...
q.e: If a pilot takes off without a flight plan but suddenly requires one (e.g., encountering deteriorating weather and needing an IFR clearance or crossing a border), they can file an Airborne Flight Plan (AFIL) via radio by calling the regional Flight Information Service (FIS) frequency.

q.t: In comparison to the true airspeed in still air conditions, the TAS in a strong tailwind will be...
q.e: A strong tailwind pushes the aircraft towards its destination for free. To maximize range (fuel efficiency per mile over the ground), the pilot should reduce engine power and fly at a slightly lower True Airspeed (TAS), letting the tailwind do the work and saving fuel.

q.t: What happens to the true airspeed at a constant indicated airspeed during a climb?
