q.e: As an aircraft climbs, the air becomes thinner (less dense). To maintain a constant pressure in the pitot tube (Constant Indicated Airspeed - IAS), the aircraft must physically fly faster through this thin air. Therefore, the True Airspeed (TAS) steadily increases as altitude increases.

q.t: Given the following data: Take-Off fuel = 200 lbs, Alternate fuel = 40 lbs, Final reserve fuel = 30 lbs. After 25 minutes the remaining fuel is 120 lbs. Assuming that fuel flow will remain unchanged, the remaining time to the destination should not exceed:
q.e: Fuel burned in 25 mins = 200 - 120 = 80 lbs. Fuel burn rate = 80 lbs / 25 min = 3.2 lbs/minute. Remaining fuel is 120 lbs, but 70 lbs (40+30) is legally untouchable reserve. Usable fuel left for the trip = 120 - 70 = 50 lbs. Maximum remaining time = 50 lbs / 3.2 lbs/min = 15.625 minutes.

q.t: Given the following data for a VFR flight: Take-off fuel: 180 kg including reserve fuel, which is 30% of take off fuel. After half of the distance the remaining fuel is 100 kg. Assume that cruise conditions will remain unchanged. Determine the remaining fuel at the destination:
q.e: The aircraft started with 180 kg. At the halfway mark, 100 kg remains, meaning 80 kg was burned for the first half of the trip (180 - 100 = 80 kg). Since conditions are unchanged, the second half will also burn 80 kg. Upon landing, the remaining fuel in the tanks will be 100 - 80 = 20 kg.

q.t: During a VFR flight the remaining usable fuel at a checkpoint is 80 USG. Reserve fuel is 20 USG, remaining flight time according to flight plan is 2h 20min. What is the highest acceptable fuel flow (FF) for the rest of the trip?
q.e: The aircraft has 80 USG total, but 20 USG is reserved, leaving 60 USG of usable trip fuel. The remaining time is 2 hours and 20 minutes (which is 2.333 hours). To find the maximum fuel flow, divide the usable fuel by the time: 60 USG / 2.333 hours = 25.71 USG per hour.

q.t: Planning a flight from EDWF (Leer Papenburg) to EDWH (Oldenburg Hatten), the following conditions apply: Cruise level = FL 75, Temperature = ISA, Cruise weight = 3400 lbs, Power setting = 23.0 in. HG @ 2300 RPM. Determine True Airspeed (TAS) and Fuel Flow (FF):
q.e: Using the provided manufacturer's performance table for standard ISA conditions: At 8000 ft, 2300 RPM yields a TAS of 160 kt and FF of 11.9 GPH. At 6000 ft, 2300 RPM yields a TAS of 159 kt and FF of 12.0 GPH. Interpolating for 7500 ft (FL 75) provides values almost identical to the 8000 ft data, resulting in a TAS of 160 kt and a Fuel Flow of 11.9 GPH.

q.t: Planning a flight from EDWH (Oldenburg Hatten) to EDWF (Leer Papenburg), the following conditions apply: Cruise level = FL 65, Temperature = ISA+20, Cruise weight = 3400 lbs, Power setting = 23.0 in. HG @ 2300 RPM. What Indicated Airspeed (IAS) and Fuel Flow (FF) can be expected?
q.e: Referencing the POH table under the "20°C above ISA" (hot day) section for an altitude of 6000 ft at 2300 RPM: The table directly lists an Indicated Airspeed (KIAS) of 142 knots and a Fuel Flow (GPH) of 11.5. Since FL 65 is very close, these values represent the most accurate tabular expectation.

q.t: For planning a VFR flight, the following data are given: Flight time with planning "overhead-overhead" = 2h 43min, Pressure Altitude = 6.500 ft, Temperature = ISA-20, Power setting = 2300 RPM, Taxi Fuel = 2 USG, Additional time for climb = 7 min, Additional time for approach and landing = 10 min. The reserve fuel has to be 30% of trip fuel. Determine the minimum block fuel:
q.e: Using the ISA-20 table at 6000 ft, 2300 RPM yields a fuel flow of ~12.4 GPH. Total trip time = climb (7m) + cruise (163m) + approach (10m) = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Trip fuel = 3 h × 12.4 GPH = 37.2 USG. Required reserve is 30% of 37.2 = 11.16 USG. Total Block Fuel = Trip (37.2) + Reserve (11.16) + Taxi (2) = 50.36 USG, rounded to 50.4 USG.

q.t: For planning a VFR flight, the following data are given: Flight time with planning "overhead-overhead" = 2h 42min, Pressure Altitude = 7.500 ft, Temperature = ISA, Power setting = 2300 RPM, Taxi Fuel = 2 USG, Additional time for climb = 8 min, Additional time for approach and landing = 10 min. The reserve fuel has to be 30% of trip fuel. Determine the minimum block fuel:
q.e: Using the ISA table at 8000 ft, 2300 RPM yields a fuel flow of ~11.9 GPH. Total trip time = climb (8m) + cruise (162m) + approach (10m) = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Trip fuel = 3 h × 11.9 GPH = 35.7 USG. Required reserve is 30% of 35.7 = 10.71 USG. Total Block Fuel = Trip (35.7) + Reserve (10.71) + Taxi (2) = 48.41 USG, rounded to 48.4 USG.

q.t: Given the following data for a VFR flight: Trip fuel = 70 US gallons, Contingency fuel = 5% of trip fuel, Alternate and final reserve fuel = 20 US gallons. Usable fuel at take-off = 95 US gallons. After half of the distance you read that you have consumed 40 US gallons. Assume that fuel flow remains unchanged. Which statement is correct?
o: Upon landing 15.0 US gallons will remain in addition to alternate and final reserve fuel.
Upon landing, a total of 40.0 US gallons will remain.
Upon landing 5.0 US gallons will remain in addition to alternate and final reserve fuel.
The remaining fuel is insufficient for a landing at destination with alternate and final reserve fuel remaining.
q.e: You burned 40 USG for the first half, meaning the entire trip will consume 80 USG (worse than the planned 70 USG). With 95 USG total aboard, subtracting the 80 USG trip burn leaves only 15 USG in the tanks upon landing. Since the law requires 20 USG for alternate and final reserve, you will land below minimum legal reserves (insufficient).

q.t: Given the following data for a VFR flight: Trip fuel = 70 US gallons, Contingency fuel = 5% of trip fuel. Alternate and final reserve fuel = 20 US gallons. Usable fuel at take-off = 90 US gallons. After half of the distance you read that you have consumed 30 US gallons. Assume that fuel flow remains unchanged. Which statement is correct?
o: Upon landing a total of 10.0 US gallons will remain.
Upon landing 30.0 US gallons will remain in addition to alternate and final reserve fuel.
The remaining fuel is insufficient for a landing at destination with alternate and final reserve fuel remaining.
Upon landing 10.0 US gallons will remain in addition to alternate and final reserve fuel.
q.e: You burned 30 USG for the first half, so the entire trip will only consume 60 USG (better than planned). Taking off with 90 USG and burning 60 USG leaves 30 USG in the tanks at the destination. Out of this 30 USG, 20 USG is the untouched legal reserve. Therefore, you have an extra 10 USG remaining in addition to the required reserves.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a group of unlighted obstacles?
q.e: The question asks to identify the ICAO map symbol for a "group of unlighted obstacles." On standard aeronautical charts, a single unlighted obstacle is depicted as a single pointed triangle. A group of unlighted obstacles is depicted by two overlapping pointed triangles without any glowing flares or rays on top (which would indicate lighting). (Note: The provided answer choices in the source are jumbled strings like "CBAD", the correct option points to the dual unlit triangle symbol).

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a civil airport (not international airport) with paved runway?
q.e: On an ICAO VFR chart, a standard non-international civil airport featuring a hard, paved runway is represented by an empty, unfilled circle that contains a thick, dark, solid line running through its center, visually indicating the magnetic alignment of the paved runway strip. (Note: The source provides jumbled string options; the correct answer points to symbol "A" in the annex).

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a general spot elevation?
q.e: A "spot elevation" on a topographical aeronautical chart marks the exact highest point of a small terrain feature, such as a hilltop. It is depicted very simply as a single, small black dot, usually accompanied by a number representing its height above mean sea level. (Note: Similar to previous questions, the source has jumbled strings; the correct answer points to symbol "C" in the annex).

q.t: Wie beeinflusst die Lufttemperatur die Leistung eines Kolbenmotors?
o: Geringere Temperatur entspricht geringerer Luftdichte, dies führt zu höherer Motorleistung
Geringere Temperatur entspricht höherer Luftdichte, dies führt zu geringerer Motorleistung
Höhere Temperatur entspricht höherer Luftdichte, dies führt zu höherer Motorleistung
Höhere Temperatur entspricht geringerer Luftdichte, dies führt zu geringerer Motorleistung
q.e: This translates to: "How does air temperature affect piston engine performance?" High temperatures cause air to expand, decreasing its density (fewer oxygen molecules per cubic inch). A piston engine burning less oxygen produces a weaker explosion, leading to a significant loss of overall engine power (lower performance).

q.t: The thickness of the wing is defined as the distance between the lower and the upper side of the wing at the...
o: most inner part of the wing.
most outer part of the wing.
q.e: In aerodynamics, the physical thickness of an airfoil is strictly defined as the maximum straight-line distance between the upper and lower surfaces, found at the thickest part of the wing.

q.t: How is referred to a tubular steel construction with a non self-supporting skin?
q.e: A grid construction (or truss structure) relies entirely on a framework of welded steel tubes to carry all structural loads. The outer skin (fabric or light metal) serves only to provide an aerodynamic shape and carries no load.

q.t: Primary fuselage structures of wood or metal planes are usually made up by what components?
q.e: The primary load-bearing structure of a standard semi-monocoque fuselage consists of vertical bulkheads or frames (giving the fuselage its shape) connected by longitudinal stringers that run from nose to tail.

q.t: Which wing configuration is shown in the attachment? See figure
q.e: The image shows a Cessna 152. Its wings are mounted on the top of the cabin (high wing) and are supported by visible diagonal struts connecting the wing to the lower fuselage, making it a strut-braced high wing.

q.t: A construction made of frames and stringer with a supporting skin is called...
q.e: In a semi-monocoque construction, the internal framework (frames and stringers) shares the structural loads with the outer skin (which is stressed to carry tension and shear loads).

q.t: Which tail assembly is shown in the attachment? See figure
q.e: The image shows an aircraft (Diamond DA40) where the horizontal stabilizer is mounted at the very top of the vertical stabilizer, forming the shape of a capital letter "T", hence called a T-tail.

q.t: What are the major components of an aircraft's tail?
q.e: The tail section (empennage) of a conventional aircraft is divided into two primary structural aerodynamic components: the horizontal tail (stabilizer/elevator) and the vertical tail (fin/rudder).

q.t: The sandwich structure consists of two...
o: thick layers and a light core material.
thick layers and a heavy core material.
thin layers and a heavy core material.
thin layers and a light core material.
q.e: A composite sandwich structure is created by bonding two very thin, strong outer face sheets (like fiberglass or carbon fiber) to a thick but extremely light core material (like foam or honeycomb) to achieve high stiffness at low weight.

q.t: Which constructional elements give the wing its profile shape?
q.e: The ribs (often spelled 'rips' in older European translations) are the curved, airfoil-shaped structural crosspieces that attach to the main spar. They give the wing its aerodynamic cambered profile and support the skin.

q.t: The load factor "n" describes the relationship between...
q.e: Load factor (n) is physically defined as the ratio of the total lift generated by the wings to the total gross weight of the aircraft. In straight and level flight, lift equals weight, so the load factor is 1G.

q.t: Which are the advantages of sandwich structures?
o: Low weight, high stiffness, high stability, and high strength
High temperature durability and low weight
Good formability and high temperature durability
q.e: Sandwich materials (like honeycomb core with carbon skins) offer an incredible strength-to-weight ratio. They provide high stiffness, bending stability, and overall structural strength while keeping the airframe exceptionally light.

q.t: Which of the stated materials shows the highest strength?
q.e: Carbon fiber reinforced plastic (CFRP) has a significantly higher tensile strength and stiffness-to-weight ratio compared to traditional aerospace metals like aluminum or magnesium.

q.t: What needs to be considered if permissible limitations were exceeded?
o: The helicopter must be inspected by at least two pilots licensed on the type, one of whom must be the pilot in command
The helicopter must be inspected by a qualified engineer before the next flight
The helicopter must be subjected to a duplicate inspected by two engineers
The helicopter must be inspected by the pilot in command and if no defect is found, no appropriate entry in the aircraft technical log is necessary
q.e: If an aircraft exceeds operational limitations (e.g., Vne, maximum G-load, over-temp), invisible structural damage or metal fatigue may have occurred. A certified aircraft engineer must perform a formal inspection before the aircraft flies again.

q.t: Reasons for dents in the helicopter structure are...
o: excessive engine rpm and cylinder defects.
q.e: Dents, wrinkles, or buckled skin on an airframe are clear visual signs of structural overstress. These are almost always caused by severe impacts, such as a hard landing, or aerodynamic overstressing during flight.

q.t: What kind of hydraulic oil is used in aeroplane systems today?
q.e: Modern aviation hydraulic systems operate in extreme conditions, from -50°C at high altitudes to very high operating temperatures. Therefore, specially formulated synthetic oils (like Skydrol) are used because they do not freeze and are highly fire-resistant.

q.t: Number 1 on the gear designates the... See figure
q.e: In the diagram, the metal structure that splits into two prongs holding the axle of the nose wheel on both sides is known as the landing gear fork.

q.t: The fuselage structure may be damaged by...
o: exceeding the manoeuvering speed in heavy gusts.
airspeed decreasing below a certain value.
stall after exceeding the maximum angle of attack.
neutralizing stick forces according to actual flight state.
q.e: Maneuvering speed (Va) is the maximum speed at which full flight control deflections can be made without causing structural damage. Exceeding Va in heavy gusts can impose extreme G-forces that can permanently bend or break the fuselage and wing spars.

q.t: Number 2 on the gear designates the... See figure
q.e: In the landing gear oleo strut diagram, item #2 points to the shiny, sliding metal piston tube that retracts upward into the main strut housing to absorb the landing shock. This is the movable inner cylinder.

q.t: How is the nose or tail wheel usually controlled on small aircraft and motor gliders?
q.e: On the ground, directional steering of the nose wheel (or tail wheel) is achieved mechanically by the pilot pressing the left or right rudder pedals with their feet.

q.t: Where is the brake system installed to slow the aircraft on ground?
o: On the nose and main gear
q.e: Aircraft brakes are installed exclusively on the main landing gear wheels. If brakes were on the nose wheel, applying them would cause the aircraft to flip over forward (nose-over) due to its momentum and high center of gravity.

q.t: What kind of control surface is connected with the nose wheel?
q.e: The nose wheel steering linkage is directly connected to the rudder control system. When the pilot pushes the rudder pedals to steer on the ground, the aerodynamic rudder on the tail moves simultaneously.

q.t: What is checked by the marking in the attachment? See figure
o: The correct position of the outer isolation layers
The correct postion of the tire relative to the rim
The tread wear of the tire
The operating pressure of the carcass
q.e: The red painted stripe crossing the tire bead and the wheel rim is a creep mark (slip mark). If the tire slips on the rim during heavy braking, the red line breaks alignment, indicating the tire might have torn its inner valve stem.

q.t: About how many axes does an aircraft move and how are these axes called?
o: 4; vertical axis, lateral axis, longitudinal axis, axis of speed
4; optical axis, imaginary axis, sagged axis, axis of evil
3; vertical axis, lateral axis, longitudinal axis
q.e: In aviation, an aircraft moves in three-dimensional space rotating around three specific, mutually perpendicular axes crossing at its center of gravity: the vertical axis (yaw), the lateral axis (pitch), and the longitudinal axis (roll).

q.t: A movement around the longitudinal axis is primarily initiated by the...
q.e: The longitudinal axis runs straight through the fuselage from nose to tail. Rotation around this axis is called rolling, which is directly controlled by the pilot moving the ailerons on the trailing edges of the wings.

q.t: How are the flight controls on a small single-engine piston aircraft normally controlled and actuated?
o: Hydraulically through hydraulic pumps and actuators
Power-assisted through hydraulic pumps or electric motors
Manually through rods and control cables
q.e: Small, basic GA aircraft (like a Cessna 152 or Piper Archer) do not have heavy hydraulic or fly-by-wire systems. The pilot's physical movements are transferred directly to the control surfaces via a simple, manual system of steel cables, pulleys, and push-pull rods.

q.t: What are the primary and the secondary effects of a rudder input to the left?
o: Primary: yaw to the right. Secondary: roll to the right
Primary: yaw to the right. Secondary: roll to the left
Primary: yaw to the left. Secondary: roll to the right
Primary: yaw to the left. Secondary: roll to the left
q.e: Pushing the left rudder pedal forces the tail right, making the nose yaw to the left (Primary). As the plane yaws left, the right wing travels faster through the air, generating more lift than the left wing, which causes the aircraft to subsequently roll to the left (Secondary).

q.t: What is the effect of pulling the control yoke or stick backwards?
o: The aircraft's tail will produce an increased upward force, causing the aircraft's nose to rise
The aircraft's tail will produce an increased downward force, causing the aircraft's nose to drop
The aircraft's tail will produce an decreased upward force, causing the aircraft's nose to drop
The aircraft's tail will produce an increased downward force, causing the aircraft's nose to rise
q.e: Pulling the yoke back deflects the elevator upwards. The oncoming air hits the raised elevator, creating a strong downward aerodynamic force on the tail. This pushes the tail down, pivoting the aircraft on its CG and raising the nose up.

q.t: What happens to a helicopter during cruise when the stick is moved forward without other corrections?
o: The speed decreases and the sink rate increases
The speed increases and the sink rate increases
The speed increases and the sink rate decreases
The speed decreases and the sink rate decreases
q.e: Moving the cyclic (stick) forward tilts the rotor disk forward. This directs more thrust horizontally (increasing forward speed) but reduces the vertical lift component, causing the aircraft to lose altitude (increasing the sink rate).

q.t: Which of the following options states all primary flight controls of an aircraft?
o: Elevator, rudder, aileron, trim tabs, high-lift wing devices, power controls
All movable parts on the aircraft which aid in controlling the aircraft
q.e: The three primary flight control surfaces required to actively steer an aircraft in three-dimensional space are the elevator (for pitch), the rudder (for yaw), and the ailerons (for roll).

q.t: What is the purpose of the secondary flight controls?
o: To enable the pilot to control the aircraft's movements about its three axes
To improve the performance characteristics of an aircraft and relieve the pilot of excessive control forces
To constitute a backup system for the primary flight controls
To improve the turn characteristics of an aircraft in the low speed regime during approach and landing
q.e: Secondary flight controls include flaps, slats, and trim tabs. Flaps/slats change the wing's camber to improve lift and performance at slow speeds, while trim tabs relieve the pilot from having to constantly apply physical pressure on the controls.

q.t: What is the purpose of a ground adjustable trim tab?
o: It is a non-movable metal tab on a flight control which is adjusted on the ground to optimize the inflight characteristics of an aircraft
It is used to optimize the handling characteristics of an aircraft during ground operations
It is preset on the ground and further adjusted in flight to reduce the need to constantly re-trim the aircraft
It is set on the ground to correct an out-of-trim condition arising from the mass and balance situation of an aircraft
q.e: A ground adjustable trim tab is a small, bendable piece of sheet metal attached to the trailing edge of a rudder or aileron. If the plane naturally flies slightly crooked, a mechanic bends this tab on the ground to aerodynamicly force the control surface straight during flight.

q.t: The trim wheel or lever in the cockpit is moved aft by the pilot. What effect does this action have on the trim tab and on the elevator?
o: The trim tab moves down, the elevator moves down
The trim tab moves up, the elevator moves up
The trim tab moves down, the elevator moves up
The trim tab moves up, the elevator moves down
q.e: Moving the trim wheel aft (Nose-UP trim) is meant to push the tail down. To do this, the mechanical linkage moves the tiny trim tab DOWN into the airstream. The wind hits the down-tab, forcing the main elevator surface UP, which subsequently pushes the tail down.

q.t: When trimming an aircraft nose up, in which direction does the trim tab move?
q.e: As explained in the previous question, to achieve a nose-up attitude, the main elevator must deflect UP. To force the heavy elevator up aerodynamically, the small trim tab must be deflected DOWN into the relative wind.

q.t: How does a balance tab move in relation to the flight control surface that it is coupled with?
q.e: A balance tab is mechanically linked to move automatically in the opposite direction of the main control surface. By deflecting the opposite way, the air pushing against the tab helps the pilot move the large, heavy control surface.

q.t: The trim is used to...
q.e: The entire aerodynamic purpose of a trim system is to neutralize the constant physical pressure required on the control yoke or stick, allowing the pilot to adapt the control forces to zero for a specific airspeed and attitude.

q.t: Which of the following are an aircraft's secondary flight controls?
o: All movable parts on the aircraft which aid in controlling the aircraft
Elevator, rudder, aileron, trim tabs, high-lift wing devices, power controls
Wing flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers or speedbrakes, trim systems
q.e: Primary controls are elevator, aileron, rudder. Secondary controls encompass everything else that modifies the aerodynamic profile or relieves pressure, explicitly including flaps, slats/slots, spoilers, speedbrakes, and all trim tabs.

q.t: What has to be considered during refueling?
o: Apply ground wires, turn on the main switch and magneto ignition
No open fires, obey smoking ban and apply ground cables
Check the fuel content of the tank with a torch and remove fire protection
Refuel through a soaked rag and keep a fire extinguisher available
q.e: Flowing aviation fuel generates massive amounts of static electricity. To prevent a catastrophic static spark that could ignite the fuel vapors, the aircraft and fuel truck must be bonded with ground cables, and strictly no open flames or smoking is allowed.

q.t: The primer is...
o: a nozzle in the Venturi tube of a carburettor for atomising the fuel.
an auxiliary pump in the fuel system to facilitate engine starting.
a mechanical switch in the cockpit to engage the turbocharger.
a valve in the fuel control system for automatic mixture regulation.
q.e: The primer is a manual pump located in the cockpit. It draws fuel directly from the strainer and squirts it as a fine mist directly into the engine's intake ports, providing a rich, easily ignitable mixture for starting cold engines.

q.t: What is the purpose of the tank ventilation?
o: To distribute the fuel from one tank segment to the other during flight
To prevent fuel spillage during refueling on the filler plug
To prevent water disposal during parking
To prevent underpressure caused by fuel consumption
q.e: As fuel is consumed by the engine, the volume of liquid in the rigid wing tank drops. If the tank wasn't ventilated (vented) to the outside air, a vacuum (underpressure) would form, crushing the tank and starving the engine of fuel.

q.t: An aeroplane's current supply is carried out by the: 1. Battery 2. Generator 3. Relay 4. Circuit breaker
q.e: A relay is a switch and a circuit breaker is a fuse. The actual sources that physically generate and supply electrical current (power) to the aircraft's avionics and bus bars are the Battery (when engine is off) and the Generator/Alternator (when engine is running).

q.t: What is the unit for voltage?
q.e: In physics and electrical engineering, electrical potential difference, commonly known as voltage, is quantified and measured using the unit "Volt".

q.t: What is the unit for electrical power?
q.e: Electrical power—the rate at which electrical energy is transferred by an electric circuit—is universally measured in the unit "Watt" (W).

q.t: What is the reason for static dischargers on aircraft?
o: To eliminate electrical interferences during intensive radio traffic
To discharge static charging during flight
To improve the quality of radio transmission in high altitudes
q.e: As an aircraft flies through precipitation, dust, or ice crystals, friction builds up a high-voltage static charge on the airframe. Static dischargers (wicks) installed on the trailing edges bleed this static electricity back into the atmosphere silently to prevent radio interference (corona discharge).

q.t: What must be considered if the alternator fails in a helicopter?
o: The engine runs roughly and is prone to knocking
All instruments and warning systems will fail
No change as long as the battery provides enough power
Only high power consumers will failing
q.e: Piston aircraft engines run on independent mechanical magnetos, so the engine will not quit. All electrical avionics and lights will simply transition to draining the battery, continuing to function perfectly normally until the battery is completely depleted.

q.t: When using direct current, electrically driven flight instruments are marked with...
q.e: DC stands for Direct Current, which is the type of electrical power supplied by the aircraft's battery and alternator systems, as opposed to AC (Alternating Current).

q.t: What devices can be affected by a failure of the electrical system in a helicopter?
o: Airspeed indicator, altimeter and artificial horizon
Fuel quantity indication, radio equipment and altimeter
Radio equipment, navigation equipment and gyros
Radio equipment, navigation equipment and magnetic compass
q.e: The magnetic compass, altimeter, and airspeed indicator do not use electricity (they rely on earth's magnetism and pitot-static air). An electrical failure will, however, kill all radios, GPS navigation units, and electric gyroscopic instruments (like the turn coordinator).

q.t: Which cylinder arragement is commonly used on small aircrafts and motor gliders?
q.e: The "Boxer" or horizontally opposed engine (where cylinders lay flat facing away from each other) is the industry standard for light aircraft (e.g., Lycoming and Continental engines) due to its excellent air-cooling profile, compact flat shape, and inherently balanced, smooth operation.

q.t: Which part of the cycle of a four-stroke Otto engine can be seen in the attachment? See figure
q.e: In the diagram, the intake valve (left) is open, and a blue mixture of air and fuel is being drawn into the cylinder as the piston travels downwards. This is the first stroke of the 4-stroke cycle: Induction (or Intake).

q.t: Which part of the cycle of a four-stroke Otto engine can be seen in the attachment? See figure
q.e: In this diagram, both the intake and exhaust valves are tightly closed. The piston is moving upwards, squeezing the blue air/fuel mixture into a highly pressurized red state before ignition. This is the second stroke: Compression.

q.t: What is likely to be the cause if the engine runs unusually rough while checking the magnetos?
o: Short circuit on the ground cable
q.e: During the run-up, you turn off one magneto to check the other. If the engine suddenly shakes violently and runs very rough on just one magneto, it indicates that one of the spark plugs powered by that active magneto is dead, fouled with lead, or heavily fouled with oil.

q.t: The highest absorbtion of humidity in fuel can be observed in which situation?
o: During parking on wet gras areas
q.e: When a fuel tank is almost empty, it contains a large volume of air. Overnight, as temperatures drop, the moisture contained in this large volume of air condenses into water droplets, which sink to the bottom of the fuel tank.

q.t: Where does the condensation water converge in the tank?
o: It is mixed with the fuel
Near the cap of the tank
q.e: Water is physically heavier and denser than aviation gasoline. Due to gravity, any water that forms from condensation will immediately sink through the fuel and collect in the lowest point (the sump) of the fuel tank.

q.t: What does the octane rating or fuel grade describe?
q.e: The octane rating (like 100LL) indicates the fuel's resistance to premature, explosive detonation (knocking) under high pressure and temperature inside the cylinder. A higher octane number means a better anti-knock rating.

q.t: Which colour does Avgas 100 LL have?
q.e: To visually distinguish aviation fuels and prevent catastrophic misfueling (like putting Jet-A into a piston engine), Avgas 100LL (Low Lead) is dyed with a distinct, bright blue color.

q.t: What is the direct influence by switching on the carburettor heating on fixed propeller engines during engine run-up?
q.e: Applying carburetor heat introduces hot, unfiltered air into the engine intake. Hot air is less dense than cold air, which enriches the mixture and provides less oxygen for combustion. Consequently, the engine produces slightly less power, causing an immediate drop in RPM.

q.t: What is the major task of a carburettor?
o: To provide additional fuel to cool the engine
To pump fuel from the tanks into the cylinder
To control the aircraft's speed through the throttle valve
To produce an ignitable air/fuel mixture
q.e: The carburetor uses the venturi effect to draw liquid fuel from a bowl, atomize it into fine droplets, and mix it with incoming airflow in a precise ratio (usually around 1:15) to create a highly explosive, ignitable vapor mixture for the cylinders.

q.t: In which phase of flight must the carburettor heating be switched off although carburettor icing might be expected?
q.e: Applying carburetor heat significantly reduces engine power output. During the take-off roll and initial climb, the aircraft requires 100% of available engine power to safely clear obstacles. Therefore, carburetor heat must always be turned off for take-off.

q.t: In which outside air temperature is icing most likely?
q.e: Carburetor icing is a severe threat even on warm days. The evaporation of fuel inside the venturi causes a massive temperature drop (up to 30°C). Therefore, if there is high humidity, thick ice can form inside the carburetor even when the outside air is as warm as +20°C.

q.t: What is the task of cooling fins on air-cooled engine cylinders?
o: Increasing the airflow thus improving cooling of cylinder parts
Leading the airflow to parts designated to be cooled
Cooling of the cylinder surrounding airflow and forwarding to hotter engine parts
Quick heat transfer to the surrounding air flow by expanding the surface
q.e: Aviation engines do not use liquid radiators due to weight. Instead, the cylinders are cast with dozens of thin metal fins. These fins exponentially increase the surface area of the hot metal exposed to the rushing ram air, ensuring rapid and efficient heat dissipation.

q.t: Cylinder head temperature indication relates to...
q.e: Airflow is never perfectly equal across all cylinders in an air-cooled engine; one cylinder usually runs the hottest due to its location in the cowling. The CHT (Cylinder Head Temperature) sensor is always installed on this specific, hottest "critical cylinder" to prevent engine meltdown.

q.t: What happens during oil filter clocking?
o: A bypass valve opens thus enabling the circulation to continue, debris will not be filtered
The oil circulation will end after 30 minutes so that a proper engine run will not be guaranteed
The oil circulation will end after 15 minutes so that a proper engine run will not be guaranteed
A bypass valve opens thus enabling the circulation to continue, debris will be filtered by an alternate filter
q.e: If the oil filter becomes completely clogged (clocked) with carbon or metal shavings, oil pressure would skyrocket and flow would stop, seizing the engine. To prevent this fatal outcome, a spring-loaded bypass valve opens, sending unfiltered, dirty oil to the engine to keep it running until you can land.

q.t: How should an Otto engine be shut down?
o: By closing the throttle lever completely
By moving the propeller to the feathered position
q.e: Piston (Otto) aircraft engines are shut down by pulling the mixture control knob completely out to the "Idle Cut-Off" position. This physically starves the engine of all fuel, ensuring that no unburned fuel is left in the cylinders which could cause accidental engine firing later.

q.t: Piston engines of helicopters have...
q.e: For redundancy and safety, certified aviation piston engines (whether in airplanes or helicopters) are mandated to have two entirely separate, self-generating magneto ignition systems firing two spark plugs per cylinder. If one fails, the engine continues running on the other.

q.t: How do you call fuel mixtures with a high amount of fuel?
q.e: In engine terminology, a fuel-air mixture that contains a high proportion of fuel relative to the amount of oxygen is referred to as a "Rich" mixture. It is typically used for engine starting, take-off, and high-power cooling.

q.t: The angle indicated by arrow number 1 shows the propeller's... See figure
q.e: In the provided propeller blade cross-section, the angle measured between the blade's chord line (C) and the propeller's flat plane of rotation (R) is structurally fixed by the manufacturer (or the governor). This is the blade pitch angle, or the geometric angle of incidence.

q.t: How should a power increase be executed on a constant-speed propeller, provided that no other procedure is described in the flight manual?
q.e: To avoid disastrous over-pressurization and detonation inside the engine cylinders, you must never push high manifold pressure into an engine running at low RPM. The correct rule is: Always increase RPM (prop lever forward) FIRST, then increase manifold pressure (throttle forward) SECOND.

q.t: How should a power decrease be executed on a constant-speed propeller, provided that no other procedure is described in the flight manual?
q.e: Following the same logic to prevent over-stressing the engine, when reducing power, you must reduce the combustion pressure (throttle backwards) FIRST, and only after the pressure is low can you safely pull back the prop lever to decrease the RPM (decrease RPM SECOND).

q.t: With increasing altitude and unchanged mixture setting, the air/fuel mixture...
q.e: As the aircraft climbs, the air becomes less dense (fewer oxygen molecules). If the carburetor continues to inject the exact same volume of fuel as it did at sea level, the ratio of fuel to oxygen becomes highly saturated, meaning the mixture becomes excessively "rich".

q.t: With increasing altitude, the power of a carburettor engine...
o: first decreases, from 5000 ft on increases.
q.e: Normally aspirated (non-turbocharged) piston engines rely purely on ambient atmospheric pressure to suck air into the cylinders. As altitude increases and air density drops, the engine breathes in less oxygen per stroke, resulting in a continuous and unavoidable decrease in horsepower.

q.t: During ignition check the ignition is switched to OFF for a short moment and subsequently back to BOTH. What happens to the RPM if the ignition system is properly grounded?
o: The RPM increases once switched to OFF and resumes the previous value when switched back to BOTH
The RPM increases once switched to OFF and resumes a value below the previous one when switched back to BOTH
The RPM decreases once switched to OFF and resumes a value below the previous one when switched back to BOTH
The RPM decreases once switched to OFF and resumes the previous value when switched back to BOTH
q.e: This is a "grounding check" done at idle. By briefly turning the key to OFF, you test if the P-lead wires are properly grounding the magnetos. If they are, the spark dies and the engine RPM abruptly drops (engine tries to die). Switching back to BOTH restores the spark and the RPM instantly recovers.

q.t: Which gauges involve a measurement of temperature?
o: Engine lubricant, exhaust gas, outside air, cabin air, directional gyro
Engine oil, cylinder head, exhaust gas, altimeter, airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator
Engine lubricant, engine cooling fluid, cylinder head, exhaust gas, outside air, cabin air
Engine lubricant, cylinder head, exhaust gas, suction, outside air, cabin air
q.e: Aviation instrument panels are filled with temperature gauges to monitor engine health and environment: Oil Temp (lubricant), Coolant Temp (for liquid-cooled engines like Rotax), Cylinder Head Temp (CHT), Exhaust Gas Temp (EGT), Outside Air Temp (OAT), and Cabin Temp.

q.t: Fuel quantity in small aircraft is most commonly measured through a level sensor. The European Certification Specifications CS 23 require that...
o: if no fuel quantity indicator is available to the pilot in flight, the pilot must check the fuel quantity before commencing the flight and recalculate the remaining fuel on board in regular intervals during the flight.

at least one fuel quantity indicator must be available to indicate the total amount of fuel abord an aircraft. This Indicator must be calibrated adequately to indicate the correct amount of fuel during all phases of flight.
if the fuel indicator fails, the pilot must land at the next available airport.

a fuel quantity indicator must be available for each tank and the indicator must be calibrated to read "zero" during level flight when the quantity of fuel remaining in the tank is equal to the unusable fuel supply.
q.e: Aviation fuel float gauges are notoriously inaccurate due to aircraft pitching and banking. Therefore, certification rules demand only one absolute truth: the gauge MUST accurately hit the "Zero" mark exactly when the tank dries up to the unusable fuel level, giving the pilot an unmistakable warning of impending engine starvation.

q.t: Which of the instruments listed below obtain their readings through pressure measurement?
o: Airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass, oil pressure gauge, fuel pressure gauge
Oil pressure gauge, fuel pressure gauge, fuel quantity gauge, manifold pressure gauge, differential pressure gauge, altimeter
Airspeed indicator, vertical speed indicator, altimeter, directional gyro, turn and bank coordinator, oil pressure gauge, fuel pressure gauge
Oil pressure gauge, fuel pressure gauge, manifold pressure gauge, altimeter, vertical speed indicator, airspeed indicator, suction gauge
q.e: Pressure operates a vast array of mechanical aircraft instruments. Liquids under pressure drive the Oil and Fuel pressure gauges. Vacuum (suction) pressure drives gyros. Manifold absolute pressure (MAP) reads engine intake air. Finally, ambient air pressure variations drive the entire Pitot-Static trio: Altimeter, VSI, and Airspeed Indicator.

q.t: The Pitot / static system is required to...
o: correct the reading of the airspeed indicator to zero when the aircraft is static on the ground.
prevent potential static buildup on the aircraft.
prevent icing of the Pitot tube.
measure total and static air pressure.
q.e: The fundamental aerodynamic purpose of the aircraft's pitot-static system is to capture the stagnant, undisturbed ambient air pressure (Static pressure) and the ram-air pressure caused by the aircraft's forward motion (Total pressure) to feed the flight instruments.

q.t: Which pressure is sensed by the Pitot tube?
q.e: The pitot tube is a forward-facing open pipe. It catches the brute-force impact of the oncoming wind. This captured pressure consists of BOTH the dynamic pressure of the moving air AND the existing static pressure of the atmosphere combined. In physics, this combined force is called the "Total Pressure."

q.t: QFE is the...
o: altitude above the reference pressure level 1013.25 hPa.
barometric pressure adjusted to sea level, using the international standard atmosphere (ISA).
barometric pressure at a reference datum, typically the runway threshold of an airfield.
q.e: QFE (Field Elevation) is the literal, physical barometric pressure measured directly on the tarmac of an aerodrome. If you dial QFE into your altimeter while parked, the instrument will read exactly zero feet.

q.t: QNE is the...
o: barometric pressure at a reference datum, typically the runway threshold of an airfield.
barometric pressure adjusted to sea level, using the international standard atmosphere (ISA).
altitude above the reference pressure level 1013.25 hPa.
q.e: QNE is the aviation code for the standard altimeter setting (1013.25 hPa or 29.92 inHg). When pilots climb into the high-altitude airways (Flight Levels), they all dial QNE into their subscales to ensure standard vertical separation based on this theoretical pressure altitude, regardless of local weather.

q.t: Which is the purpose of the altimeter subscale?
o: To set the reference level for the altitude decoder of the transponder
To correct the altimeter reading for system errors
To adjust the altimeter reading for non-standard temperature
To reference the altimeter reading to a predetermined level such as mean sea level, aerodrome level or pressure level 1013.25 hPa
q.e: The Kollsman window (subscale) allows the pilot to manually calibrate the altimeter's internal aneroid wafers against changing daily weather systems. By turning the knob, the pilot sets a baseline pressure reference (like QNH for sea level, or 1013 for standard) so the needles indicate the correct altitude relative to that chosen datum.

q.t: In which way may an altimeter subscale which is set to an incorrect QNH lead to an incorrect altimeter reading?
o: If the subscale is set to a higher than actual pressure, the indication is too low. This may lead to much greater heights above the ground than intended
If the subscale is set to a lower than actual pressure, the indication is too high. This may lead to much closer proximity to the ground than intended
If the subscale is set to a lower than actual pressure, the indication is too low. This may lead to much closer proximity to the ground than intended
If the subscale is set to a higher than actual pressure, the indication is too high. This may lead to much closer proximity to the ground than intended
q.e: From High to Low, Look out Below. If you leave a high QNH (e.g., 1030) set in your window but fly into a low-pressure storm system (e.g., 990), your altimeter thinks it's still in dense air and reads artificially HIGH (e.g., indicating a safe 4000 ft). In reality, the low pressure means you are sinking dangerously LOW, potentially flying into terrain while the instrument lies to you.

q.t: Lower-than-standard temperature may lead to...
o: a correct altitude indication as long as the altimeter subscale is set to correct for non-standard temperature.
a blockage of the Pitot tube by ice, freezing the altimeter indication to its present value.
an altitude indication which is too low.
an altitude indication which is too high.
q.e: From Hot to Cold, Don't Be Bold. Freezing cold air severely compresses the atmospheric column, causing pressure levels to sag closer to the earth. Your altimeter, calibrated for warmer ISA conditions, doesn't know the air shrank. It happily points to a falsely HIGH altitude (e.g., showing 5000 ft), while your aircraft is physically flying much closer to the dangerous mountain peaks below.

q.t: A flight level is a...
q.e: Flight Levels (e.g., FL 100, FL 350) do not measure tape-measure distance to the ground or the sea. They are theoretical, isobaric planes in the sky derived purely from the standard pressure setting of 1013.25 hPa. Therefore, a Flight Level is strictly a "Pressure Altitude."

q.t: A true altitude is...
o: a height above ground level corrected for non-standard pressure.
a pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature.
a height above ground level corrected for non-standard temperature.
an altitude above mean sea level corrected for non-standard temperature.
q.e: While indicated altitude (QNH) is your height above the sea, it is flawed by extreme temperatures. If you take out a flight computer and mathematically correct your indicated altitude for the massive shrinking or expanding effect of extreme cold or heat (OAT deviations from ISA), the resulting pinpoint-accurate distance from the ocean is your True Altitude.

q.t: During a flight in colder-than-ISA air the indicated altitude is...
q.e: Reiterating the temperature trap: Since cold air contracts and sinks, the real physical altitude of the aircraft drops down closer to the ground. However, the uncorrected altimeter on the dashboard remains oblivious to the cold and displays a falsely HIGH indicated number, making you think you are safer than you actually are.

q.t: During a flight in an air mass with a temperature equal to ISA and the QNH set correctly, the indicated altitude is...
q.e: If you hit the meteorological jackpot and fly on a perfect day where the temperature flawlessly matches the theoretical ISA model (+15°C at sea level, dropping 2° per 1000 ft), the altimeter's internal math works perfectly. Your indicated dial reading will exactly match your True tape-measure Altitude above the ocean.

q.t: Which instrument can be affected by the hysteresis error?
q.e: When an aircraft performs a massive, rapid descent from high altitude, the corrugated metal aneroid capsules inside the Altimeter are violently crushed by the changing pressure. When leveling off, the metal has "memory" and is sluggish to snap back into its original shape. This metallic lag causes the altimeter to temporarily read incorrectly, an effect known as Hysteresis.

q.t: The measurement of altitude is based on the change of the...
q.e: The atmosphere is a giant ocean of air stacked on top of us. As you climb, there is less air above pushing down, so the ambient weight of the atmosphere decreases. The altimeter's sole job is to measure this decaying, calm, undisturbed ambient weight, which is purely the Static Pressure.

q.t: Which of the following options states the working principle of a vertical speed indicator?
o: Total air pressure is measured and compared to static pressure
Measuring the vertical acceleration through the displacement of a gimbal-mounted mass
Static air pressure is measured and compared against a vacuum
Measuring the present static air pressure and comparing it to the static air pressure inside a reservoir
q.e: The Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI) consists of a sealed metal reservoir with a tiny, calibrated leak (capillary tube) to the outside static air. When you climb, the outside pressure drops instantly, but the air trapped inside the reservoir bleeds out slowly through the tiny leak. The instrument measures this temporary pressure difference between the "now" (outside) and the "past" (inside) to display your climb rate in feet per minute.

q.t: The vertical speed indicator measures the difference of pressure between...
o: the present dynamic pressure and the static pressure of a previous moment.
the present total pressure and the total pressure of a previous moment.
the present dynamic pressure and the dynamic pressure of a previous moment.
the present static pressure and the static pressure of a previous moment.
q.e: As detailed above, the VSI mechanically pits the instantaneous, newly changing outside Static pressure against the delayed, older Static pressure trapped inside its internal thermos-like reservoir. The resulting pressure battle drives the needle up or down.

q.t: Calibrated airspeed (CAS) equals...
o: ground speed (GS) corrected for instrument and position error.
indicated airspeed (IAS) corrected for instrument and position error.
q.e: The airspeed indicator in the cockpit (IAS) is a mechanical gauge susceptible to friction, and the pitot tube on the wing is subject to airflow distortion from the aircraft's nose and flaps (Position error). Engineers calculate these flaws, and when you subtract these physical and aerodynamic lies from the IAS, you get the pure, refined Calibrated Airspeed (CAS).

q.t: At higher altitudes, true airspeed (TAS) tends to be higher than calibrated airspeed (CAS). A rough estimate of the TAS can be obtained by...
o: subtracting 10 % of the CAS for every 1000 m altitude.
subtracting 2 % of the CAS for every 1000 ft altitude.
adding 10 % of the CAS for every 1000 ft altitude.
adding 2 % of the CAS for every 1000 ft altitude.
q.e: Because air gets thinner at altitude, fewer air molecules hit the pitot tube, causing the airspeed needle (CAS) to artificially read low. To find your actual speed through the airmass (True Airspeed), you use a pilot's rule of thumb: Add 2% to your indicated speed for every 1,000 feet you have climbed above sea level.

q.t: An aircraft cruises on a heading of 180° with a true airspeed of 100 kt. The wind comes from 180° with 30 kt. Neglecting instrument and position errors, which will be the approximate reading of the airspeed indicator?
q.e: This is a classic trap. The airspeed indicator measures the aircraft's speed RELATIVE to the block of air it is flying inside. The pitot tube doesn't know and doesn't care what the wind is doing relative to the ground. If you are plowing through the airmass at a True Airspeed of 100 knots, the indicator will proudly display 100 knots, regardless of whether a 30-knot headwind is slowing your Ground Speed (GS) down to 70 knots over the trees.

q.t: Which of the following factors could cause an erroneous airspeed indication?
o: The earth wire is still attached
The boost pressure line is defective
The aircraft is covered with adhesive foils
q.e: A functional airspeed indicator relies entirely on clear, unblocked pneumatic plumbing from the outside world. If a mechanic or pilot leaves adhesive tape (foils) covering the static ports or pitot tube after washing or painting the aircraft, the instrument is totally blinded and will show catastrophic errors or remain dead at zero.

q.t: Which of the following states the working principle of an airspeed indicator?
o: Dynamic air pressure is measured by the Pitot tube and converted into a speed indication by the airspeed indicator
Static air pressure is measured and compared against a vacuum.
Total air pressure is measured by the static ports and converted into a speed indication by the airspeed indicator
Total air pressure is measured and compared against static air pressure.
q.e: The forward-facing pitot tube acts as a ram, catching the violent "Total Pressure" of the wind. To find out how much of that impact is purely due to your forward speed, the instrument mechanically subtracts the calm, ambient "Static Pressure" (piped in from the side of the fuselage). The remaining force is pure Dynamic Pressure, which expands a diaphragm to push the airspeed needle.

q.t: What values are usually marked with a red line on instrument displays?
q.e: Across all aviation instruments—whether measuring terrifying structural airspeeds (Vne), engine RPM, or blistering cylinder head temperatures—a stark Red Line represents the absolute "Operational Limit." Crossing this redline guarantees severe mechanical damage, engine failure, or in-flight structural break-up.

q.t: What is necessary for the determination of speed (IAS) by the airspeed indicator?
o: The difference between the standard pressure and the total pressure
The difference between the total pressure and the dynamic pressure
The difference between the dynamic pressure and the static pressure
The difference betweeen the total pressure and the static presssure
q.e: Reiterating the mechanical magic of the ASI: It takes the brute-force impact of the headwind (Total Pressure from the pitot tube) and subtracts the ambient atmospheric weight (Static Pressure from the static port). The resulting differential drives the needle across the dial.

q.t: What is the meaning of the white arc on the airspeed indicator?
q.e: The thick white band painted on the airspeed dial dictates the structural safety envelope for deploying the large, fragile aluminum flaps beneath the wing. The bottom of the white arc is the stall speed with flaps down (Vso), and the top is the maximum speed you can fly before the wind tears the extended flaps off the hinges (Vfe).

q.t: What is the meaning of the red range on the airspeed indicator?
o: Speed which must not be exceeded within bumpy air
Speed which must not be exceeded with flaps extended
Speed which must not be exceeded in turns with more than 45° bank
Speed which must not be exceeded regardless of circumstances
q.e: The red radial line (Vne - Velocity Never Exceed) marks the ultimate redline of the airframe. Pushing the nose down and accelerating past this mark, regardless of how smooth the air is, will cause the wings and tail to begin an uncontrollable, vibrating resonance (flutter) that will instantly shatter the aircraft in mid-air.

q.t: The compass error caused by the aircraft's magnetic field is called...
q.e: The cockpit is an electromagnetic nightmare: running alternators, buzzing radios, moving steel control columns, and metal engine blocks. This localized metallic junk creates its own tiny magnetic field inside the cabin, which attracts and pulls the floating compass needle away from True North. This localized aircraft error is called "Deviation."

q.t: The indication of a magnetic compass deviates from magnetic north direction due to what errors?
o: Inclination and declination of the earth's magnetic field
q.e: A wet magnetic compass is a flawed, bouncing instrument. It suffers from internal cockpit interference (Deviation). Furthermore, because the compass card hangs on a pivot like a pendulum, whenever the pilot pitches down to speed up (Acceleration error) or banks hard to the side (Turning error), the heavy card swings and physically dips, giving wildly false and confusing heading readings.

q.t: Which of the mentioned cockpit instruments is connected to the pitot tube?
q.e: Out of the "Holy Trinity" of pneumatic flight instruments (Altimeter, VSI, ASI), ONLY the Airspeed Indicator requires the violent, forward-facing ram-air pressure to measure how fast the plane is piercing the sky. Therefore, it is the sole instrument connected via tubing to the Pitot probe on the wing.

q.t: Which cockpit instruments are connected to the static port?
o: Airspeed indicator, direct-reading compass, slip indicator
Altimeter, vertical speed indicator, airspeed indicator
q.e: The static port provides a calm, undisturbed sample of the ambient atmospheric pressure outside the aircraft. This baseline reference is absolutely vital for the Altimeter (to measure height), the Vertical Speed Indicator (to measure climbing pressure drops), AND the Airspeed Indicator (to subtract from the pitot pressure). All three rely on this static line.

q.t: An aircraft in the northern hemisphere intends to turn on the shortest way from a heading of 270° to a heading of 360°. At approximately which indication of the magnetic compass should the turn be terminated?
q.e: Northern Turning Error (UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South). Because the magnetic field lines dip sharply into the earth in the northern hemisphere, the compass card tilts during a bank. When turning towards North (360°), the compass lags lazily behind the actual turn. If the pilot waits until the compass says 360, they will have flown way past it. Therefore, the pilot must aggressively roll out early, "undershooting" the turn by about 30 degrees, ending the turn when the compass reads 330°.

q.t: An aircraft in the northern hemisphere intends to turn on the shortest way from a heading of 360° to a heading of 270°. At approximately which indication of the magnetic compass should the turn be terminated?
q.e: Unlike turns to the North or South, turning onto a pure East (090) or West (270) heading doesn't trigger the magnetic dipping lag. The compass needle remains remarkably stable and true. Therefore, the pilot can trust the instrument and simply roll the wings level exactly when the compass hits 270°.

q.t: The term "static pressure" is defined as pressure...
o: resulting from orderly flow of air particles.
q.e: Static pressure is the pure, raw weight of the atmospheric column of air sitting on top of the aircraft. It represents the pressure of the air mass in its natural, undisturbed state, completely devoid of any dynamic ram-effects caused by the aircraft's speeding nose.

q.t: An aircraft in the northern hemisphere intends to turn on the shortest way from a heading of 030° to a heading of 180°. At approximately which indicated magnetic heading should the turn be terminated?
q.e: Revisiting the UNOS rule (Overshoot South). When turning towards the South (180°), the compass needle wildly leads and races AHEAD of the aircraft's actual nose. If you stop turning when the compass says 180, you haven't actually reached South yet. You must keep turning, "overshooting" the target by about 30 degrees, and roll out when the manic compass reads 210°. (Once you level the wings, the compass will settle back to the real 180°).

q.t: What does the dynamic pressure depend directly on?
o: Air density and airflow speed squared
q.e: The formula for dynamic pressure (q) is 1/2 * Rho * V^2. This means the brutal force of the wind smashing into the aircraft depends linearly on the thickness of the air (Air Density), and massively on the aircraft's speed, which is squared (Airflow speed squared). Doubling your speed quadruples the wind force!

q.t: What is a cause for the dip error on the direct-reading compass?
o: Inclination of earth's magnetic field lines
q.e: At the equator, magnetic field lines run parallel to the ground. But in the northern hemisphere, the magnetic lines dive steeply down into the Earth's crust towards the magnetic core. This downward pull (Inclination/Dip) yanks the northern end of the compass needle downward, throwing the floating card off balance during banks and accelerations.

q.t: What behaviour is shown by a rotating gyro in space?
o: It moves in circles with a stadily decreasing radius
It moves in accordance with the body surrounding it
It swings from east to west like a pendulum
It tends to maintain its position in space
q.e: The principle of "Gyroscopic Rigidity in Space." A heavy brass rotor spinning at 20,000 RPM inside an instrument case becomes incredibly stable. It vehemently refuses to tilt or change its orientation. If the aircraft loops or rolls around it, the spinning gyro remains completely stationary relative to the universe, providing the pilot with an unwavering artificial horizon.

q.t: A gyro which is rotating in space responds to forces being applied to it by an evasive movement...
o: at an angle of 180° to the force being applied.
at an angle of 45° to the force being applied.
at an angle of 90° to the force being applied.
q.e: This is "Gyroscopic Precession." If you take a spinning gyroscope and push hard on the top of it, it does not tilt backwards as expected. Instead, the force is carried around by the rotation and manifests exactly 90 degrees later in the direction of spin, causing the gyro to tilt completely to the side. This bizarre physics trick is utilized in aircraft Turn Coordinators.

q.t: The bank angle of a 2-minutes circle depends on the...
q.e: A 2-minute turn (Rate 1 turn) means flying a perfect 360-degree circle in 120 seconds (3 degrees per second). To achieve this geometry, a slow trainer plane only needs to tilt its wings a gentle 15 degrees. But a jet fighter traveling at an immense True Airspeed (TAS) covers so much distance that it must bank aggressively (e.g., 60 degrees) just to wrench its flight path into that same tight 2-minute circle.

q.t: A turn and bank (or turn and slip) coordinator provides information regarding...
o: the coordination of the turn and slip angle.
the pitch and bank angle of the aircraft.
the rate of turn and bank angle of the aircraft.
the rate of turn and coordination, i.e. slip or skid, of the turn.
q.e: This iconic "Bat and Ball" instrument does two things. The miniature airplane model on the dial reacts to a tilted internal gyro, showing exactly how fast the nose is sweeping across the horizon (Rate of turn). Meanwhile, the black glass ball sitting in the curved fluid tube acts as a gravity pendulum, indicating whether the pilot's rudder inputs are balanced, or if the plane is sliding sideways (Slip or Skid).

q.t: The airspeed indicator is unservicable. The airplane may only be operated...
o: if only airfield patterns are flown.
if no maintenance organisation is around.
when a GPS with speed indication is used during flight.
when the airspeed indicator is fully functional again.
q.e: Aviation law and common sense dictate a zero-tolerance policy for a dead Airspeed Indicator. A GPS only shows ground speed, which is useless for knowing if your wings are about to stall and drop you from the sky. The ASI is a required, primary life-saving flight instrument. If it is broken, the aircraft is legally grounded and completely prohibited from flying until repaired.

q.t: Which light colour advises the pilot to the condition "corrective action may be required in the future"?
q.e: Cockpit warning lights follow a strict psychological color code. Green means normal operation. A glaring Red light screams "Immediate catastrophic danger, act now or die!" However, a glowing Amber (Yellow/Orange) "Caution" light signifies a degradation or system anomaly that isn't instantly lethal, but demands the pilot's heightened awareness and corrective troubleshooting to prevent it from worsening.

q.t: The Caution Area is marked on an airspeed indicator by what color?
q.e: The bold Yellow Arc painted on the glass of the airspeed indicator represents the "Caution Range." When the needle sweeps into this yellow zone, the aircraft is flying dangerously fast. The airframe can handle it only if the air is completely dead calm. If a sudden thunderstorm gust hits the plane at this speed, the wings could be structurally bent or ripped off.

q.t: An attitude director indicator (ADI) combines the information provided by...
o: the attitude indicator and the relative bearing indicator.
the directional gyro and the rate gyro.
the attitude indicator and the radio magnetic indicator.
the attitude indicator and the flight director.
q.e: Found in high-end glass cockpits and airliners, the ADI doesn't just show a dumb, passive artificial horizon (Attitude Indicator). It overlays active, glowing crosshairs or V-bars (the Flight Director) driven by the navigation computer. These command bars visually tell the pilot exactly where to pitch and roll the yoke to perfectly capture an ILS glideslope or follow a GPS route.

q.t: What does the abbreviation HSI stand for?
q.e: The HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator) is a complex, top-tier navigational instrument. Instead of forcing the pilot to look at a compass on the ceiling and a VOR dial on the panel and mentally combine them, the HSI mechanically merges a rotating gyro-compass card with a course deviation needle into one single, glorious, top-down map-like view of the aircraft's navigation situation.

q.t: A horizontal situation indicator (HSI) combines the information provided by...
o: the attitude indicator and the flight director.
the rate gyro and the slip indicator.
the directional gyro and the flight director.
the directional gyro and the VHF navigation receiver.
q.e: As detailed above, the HSI features an outer rotating compass ring driven by a remote Directional Gyro (heading). Nested directly in the center of this compass is a moving course deviation needle (CDI) driven by the VHF Navigation Receiver (catching VOR/LOC radio signals). It flawlessly blends your heading and your radio tracking into one instrument.

q.t: What difference in altitude is shown by an altimeter, if the reference pressure scale setting is changed from 1000 hPa to 1010 hPa?
q.e: The classic "30 feet per hPa" rule of thumb. You turned the altimeter subscale knob UP by 10 hPa (from 1000 to 1010). The internal gears of the instrument respond by artificially winding the altitude needle UP by 300 feet (10 * 30 ft = 300 ft). To convert 300 feet into metric distance, you multiply by 0.3, yielding approximately 90 meters (with 80 meters being the closest correct multiple-choice option for the metric rounding used in EASA tests).

q.t: When is it necessary to adjust the pressure in the reference scale of an alitimeter?
o: Once a month before flight operation
Every day before the first flight
Before every flight and during cross country flights
q.e: The atmosphere is a living, breathing ocean; barometric pressure drops and rises constantly with passing weather fronts. To prevent flying 500 feet too low and hitting a radio mast, the pilot bears the absolute responsibility to actively tune the altimeter's Kollsman window to the freshest, most local QNH pressure setting broadcasted by the tower before takeoff, and continuously update it via radio along the route during cross-country flights.

q.t: The altimeter's reference scale is set to airfield pressure (QFE). What indication is shown during the flight?
q.e: QFE is a highly localized, club-level altimeter setting. The pilot twists the knob until the altimeter forces the needles down to read exactly "Zero" while parked on the runway. Upon taking off and flying the traffic pattern, the altimeter acts like a tape measure dropped directly from the belly of the plane to the runway tarmac below, indicating pure Height (AGL) strictly above that specific airfield.

q.t: A vertical speed indicator connected to a too big equalizing tank results in...
q.e: The Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI) relies on a delicate volume of air trapped in a small internal thermos (reservoir). If a mechanic accidentally plumbs the VSI into an oversized, massive reservoir tank, climbing the aircraft will cause an excessively massive volume of air to try and escape through the tiny capillary leak all at once. This huge pressure backlog will slam against the diaphragm, causing the needle to wildly over-read and show an indication that is terrifyingly and falsely high!

q.t: A vertical speed indicator measures the difference between...
o: instantaneous total pressure and previous total pressure.
instantaneous static pressure and previous static pressure.
q.e: The VSI is the only instrument that compares the "Now" against the "Past". It takes the raw, instantaneous Static pressure fed directly from the outside port, and mechanically fights it against the older, delayed Static pressure slowly bleeding out of its internal trapped reservoir. The difference between these two static pressures moves the climb/descent needle.

q.t: The term "inclination" is defined as...
o: angle between magnetic and true north.
angle between airplane's longitudinal axis and true north.
angle between earth's magnetic field lines and horizontal plane.
q.e: Near the Earth's equator, magnetic field lines float horizontally, parallel to the ground. However, near the North and South poles, these massive magnetic lines dive steeply down, plunging into the Earth's crust. This sharp, downward diving angle of the magnetic field relative to the flat horizontal horizon is mathematically termed "Inclination" (or Magnetic Dip).

q.t: What does the slip indicator show?
q.e: The slip indicator is the simple black glass ball swimming in fluid at the bottom of the Turn Coordinator. This ball has absolutely zero connection to the real horizon or the ground. It is blindly thrown around by the combined sum of gravity and centrifugal turning forces inside the aircraft. It therefore rests at the lowest point of this combined force field, indicating to the pilot the "Apparent Vertical" (the perceived "down" inside the maneuvering cockpit).

q.t: The slip indicator's ball (apparent vertical) has moved to the right during a right turn. By what actions may the ball led back to middle position?
o: Reduce rate of turn, reduce bank
Increase bank, increase rate of turn
Reduce bank, increase rate of turn
q.e: In a right turn, the ball fell to the right (the inside of the turn). The aircraft is "Slipping" into the turn because it is banked too steeply for the lazy rate it is turning at. To rescue the ball and coordinate the flight, the pilot must "Step on the ball" (push right rudder to aggressively increase the rate of turn) AND simultaneously raise the right wing slightly (reduce the excessive bank angle).

q.t: What is the purpose of winglets?
o: Increase of lift and turning manoeuvering capabilities.
To increase efficiency of aspect ratio.
Increase gliging performance at high speed.
q.e: Winglets are the vertical, shark-fin-like upward extensions bolted to the very tips of modern airliner wings. They act as physical aerodynamic fences, blocking the high-pressure air from underneath the wing from violently curling around the tip to the top. By breaking up these massive, energy-stealing wingtip vortices, winglets drastically reduce Induced Drag, saving tons of fuel on long flights.

q.t: What engines are commonly used with Touring Motor Gliders (TMG)?
q.e: Touring Motor Gliders (TMG) require extremely reliable, fuel-efficient, and relatively smooth-running powerplants for long-distance cruising. The aviation industry universally relies on flat, horizontally-opposed, air-cooled 4-cylinder, 4-stroke engines (like the famous Rotax 912 or Limbach series) to perfectly fulfill this role in the nose of TMGs.

q.t: What is the purpose of engine oil in piston engine?
o: Cooling of the engine and lubrication of propeller shaft.
Cooling, lubrication and increasing engine performance.
For nose reduction and bearing of the propeller shaft.
Cooling, lubrication of the engine and disposal of fine abrasion.
q.e: Aviation engine oil is the lifeblood of the powerplant, performing a grueling triple-duty: It coats the violently moving pistons in a slick film to prevent metal-on-metal destruction (Lubrication); it absorbs the searing inferno of combustion heat and carries it away to the oil cooler (Cooling); and it aggressively washes away microscopic metal shavings and carbon soot, carrying them to the filter (Disposal of fine abrasion).

q.t: The rotational axis of the Earth runs through the...
o: geographic North Pole and on the magnetic south pole.
magnetic north pole and on the geographic South Pole.
magnetic north pole and on the magnetic south pole.
geographic North Pole and on the geographic South Pole.
q.e: The Earth physically spins around an imaginary line in space. The two points where this axis of rotation intersects the Earth's surface are defined strictly as the geographic North Pole and the geographic South Pole.

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the polar axis of the Earth?
o: The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is at an angle of 23.5° to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is at an angle of 66.5° to the plane of the equator
q.e: The geographic polar axis is the theoretical line around which the Earth rotates. In a standard coordinate system, this polar axis is perfectly perpendicular (90 degrees) to the equatorial plane that divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern hemispheres.

q.t: Which approximate, geometrical form describes the shape of the Earth best for navigation systems?
q.e: The Earth is not a perfect sphere; centrifugal forces from its rotation cause it to bulge at the equator and flatten at the poles. For precise aviation and GPS navigation (like WGS-84), this shape is best modelled mathematically as an oblate ellipsoid.

q.t: Which statement about a rhumb line is correct?
o: The center of a complete cycle of a rhumb line is always the Earth's center.
A rhumb line cuts each meridian at the same angle.
The shortest track between two points along the Earth's surface follows a rhumb line.
A rhumb line is a great circle intersecting the the equator with 45° angle.
q.e: A rhumb line (or loxodrome) is a line crossing all meridians of longitude at the same, constant angle. Because meridians converge at the poles, following a constant heading (rhumb line) creates a spiral path towards the pole, making it easy to steer but not the shortest distance.

q.t: The shortest distance between two points on Earth is represented by a part of...
q.e: In spherical geometry, the absolutely shortest path between any two points on the surface of a sphere is the arc of a Great Circle (orthodrome). A great circle is any circle whose center matches the center of the Earth.

q.t: The circumference of the Earth at the equator is approximately...
q.e: The equator is a great circle consisting of 360 degrees. Every single degree contains 60 minutes of arc. Since one minute of arc on a great circle defines exactly one Nautical Mile (NM), the total circumference is 360 * 60 = 21,600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in latitude between A (12°53'30"N) and B (07°34'30"S)?
q.e: Because point A is in the Northern hemisphere and point B is in the Southern hemisphere, you must add their absolute distances from the equator together. Adding 12°53'30" to 07°34'30" yields exactly 20 degrees and 28 minutes.

q.t: Where are the two polar circles?
o: 23.5° north and south of the poles
23.5° north and south of the equator
q.e: The Earth's rotational axis is tilted at approximately 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane. The polar circles (Arctic and Antarctic) are located at 66.5° latitude, which is mathematically exactly 23.5° away from the poles (90° - 23.5°).

q.t: What is the distance between the parallels of latitude 48°N and 49°N along a meridian line?
q.e: Meridians of longitude are great circles. The difference between 48°N and 49°N is exactly one degree of latitude. One degree equals 60 minutes of arc, and 1 minute of arc on a great circle equals 1 Nautical Mile. Thus, the distance is 60 NM.

q.t: What distance corresponds to one degree difference in latitude along any degree of longitude?
q.e: As established in the previous principle: along any meridian (a line of longitude), traversing exactly one degree of latitude covers 60 minutes of arc, equating directly to a physical distance of 60 Nautical Miles.

q.t: Point A on the Earth's surface lies exactly on the parallel of latitude of 47°50'27"N. Which point is exactly 240 NM north of A?
q.e: Traveling due north means flying along a meridian. Since 1 degree equals 60 NM, traveling 240 NM corresponds to a change of exactly 4 degrees (240 / 60 = 4). Adding 4 degrees to 47°50'27"N results in 51°50'27"N.

q.t: What is the distance between the two parallels of longitude 150°E and 151°E along the equator?
q.e: The equator is the only line of latitude that is also a great circle. Therefore, moving 1 degree of longitude precisely along the equator covers 60 minutes of a great circle, which translates perfectly to 60 NM.

q.t: What is the great circle distance between two points A and B on the equator when the difference between the two associated meridians is exactly one degree of longitude?
q.e: This is a re-phrasing of the same geometric rule. Because the equator is a great circle, an angular difference of one degree translates to 60 arc-minutes, which defines a physical distance of 60 Nautical Miles.

q.t: Assume two arbitrary points A and B on the same parallel of latitude, but not on the equator. Point A is located on 010°E and point B on 020°E. The rumb line distance between A and B is always...
q.e: The distance is 10 degrees of longitude. If they were on the equator, the distance would be 10 * 60 = 600 NM. However, lines of longitude converge as you move away from the equator toward the poles. Thus, along any other parallel, 10 degrees of longitude covers less physical distance than 600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 20° of longitude?
q.e: The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, meaning it rotates 15° every hour, or 1° every 4 minutes. Moving 20° of longitude takes 20 * 4 = 80 minutes. 80 minutes is equal to 1 hour and 20 minutes (1:20 h).

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 10° of longitude?
q.e: Applying the same rotational math: The Earth rotates 1 degree every 4 minutes. Therefore, the sun transiting across 10 degrees of longitude takes exactly 10 * 4 = 40 minutes (0:40 h).

q.t: The sun moves 10° of longitude. What is the difference in time?
q.e: This question asks for the 40-minute time difference expressed in decimal hours. 40 minutes divided by 60 minutes equals 2/3 of an hour, which is mathematically 0.66 hours.

q.t: With Central European Summer Time (CEST) given as UTC+2, what UTC time corresponds to 1600 CEST?
q.e: If the local summer time (CEST) is two hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC + 2), you must subtract 2 hours from the local time to find UTC. 16:00 minus 2 hours is 14:00 UTC.

q.t: UTC is...
o: a local time in Central Europe.
local mean time at a specific point on Earth.
an obligatory time used in aviation.
q.e: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), often referred to as "Zulu time", is the mandatory, unified time standard used globally in aviation to prevent scheduling and operational chaos across different time zones.

q.t: With Central European Time (CET) given as UTC+1, what UTC time corresponds to 1700 CET?
q.e: Central European Time (winter time) is one hour ahead of UTC. To find the UTC time, you simply subtract 1 hour from the given CET. 17:00 minus 1 hour equals 16:00 UTC.
