q.t: The ideal level of arousal is at which point in the diagram?
q.e: According to the Yerkes-Dodson Law, optimal performance is reached at a moderate level of arousal (Point B).

q.t: At which point in the diagram will a pilot find himself to be overstrained?
q.e: Point D on the performance curve represents a state of high stress where performance drops sharply due to being overstrained.

q.t: Which of the following qualities are influenced by stress? 1. Attention, 2. Concentration, 3. Responsiveness, 4. Memory.
q.e: High levels of stress negatively impact all key cognitive functions, including attention, concentration, response time, and memory.

q.t: Which answer is correct concerning stress?
o: Everybody reacts to stress in the same manner
Stress can occur if there seems to be no solution for a given problem
Training and experience have no influence on the occurence of stress
Stress and its different symptoms are irrelevant for flight safety
q.e: Stress often arises when a pilot perceives that they do not have a solution or the resources to cope with a specific problem.

q.t: What clouds and weather may result from an humid and instable air mass, that is pushed against a chain of mountains by the predominant wind and forced to rise?
o: Thin Altostratus and Cirrostratus clouds with light and steady precipitation.
Overcast low stratus (high fog) with no precipitation.
Embedded CB with thunderstorms and showers of hail and/or rain.
Smooth, unstructured NS cloud with light drizzle or snow (during winter).
q.e: Humid, unstable air forced up mountains creates strong convection leading to cumulonimbus (CB) clouds.

q.t: What type of fog emerges if humid and almost saturated air, is forced to rise upslope of hills or shallow mountains by the prevailling wind?
q.e: Orographic (hill) fog forms when moist air is cooled to its dew point as it is mechanically forced up rising terrain.

q.t: What situation is called "over-development" in a weather report?
o: Development of a thermal low to a storm depression
Vertical development of Cumulus clouds to rain showers
Widespreading of Cumulus clouds below an inversion layer
Change from blue thermals to cloudy thermals during the afternoon
q.e: Over-development refers to cumulus clouds growing vertically into showers or thunderstorms due to atmospheric instability.

q.t: What is the gas composition of "air"?
o: Oxygen 21%, Nitrogen 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
Nitrogen 21%, Oxygen 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
q.e: Dry air is primarily composed of Nitrogen (approx. 78%) and Oxygen (approx. 21%).

q.t: Weather phenomena are most common to be found in which atmospheric layer?
q.e: Almost all weather occurs in the Troposphere where the vast majority of water vapor and air mass is contained.

q.t: What is the mass of a "cube of air" with the edges 1 m long, at MSL according ISA?
q.e: Standard air density at mean sea level (MSL) in the ICAO Standard Atmosphere is 1.225 kg/m³.

q.t: At what rate does the temperature change with increasing height according to ISA within the troposphere?
q.e: The ISA temperature lapse rate is approximately 2°C per 1000 ft (specifically 1.98°C/1000ft).

q.t: What is the mean height of the tropopause according to ISA?
q.e: The average height of the tropopause in standard ICAO conditions is defined as 11,000 meters.

q.t: The term "tropopause" is defined as...
o: the boundary area between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
the boundary area between the mesosphere and the stratosphere.
the height above which the temperature starts to decrease.
the layer above the troposphere showing an increasing temperature.
q.e: The tropopause is the transition boundary layer that separates the troposphere from the stratosphere.

q.t: Temperatures will be given by meteorological aviation services in Europe in which unit?
q.e: Metric units (Celsius) are the regulatory standard for aviation temperature reporting across Europe.

q.t: What is meant by "inversion layer"?
o: An atmospheric layer with constant temperature
A boundary area between two other layers
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases
An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with height
q.e: An inversion is a reversal of the normal lapse rate where temperature increases with altitude.

q.t: What is meant by "isothermal layer"?
o: An atmospheric layer where temperature increases
A boundary area between two other layers
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with height
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases
q.e: An isothermal layer has a zero lapse rate, meaning the temperature remains constant as altitude increases.

q.t: The temperature lapse rate with increasing height within the troposphere according ISA is...
q.e: In ISA, the temperature decrease of 1.98°C/1000ft corresponds to 0.65°C per 100 meters.

q.t: Which process may result in an inversion layer at about 5000 ft (1500 m) height?
o: Widespread descending air within a high pressure area
Intensive sunlight insolation during a warm summer day
Ground cooling by radiation during the night
Advection of cool air in the upper troposphere
q.e: Subsiding air in a high pressure system warms adiabatically as it sinks, often creating a subsidence inversion.

q.t: What danger arises for a helicopter during flight through a ground inversion in winter?
q.e: Rain falling from warmer air aloft into sub-freezing air below a ground inversion leads to freezing rain and severe icing.

q.t: An inversion layer close to the ground can be caused by...
o: thickening of clouds in medium layers.
q.e: Nocturnal radiation cooling of the Earth's surface cools the adjacent air, creating a radiation (ground) inversion.

q.t: What is the ISA standard pressure at FL 180 (5500 m)?
q.e: At approximately 18,000 ft (FL180), atmospheric pressure is roughly half of its sea-level value, which is 500 hPa.

q.t: The pressure which is measured at a ground station and reduced to mean sea level (MSL) by means of the actual atmospheric conditions is called...
q.e: QFF is station pressure reduced to sea level using actual temperature, unlike QNH which uses ISA values.

q.t: Which processes result in decreasing air density?
q.e: Density decreases when air expands due to heating (higher temp) or when there is less overlying mass (lower pressure).

q.t: The pressure at MSL in ISA conditions is...
q.e: The standard pressure at mean sea level (MSL) is defined as 1013.25 hPa or 29.92 inHg.

q.t: The height of the tropopause of the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is at...
q.e: 11,000 meters is approximately 36,089 feet, typically rounded to 36,000 ft in aviation materials.

q.t: The barometric altimeter indicates height above...
q.e: Altimeters are pressure gauges that indicate height based on the difference between the ambient and a selected reference pressure.

q.t: The altimeter can be checked on the ground by setting...
o: QNE and checking that the indication shows zero on the ground.
QFF and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QNH and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QFE and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
q.e: Setting QNH on the ground should make the altimeter read the official surveyed elevation of the airfield.

q.t: The barometric altimeter with QFE setting indicates...
o: height above the pressure level at airfield elevation.
q.e: QFE (Field Elevation) sets the datum to the airfield pressure, so the altimeter reads height above the field.

q.t: The barometric altimeter with QNH setting indicates...
o: height above the pressure level at airfield elevation.
q.e: QNH (Nautical Height) sets the datum to MSL pressure, providing altitude above sea level.

q.t: Given QNH 983 hPa, Altitude FL 85, OAT ISA - 10°, what is the true altitude?
q.e: Low pressure and cold temperatures make the air denser and the aircraft lower than indicated. FL85 (8500ft) corrected results in ~7600ft.

q.t: How can wind speed and wind direction be derived from surface weather charts?
o: By annotations from the text part of the chart
By alignment of lines of warm- and cold fronts.
By alignment and distance of hypsometric lines
By alignment and distance of isobaric lines
q.e: Wind flows nearly parallel to isobars, and its speed is inversely proportional to the distance between them.

q.t: Which force causes "wind"?
q.e: The pressure gradient force, pushing air from high to low pressure areas, is the fundamental cause of wind.

q.t: Above the friction layer, with a prevailing pressure gradient, the wind direction is...
o: at an angle of 30° to the isobars
q.e: Above the surface friction layer, the balance between pressure gradient and Coriolis forces results in geostrophic wind parallel to isobars.

q.t: Which of the stated surfaces will reduce the wind speed most due to ground friction?
o: Flat land, deserted land, no vegetation
Flat land, lots of vegetation cover
q.e: Rough terrain and heavy vegetation create significant mechanical friction that slows down surface air movement.

q.t: The movement of air flowing together is called...
q.e: Convergence describes air masses flowing toward each other, which typically results in lifting and cloud formation.

q.t: The movement of air flowing apart is called...
q.e: Divergence is the atmospheric process where air masses move away from each other, leading to sinking air and clearing skies.

q.t: What weather development will result from convergence at ground level?
q.e: Surface convergence forces air upward; as it rises, it cools adiabatically, leading to condensation and cloud development.

q.t: When air masses meet each other head on, how is this referred to and what air movements will follow?
o: Convergence resulting in air being lifted
Divergence resulting in air being lifted
q.e: When air masses converge, the air is forced upward (lifting), which is a key process for cloud and precipitation development.

q.t: What are the air masses that Central Europe is mainly influenced by?
o: Polar cold air and tropical warm air
q.e: The weather in Central Europe is primarily driven by the interaction of cold polar air and warm tropical/subtropical air.

q.t: With regard to global circulation within the atmosphere, where does polar cold air meets subtropical warm air?
o: At the subtropical high pressure belt
q.e: The polar front is the worldwide boundary zone where cold polar air meets warmer subtropical air masses.

q.t: Winds blowing uphill are defined as...
q.e: Anabatic winds are daytime upslope winds caused by solar heating of the mountain slopes.

q.t: Winds blowing downhill are defined as...
q.e: Katabatic winds are downslope winds driven by gravity, typically occurring at night as surface air cools and becomes denser.

q.t: Air descending behind a mountain range is defined as...
q.e: Gravity-driven air descending a slope is categorized as a katabatic wind (of which the Foehn is a specific warm type).

q.t: "Foehn" conditions usually develop with...
o: instability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
stability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
instability, high pressure area with calm wind.
stability, high pressure area with calm wind.
q.e: Foehn occurs when a moist, unstable air mass is forced over a ridge, losing moisture on the windward side and warming on the lee.

q.t: What type of turbulence is typically found close to the ground on the lee side during Foehn conditions?
q.e: Rotors are intense, turbulent vortices that form on the lee side of mountains during strong wave conditions.

q.t: Light turbulence always has to be expected...
o: below cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
above cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
below stratiform clouds in medium layers.
q.e: Thermal convection that builds cumulus clouds creates updrafts and downdrafts felt as light to moderate turbulence.

q.t: Moderate to severe turbulence has to be expected...
o: below thick cloud layers on the windward side
with the appearance of extended low stratus clouds
on the lee side of a mountain range when rotor clouds are present.
q.e: Rotor clouds signify the presence of powerful mountain waves and extreme low-level turbulence on the lee side.

q.t: Which answer contains every state of water found in the atmosphere?
q.e: Water exists in the atmosphere as vapor (gas), water droplets (liquid), and ice crystals or snow (solid).

q.t: How do dew point and relative humidity change with decreasing temperature?
o: Dew point decreases, relative humidity increases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity increases
Dew point increases, relative humidity decreases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity decreases
q.e: As air cools without adding/removing water, the dew point stays constant but relative humidity rises as it nears saturation.

q.t: How do spread and relative humidity change with increasing temperature?
o: Spread remains constant, relative humidity increases
Spread remains constant, relative humidity decreases
q.e: Warming air increases its capacity for water vapor, widening the spread and lowering the relative humidity.

q.t: The "spread" is defined as...
o: relation of actual to maximum possible humidity
difference between dew point and condensation point.
difference between actual temperature and dew point.
q.e: The spread (or dew point depression) is the numerical difference between the ambient air temperature and its dew point.

q.t: With other factors remaining constant, decreasing temperature results in...
o: increasing spread and decreasing relative humidity
decreasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
decreasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
q.e: Cooling brings the air temperature closer to the dew point, thus decreasing the spread and increasing the humidity percentage.

q.t: What process causes latent heat being released into the upper troposphere?
q.e: As water vapor condenses into liquid cloud droplets, it releases latent heat of condensation into the surrounding air.

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate is...
o: proportional to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
higher than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
lower than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
equal to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
q.e: The SALR is lower than the DALR because the heat released during condensation offsets some of the cooling from expansion.

q.t: The dry adiabatic lapse rate has a value of...
q.e: Dry air (unsaturared) cools at a constant rate of 1.0°C per 100 meters (approx. 3°C per 1000 ft) as it rises.

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate should be assumed with a mean value of:
q.e: While it varies with temperature, the saturated lapse rate is typically assumed to be around 0.6°C per 100 meters.

q.t: What weather conditions may be expected during conditionally unstable conditions?
o: Layered clouds up to high levels, prolonged rain
Towering cumulus, isolated showers of rain or thunderstorms
Sky clear of clouds, sunshine, low winds
Shallow cumulus clouds with base at medium levels
q.e: Conditionally unstable air is stable for dry air but unstable once saturated, allowing for vertical growth and showers.

q.t: Which conditions are likely for the formation of advection fog?
o: Warm, humid air moves over a cold surface
Cold, humid air moves over a warm ocean
Warm, humid air cools during a cloudy night
Humidity evaporates from warm, humid ground into cold air
q.e: Advection fog occurs when a warm, moist air mass moves over a significantly colder surface, cooling the air to saturation.

q.t: Clouds are basically distinguished by what types?
q.e: Clouds are primarily categorized as "heap" clouds (Cumulus) or "layer" clouds (Stratiform).

q.t: Clouds in high layers are referred to as...
q.e: High-level clouds (generally above 20,000 ft) are identified by the prefix "Cirro-", such as Cirrus or Cirrostratus.

q.t: What weather phenomenon designated by "2" has to be expected on the lee side during "Foehn"?
q.e: Item "2" in figure MET-001 represents wave clouds, specifically lens-shaped Altocumulus lenticularis.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show?
q.e: The figure shows individual, puffy white clouds with flat bases and vertical growth, which are characteristic Cumulus.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show?
q.e: The image displays thin, wispy, hair-like clouds at high altitude, which are classic Cirrus clouds.

q.t: What factor may affect the top of cumulus clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
q.e: Rising air in cumulus clouds is stopped when it reaches a stable layer, typically an atmospheric inversion.

q.t: What factors may indicate a tendency to fog formation?
q.e: Air that is already close to saturation (low spread) and is further cooling will rapidly reach the dew point and form fog.

q.t: What condition may prevent the formation of "radiation fog"?
q.e: A thick cloud cover acts as a blanket, trapping terrestrial radiation and preventing the surface from cooling to the dew point.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "advection fog"?
o: Cold, moist air is being moved across warm ground areas
Warm, moist air is moved across cold ground areas
Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
q.e: Advection is the horizontal movement of air; warm, moist air moving over cold ground is cooled from below into fog.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "orographic fog" ("hill fog")?
o: Evaporation from warm, moist ground into cold air
Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Warm, moist air is moved across a hill or a mountain range
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
q.e: Orographic fog is caused by the mechanical lifting and subsequent adiabatic cooling of moist air over rising terrain.

q.t: What factors are required for the formation of precipitation in clouds?
o: Calm winds and intensive sunlight insolation
The presence of an inversion layer
q.e: Updrafts are necessary to keep droplets suspended long enough for them to grow into sizes heavy enough to fall as rain.

q.t: The formation of medium to large precipitation particles requires...
q.e: Larger particles (like heavy rain or hail) require powerful updrafts to support their weight during the growth phase.

q.t: Which type of cloud is associated with prolonged rain?
q.e: Nimbostratus is a thick, uniform, dark grey layer cloud that produces steady and continuous precipitation over large areas.

q.t: Regarding the type of cloud, precipitation is classified as...
q.e: Steady precipitation from stratiform clouds is called "rain," while intermittent precipitation from cumuliform clouds is "showers."

q.t: How is an air mass described when moving to Central Europe via the Russian continent during winter?
q.e: Air originating over the cold, dry interior of the Russian continent in winter is classified as Continental Polar (cP).

q.t: The character of an air mass is given by what properties?
o: Region of origin and track during movement
Temperatures at origin and present region
q.e: Air masses are primarily defined by the location where they form and the surfaces they pass over during their movement.

q.t: The symbol labeled (1) as shown in the picture  is a / an...
q.e: A blue line with pointed spikes (triangles) is the standard meteorological symbol for a cold front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (2) as shown in the picture  is a / an...
q.e: A red line with rounded semicircles is the standard meteorological symbol for a warm front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (3) as shown in the picture  is a / an...
q.e: A purple line with alternating triangles and semicircles represents an occluded front.

q.t: What cloud sequence can typically be observed during the passage of a warm front?
o: Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus, lowering base with rain, nimbostratus
In coastal areas forming of cumulus clouds
q.e: The approach of a warm front is characterized by gradual cloud thickening and lowering, starting with high Cirrus.

q.t: What clouds and weather can typically be observed during the passage of a cold front?
o: In coastal areas forming of cumulus clouds
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds
Strongly developed cumulus clouds (Cb) with showers, thunderstorms and gusting wind
q.e: Cold fronts involve the lifting of unstable air, often producing tall cumulonimbus clouds and violent, showery weather.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected within the warm sector of a polar front low during summer?
o: Moderate to good visibility, scattered clouds
Good visibility, some isolated high clouds
q.e: The "warm sector" between the two fronts typically features stable air and relatively fair flying conditions in summer.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected after the passage of a cold front?
o: Good visiblity, formation of cumulus clouds with showers of rain or snow
Scattered cloud layers, visbility more than 5 km
Medium visibility with lowering cloud bases
q.e: Post-cold-front air is typically clear and unstable, resulting in excellent visibility but showery cumulus development.

q.t: A boundary between a cold polar air mass and a warm subtropical air mass showing no horizontal displacement is called...
q.e: A stationary front exists when the boundary between two air masses is not moving in either direction.

q.t: What is the usual direction of movement of a polar front low?
o: Parallel to the the warm-sector isobars
Parallel to the warm front line to the south
q.e: Frontal depressions generally follow the direction of the geostrophic wind (isobars) found in the warm sector.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed during the passage of a polar front low?
o: Falling pressure in front of warm front, constant in warm sector, rising behind cold front
Rising pressure in front of warm front, constant in warm sector, rising behind cold front
Rising in front of warm front, rising in warm sector, falling behind cold front
Falling in front of warm front, constant in warm sector, falling behind cold front
q.e: Barometric pressure typically drops as the warm front approaches and reaches its minimum as the cold front passes.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed when a cold front is passing?
q.e: Pressure drops to a minimum as the front arrives and then rises sharply once the colder, denser air mass arrives.

q.t: What change of wind direction can be expected during the passage of a polar front low in Central Europe?
o: Backing at warm front, veering at cold front
Veering at warm front, backing at cold front
Backing at warm front, backing at cold front
Veering at warm front, veering at cold front
q.e: In the Northern Hemisphere, both warm and cold front passages result in a clockwise shift (veering) of the wind.

q.t: Extensive high pressure areas can be found throughout the year ...
o: over oceanic areas at latitues around 30°N/S.
in areeas showing extensive lifting processes.
in tropical areas, close to the equator.
in mid latitudes along the polar front
q.e: These are the subtropical high-pressure belts (e.g., the Azores High) driven by the descending part of the Hadley cell.

q.t: What cloud type can typically be observed across widespread high pressure areas during summer?
q.e: Widespread high pressure features descending air (subsidence), which inhibits major cloud growth, leaving only fair-weather cumulus.

q.t: What pressure pattern may result from cold-air inflow in high tropospheric layers?
o: Formation of a large ground low
Formation of a high in the upper troposphere
Formation of a low in the upper troposphere
q.e: Very cold air in the upper atmosphere is dense and occupies less volume, leading to lower pressure at that altitude (a trough).

q.t: Cold air inflow in high tropospheric layers may result in...
q.e: Cold air over warm surface air creates a steep lapse rate and high instability, fueling deep convection and thunderstorms.

q.t: How does inflowing cold air affect the shape and vertical distance between pressure layers?
o: Increase in vertical distance, low height
Decreasing vertical distance, raise in height
Decrease in vertical distance, lowering in height (low pressure)
Increasing vertical distance, raise in height
q.e: Cold air is denser; therefore, the vertical distance between pressure levels decreases, and pressure surfaces "sag" (low pressure).

q.t: What weather phenomena have to be expected around an upper-level trough?
o: Calm weather, formation of lifted fog layers
q.e: Upper troughs are areas of mass convergence and lifting, which destabilize the air and trigger showery weather.

q.t: What frontal line divides subtropical air from polar cold air, in particular across Central Europe?
q.e: The polar front is the primary boundary separating cold polar air masses from warmer subtropical air masses.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
q.e: Summer highs are dominated by sinking air, resulting in mostly clear skies, light winds, and fair-weather cumulus.

q.t: What weather conditions in Central Europe are typically found in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Large isobar spacing with strong westerly winds
Small isobar spacing with strong northerly winds
Large isobar spacing with calm winds, local systems
Small isobar spacing with calm winds, local systems
q.e: Weak pressure gradients (large isobar spacing) in a high allow for light winds and the development of local sea/land breezes.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during winter?
o: Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
q.e: In winter, high pressure often traps moist air beneath a low-level inversion, leading to persistent fog or low stratus (high fog).

q.t: What wind conditions can be expected in areas showing large distances between isobars?
o: Strong prevailing winds with rapid backing
Local wind systems with strong westerly winds
Variable winds, formation of local wind systems
Strong prevailing winds with rapid veering
q.e: When the general pressure gradient is very weak, the wind is light and dominated by local thermal and topographical effects.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected during "Foehn" on the windward side of a mountain range?
o: Layered clouds, mountains obscured, poor visibility, moderate or heavy rain
Calm wind and forming of high stratus clouds
q.e: The windward side experiences "stau" weather—lifting of moist air leading to continuous clouds and heavy precipitation.

q.t: Which of the stated wind phenomena will increase in speed since its path is narrowed by mountains?
q.e: The Mistral is a cold wind accelerated by the "funnel effect" of the Rhône valley in France.

q.t: What is the name of the the cold, katabatic wind phenomena blowing from northeast into the Adriatic Sea?
q.e: The Bora is a violent, cold, northeasterly downslope wind that affects the Adriatic coast in winter.

q.t: Which of the following conditions are most favourable for ice accretion?
o: Temperatures between 0° C and -12° C, presence of supercooled water droplets
Temperaturs below 0° C, strong wind, clear sky
q.e: Icing is most severe when an aircraft strikes supercooled liquid droplets that are between 0°C and -12°C.

q.t: What temperatures are most dangerous with respect to airframe icing?
q.e: The range between 0°C and -12°C is critical because clouds contain large amounts of liquid water that freezes upon impact.

q.t: Which type of ice forms by very small water droplets and ice crystals hitting the front surfaces?
q.e: Rime ice forms when small droplets freeze instantly upon impact, trapping air and creating a rough, opaque white deposit.

q.t: Which type of ice forms by large, supercooled droplets hitting the front surfaces of an aircraft?
q.e: Clear ice forms when large droplets spread out before freezing completely, creating a heavy, transparent, and smooth layer.

q.t: What situation may result in the occurrence of severe wind shear?
o: Flying ahead of a warm front
During final approach, 30 min after a heavy shower
When a shower is visible close to the airfield
q.e: Rain showers and thunderstorms produce localized, violent downdrafts (microbursts) and shifting winds near the surface.

q.t: What conditions are favourable for the formation of thunderstorms?
o: Warm humid air, conditionally unstable environmental lapse rate
Warm and dry air, strong inversion layer
Clear night over land, cold air and patches of fog
Calm winds and cold air, overcast cloud cover
q.e: Deep convection requires a trigger, moisture, and an unstable lapse rate to allow clouds to grow to great heights.

q.t: What conditions are mandatory for the formation of thermal thunderstorms?
o: Conditionally unstable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and low humidity
Conditionally unstable, low temp and humidity
q.e: Solar heating (high temp) provides the trigger for moist air to rise through an unstable atmosphere.

q.t: With regard to thunderstorms, strong up- and downdrafts appear during the...
q.e: The mature stage is reached when precipitation begins to fall, creating a downdraft alongside the existing updraft.

q.t: Which stage of a thunderstorm is dominated by updrafts?
q.e: The initial or "Cumulus" stage consists of rising air currents as the cloud rapidly grows vertically.

q.t: What danger is most immenent when an aircraft is hit by lightning?
o: Surface overheat and damage to exposed aircraft parts
q.e: Lightning strikes can cause structural pitting, "burning" of surfaces, and damage to external sensors or antennas.

q.t: Heavy downdrafts and strong wind shear close to the ground can be expected...
o: during approach with a strong sea breeze
during summer days with flatted Cu clouds
near the rainfall areas of heavy showers or thunderstorms
q.e: Microbursts and strong shear are concentrated in the area where heavy rain or hail falls from a cumulonimbus cloud.

q.t: What phenomenon is caused by cold air downdrafts with precipitation from a fully developed thunderstorm cloud?
q.e: The gust front is the leading edge of the cold, dense air that spreads out horizontally at the surface under a thunderstorm.

q.t: What has to be considered when taking off in a ground inversion?
o: Due to low temperatures, icing is expected
Sudden increase in speed has to be expected
During climb, a sudden decrease in speed and climb performance has to be expected
q.e: When climbing out of cold air into warmer air aloft, the decrease in air density can cause a significant loss of performance and airspeed.

q.t: What danger is most imminent during an approach to an airfield situated in a valley, with strong wind aloft blowing perpendicular?
o: Wind shear during descent, wind direction may change by 180°
q.e: Mountain waves and local topography can cause the surface wind in a valley to blow in the opposite direction of the wind aloft.

q.t: What kind of reduction in visibility is not very sensitive to changes in temperature?
q.e: Haze is composed of dry particles (dust/pollution) and is not affected by saturation or temp-dew point spread.

q.t: Information about pressure patterns and frontal situation can be found in which chart?
q.e: A surface analysis chart (Wetterkarte) is the standard map for isobars and current frontal positions.

q.t: Which weather chart shows the actual air pressure as in MSL along with pressure centers and fronts?
q.e: Surface charts provide a snapshot of the actual pressure distribution and fronts at sea level for a specific time.

q.t: What information can be obtained from satallite images?
o: Overview of cloud covers and front lines
q.e: Satellites provide visual and infrared views showing the horizontal extent of clouds and frontal systems.

q.t: What chart shows areas of precipitation?
q.e: Ground-based weather radar detects hydrometeors (rain, snow, hail) and shows their intensity and movement.

q.t: What information is NOT found on Low-Level Significant Weather Charts (LLSWC)?
q.e: LLSWCs are forecast products that show expected hazards, not real-time observed radar data.

q.t: Measured pressure distribution in MSL and corresponding frontal systems are displayed by the...
q.e: The surface chart is the primary tool for displaying observed (not just forecast) pressure patterns and fronts.

q.t: In a METAR, "heavy rain" is designated by the identifier...
q.e: In the METAR code, the "+" prefix indicates "heavy" intensity, and "RA" stands for rain.

q.t: In a METAR, "(moderate) showers of rain" are designated by the identifier...
q.e: The code "SH" denotes showers and "RA" denotes rain; together they mean showery rain.

q.t: What information can be found in the ATIS, but not in a METAR?
q.e: ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) includes specific airport operational data like the active runway.

q.t: Weather and operational information about the destination aerodrome can be obtained during the flight by...
q.e: Pilots listen to the ATIS frequency as they approach a destination to get current weather and landing instructions.

q.t: SIGMET warnings are issued for...
q.e: SIGMET (Significant Meteorological Information) warnings cover hazardous weather for an entire Flight Information Region.

q.t: An inversion is a layer ...
o: with increasing temperature with increasing height.
q.e: An inversion occurs when the normal decrease of temperature with altitude is reversed.

q.t: What can be expected for the prevailling wind with isobars on a surface weather chart showing large distances?
o: Low pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
q.e: Wide spacing between isobars indicates a small pressure difference, resulting in weak surface winds.

q.t: What is referred to as mountain wind?
o: Wind blowing down the mountain side during the night
q.e: At night, the slopes cool down; the air becomes denser and flows down into the valley, creating a mountain wind.

q.t: Under which conditions "back side weather" can be expected?
o: After passing of a warm front
During Foehn at the lee side
After passing of a cold front
q.e: "Rückseitenwetter" refers to the clear, cold, and unstable air mass that follows the passage of a cold front.

q.t: What wind is reportet as 225/15?
q.e: Winds are reported from the direction they blow (225° is SW) and speed is in knots (kt).

q.t: How does air temperatur change in ISA from MSL to approx. 10.000 m height?
q.e: Standard temperature starts at +15°C and decreases by ~2°C/1000ft, reaching approx. -50°C at 32,800ft (10km).

q.t: What weather is likely to be experienced during "Foehn" in the Bavarian area close to the alps?
o: Nimbostratus in northern alps, rotor clouds lee side
Nimbostratus in the southern alps, rotor clouds at the lee side, warm and dry wind
q.e: Foehn in the northern Alps involves moisture from the south (Italy) causing rain there and warm/dry air in Germany.

q.t: Mountain side updrafts can be intensified by ...
o: By warming of upper atmospheric layers
thermal radiation of the windward side during night
Solar irradiation on the lee side
Solar irradiation on the windward side
q.e: Direct sunlight on the slopes adds thermal convection to the mechanical lifting of air, strengthening the updrafts.

q.t: In which situations should a pilot use blind transmissions?
o: traffic situation at an airport allows transmission without acknowledgement
pilot has flown into cloud or fog unintentionally
no radio communication established, but evidence exists that transmissions are received
transmission containing important info is to be sent to several stations
q.e: Blind transmission is used when you cannot establish two-way communication but believe the ground station can hear you.

q.t: Leaving a control frequency (except when reaching final parking position)...
o: is not mandatory to be reported
q.e: Pilots must obtain approval from ATC before leaving a controlled frequency.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term "abeam"?
q.e: ABM is the official ICAO abbreviation for the term "abeam".

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term "visual flight rules"?
q.e: VFR is the standard abbreviation for Visual Flight Rules.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term "obstacle"?
q.e: OBST is the standard aviation abbreviation for an obstacle.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "FIS" stand for?
q.e: FIS stands for Flight Information Service.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "FIR" stand for?
q.e: FIR stands for Flight Information Region.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "H24" stand for?
q.e: H24 indicates a service that is available 24 hours a day.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "HX" stand for?
q.e: HX indicates that there are no specific or fixed opening hours.

q.t: The altimeter has to be set to what value in order to show zero on ground?
q.e: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at the aerodrome elevation; setting it results in zero altitude on the ground.

q.t: Which altitude is displayed on the altimeter when set to a specific QNH?
o: Altitude in relation to mean sea level
Altitude in relation to air pressure at reference airfield
Altitude in relation to 1013.25 hPa datum
Altitude in relation to highest elevation within 10 km
q.e: QNH setting displays the altitude of the aircraft relative to Mean Sea Level (MSL).

q.t: Which altitude is displayed on the altimeter when set to a specific QFE?
o: Altitude in relation to highest elevation within 10 km
Altitude in relation to air pressure at reference airfield
Altitude in relation to 1013.25 hPa datum
Altitude in relation to mean sea level
q.e: QFE setting displays the height of the aircraft above the reference airfield pressure level.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "QDR" stand for?
q.e: QDR is the magnetic bearing from a station to the aircraft.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "QUJ" stand for?
q.e: QUJ is the true bearing to be steered to reach the station.

q.t: What does the abbreviation "QTE" stand for?
q.e: QTE is the true bearing from the station to the aircraft.

q.t: Which Q-code is used for the magnetic bearing from the station?
q.e: QDR is the specific Q-code for magnetic bearing from the station.

q.t: Which Q-code is used for the true bearing from the station?
q.e: QTE is the specific Q-code for true bearing from the station.

q.t: Which Q-code is used for the true bearing to the station?
q.e: QUJ is the specific Q-code for true bearing to the station.

q.t: Which of radiotelephony messages has a higher priority than a flight safety message?
q.e: Direction finding communications have higher priority than standard flight safety messages.

q.t: What is the correct term for a message used for air traffic control?
q.e: ATC messages are categorized as Flight Safety Messages.

q.t: Distress messages are messages...
o: concerning safety of aircraft, watercraft, vehicle or person in sight
sent by agency with imminent meaning for aircraft
concerning grave and imminent threat requiring immediate assistance
q.e: Distress (MAYDAY) signals indicate a grave and imminent threat requiring immediate help.

q.t: Urgency messages are messages...
o: sent by agency with imminent meaning for aircraft
concerning safety of aircraft, watercraft, vehicle or person in sight
q.e: Urgency (PAN PAN) signals concern the safety of an aircraft or person but are not yet a distress situation.

q.t: Regularity messages are messages...
o: concerning safety of aircraft/person in sight
sent by agency of immediate concern to aircraft in flight
q.e: Regularity messages are operational messages from an aircraft operating agency.

q.t: Which of the following messages has the highest priority?
q.e: Requests for direction finding (QDM) have priority over standard ATC instructions and weather info.

q.t: What is the correct way to transmit the call sign HB-YKM?
q.e: This uses the standard ICAO phonetic alphabet: Hotel, Bravo, Yankee, Kilo, Mike.

q.t: What is the correct way to transmit the call sign OE-JVK?
q.e: This uses the standard ICAO phonetic alphabet: Oscar, Echo, Juliett, Victor, Kilo.

q.t: An altitude of 4500 ft is transmitted as...
q.e: Altitudes are transmitted in thousands and hundreds.

q.t: A heading of 285 degrees is correctly transmitted as...
q.e: Headings are always transmitted as individual digits.

q.t: A frequency of 119.500 MHz is correctly transmitted as...
o: one one niner tousand decimal five zero
one niner decimal five zero zero
one one niner decimal five zero
q.e: In some regions, frequencies are shortened if no ambiguity exists; here the trailing zeros are omitted.

q.t: The directional information "12 o'clock" is correctly transmitted as...
q.e: Twelve o'clock is the standard way to transmit relative clock positions.

q.t: Times are transmitted as...
q.e: All aviation times are transmitted in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

q.t: If there is any doubt about ambiguity, a time of 1620 is to be transmitted as...
o: one tousand six hundred two zero
q.e: To avoid ambiguity, the full four digits are transmitted individually.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase "Roger"?
o: Permission for proposed action is granted
An error has been made in this transmission
I understand your message and will comply with it
I have received all of your last transmission
q.e: Roger only means the transmission was received; it does not mean "yes" or "will comply".

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase "Correction"?
o: Error made in transmission, correct version is...
q.e: Used to correct a mistake made during the current transmission.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase "Approved"?
o: Permission for proposed action is granted
q.e: "Approved" signifies that the pilot's requested action is authorized.

q.t: Which phrase does a pilot use to check readability?
q.e: "How do you read?" is the standard query to check signal strength and clarity.

q.t: Which phrase is used by a pilot to fly through controlled airspace?
q.e: "Request" is the official term for asking for a clearance or service.

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot if a transmission is answered with "yes"?
q.e: "Affirm" is the correct radiotelephony term for "yes".

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot if a transmission is answered with "no"?
q.e: "Negative" is the correct radiotelephony term for "no".

q.t: Which phrase is used to show ready for take-off?
q.e: Pilots state they are "Ready for departure" to avoid using the word "take-off" prematurely.

q.t: What phrase is used to inform about a go-around?
q.e: "Going around" is the standard phrase for an aborted landing.

q.t: What is the call sign of the aerodrome control?
q.e: "Tower" is the suffix for aerodrome control service.

q.t: What is the call sign of surface movement control?
q.e: "Ground" is the suffix for surface movement control.

q.t: What is the call sign of flight information service?
q.e: "Information" is the suffix for flight information services.

q.t: What is the correct abbreviation of the call sign D-EAZF?
q.e: Call signs are abbreviated using the first character and at least the last two.

q.t: In what case is the pilot allowed to abbreviate the call sign?
o: If there is little traffic in traffic circuit
After the ground station has used the abbreviation
q.e: A pilot may only use an abbreviated call sign after the ground station has initiated its use.

q.t: What is the correct way of using call sign at first contact?
q.e: The full call sign must be used for initial contact with any station.

q.t: What is the correct way of establishing radio communication?
q.e: Communication is established by stating the station called followed by the station calling.

q.t: Correct way of acknowledging instruction "Call Hamburg Tower on 121.275"?
q.e: Frequency changes are acknowledged by repeating the frequency.

q.t: What does a readability of 1 indicate?
q.e: Scale 1-5: 1 is the lowest, meaning unreadable.

q.t: What does a readability of 2 indicate?
q.e: Scale 1-5: 2 means readable now and then.

q.t: What does a readability of 3 indicate?
q.e: Scale 1-5: 3 means readable but with difficulty.

q.t: What does a readability of 5 indicate?
q.e: Scale 1-5: 5 is the highest, meaning perfectly readable.

q.t: Which information from ground station does not require readback?
q.e: Wind information is for situational awareness and generally doesn't require a strict readback like clearances.

q.t: Which information from ground station does not require readback?
q.e: Traffic information is an advisory and does not require a readback.

q.t: Correct acknowledgement of complex instruction?
o: ...then turn right heading 220, runway 12, cleared for take-off
q.e: Readbacks must include key clearance elements like heading, runway, and authorization.

q.t: Correct acknowledgement for "Next report PAH"?
q.e: "Wilco" (Will Comply) is used to acknowledge an instruction that will be followed.

q.t: Correct acknowledgement for "Squawk 4321, Call Bremen Radar on 131.325"?
q.e: Combines the essential squawk code with "wilco" for the frequency change.

q.t: Correct acknowledgement for "You are now entering airspace Delta"?
q.e: Position information or status updates are acknowledged with "Roger".

q.t: FEW cloud coverage in METAR?
q.e: FEW indicates 1 to 2 oktas (eighths) of cloud cover.

q.t: SCT cloud coverage in METAR?
q.e: SCT (Scattered) indicates 3 to 4 oktas (eighths) of cloud cover.

q.t: BKN cloud coverage in METAR?
q.e: BKN (Broken) indicates 5 to 7 oktas (eighths) of cloud cover.

q.t: Transmitting 12 km visibility?
q.e: In METAR, visibility of 10km or more is often transmitted as "10 kilometers or more".

q.t: When is visibility transmitted in meters?
q.e: Visibility is given in meters when it is below 5 km.

q.t: When is visibility transmitted in kilometers?
q.e: Visibility is expressed in kilometers when it exceeds 5 km.

q.t: What is broadcasted on VOLMET?
q.e: VOLMET is a worldwide network of radio stations that broadcast METAR reports.

q.t: Facility used for ATIS?
q.e: ATIS can often be broadcast over the voice frequency of a VOR station.

q.t: Obtaining met info during cross-country flight?
q.e: VOLMET provides meteorological information for aircraft in flight.

q.t: Transponder code for radio failure?
q.e: 7600 is the international transponder code for a communications failure.

q.t: Phrase to begin blind transmission?
q.e: "Transmitting blind" is the standard phrase to warn stations you cannot hear them.

q.t: Frequency for blind transmission?
q.e: Blind transmissions should be made on the frequency where communication was last attempted.

q.t: How often shall a blind transmission be made?
q.e: The document specifies two times for blind transmissions.

q.t: When to set 7600?
q.e: Set 7600 specifically when you lose radio communication.

q.t: Radio failure in Class D airspace?
o: continue last clearance complying VFR or leave shortest route
continue last clearance leave standard routing
q.e: Standard procedure is to follow last clearance while VFR or exit the airspace immediately.

q.t: Enter Class D with radio failure?
q.e: Entry is only allowed if a prior approval/clearance was obtained.

q.t: Repeated three times for urgency?
q.e: "Pan Pan" is the signal for an urgency message.

q.t: Urgency messages defined as...
q.e: Urgency messages concern safety but not necessarily immediate threat to life.

q.t: Distress messages contain...
q.e: Distress messages always relate to immediate, grave danger.

q.t: Frequency for initial distress message?
q.e: Start the distress call on the frequency you are currently using.

q.t: Info in urgency message?
o: nature of problem, intentions, position, heading, altitude
routing, intentions, position, departure, heading, altitude
q.e: Essential info includes the problem nature, pilot intentions, and current flight state.

q.t: Transponder code for emergencies?
q.e: 7700 is the international emergency squawk code.

q.t: VHF voice communication frequency?
q.e: VHF aviation voice frequencies range from 118 to 137 MHz.

q.t: VHF voice communication frequency?
q.e: 120.50 MHz falls within the designated VHF air-band for voice.

q.t: Frequency band 118.000 to 136.975 MHz?
q.e: This specific range is the Very High Frequency (VHF) band for aviation.

q.t: Factor affecting VHF reception?
q.e: VHF is "line-of-sight," so higher altitude increases reception range.

q.t: Speed of electromagnetic wave propagation?
q.e: Electromagnetic waves (including radio) travel at the speed of light, approx 300,000 km/s.

q.t: An ATIS is valid for...
q.e: ATIS updates are usually issued every 30 minutes unless weather changes significantly.

q.t: Which ratio corresponds to the rotor disc loading?
q.e: Disc loading is the ratio of the helicopter's total mass (gross weight) to the total area of the main rotor disc.

q.t: What causes the phase lag between the displacement and the flapping of a rotor blade?
o: Rounding of the rotor blade tips
Friction in the rotor blade spindles
q.e: Due to gyroscopic precession and inertial properties, the maximum vertical displacement occurs 90° after the maximum force is applied.

q.t: If the critical angle of attack is exceeded, the...
o: transition point starts moving towards the airflow direction.
boundary layer on the upper side of the rotor blade begins to separate.
boundary layer on the lower side of the rotor blade begins to separate.
laminar boundary layer turns into a turbulent boundary layer.
q.e: A stall occurs when the critical angle of attack is exceeded, causing the airflow (boundary layer) to separate from the upper surface.

q.t: What types of airflow can be observed around a rotor blade aerofoil?
o: Laminar airflow on the entire upper surface
Laminar airflow at the leading edge, turbulent airflow further back
Turbulent airflow at the leading edge, laminar airflow further back
Turbulent airflow on the entire upper surface
q.e: Airflow typically starts as laminar at the stagnation point (leading edge) and transitions to turbulent as it moves toward the trailing edge.

q.t: What is the advantage of a turbulent airflow compared to a laminar airflow at an aerofoil with a high angle of attack?
o: It has a thinner boundary layer
The separation point moves further forward
It adheres to the aerofoil for a longer time
q.e: A turbulent boundary layer has more kinetic energy and can remain attached to the aerofoil surface longer, delaying the stall.

q.t: The virtual rotation axis of a rotor is...
o: parallel with the main rotor shaft.
perpendicular to the tip path plane.
perpendicular to the plane which contains the swash plate.
q.e: The virtual axis of rotation is always defined as being perpendicular to the plane described by the tips of the rotor blades (Tip Path Plane).

q.t: The effective angle of attack is the angle between...
o: chord line and tip path plane.
tip path plane and rotor blade.
effective airflow and tip path plane.
q.e: The effective angle of attack (AOA) is the specific angle formed between the chord line of the blade and the resultant (effective) airflow.

q.t: What kind of drag is caused by a lift-producing aerofoil?
q.e: Induced drag is a direct byproduct of the production of lift, caused by the downward deflection of air (downwash).

q.t: What force affects the braking torque of the rotor in cruise?
q.e: The rearward component of the aerodynamic force (tangential force) acts against the rotation, creating a braking torque that the engine must overcome.

q.t: The rotor thrust is...
o: perpendicular to the tip path plane.
opposite to the rotation of the rotor blade element.
parallel with the main rotor shaft.
q.e: Total rotor thrust is the resultant aerodynamic force of all blades and acts perpendicular to the Tip Path Plane.

q.t: What happens to thrust and tangential force if the rotor RPM decreases by about 10% in cruise flight?
o: The thrust and the tangential force decrease
The thrust and the tangential force increase
The thrust decreases and the tangential force remains constant
The thrust remains constant and the tangential force increases
q.e: To maintain constant thrust at lower RPM, the pitch (AOA) must be increased, which in turn increases the tangential drag force.

q.t: The effective airflow velocity of a rotor blade element varies with the distance from the rotor shaft axis, because the...
o: peripheral speed increases if the distance to the rotor blade tip decreases.
tangential force and airflow reversal vary.
drag force in direction of the rotaion axis is increased.
q.e: Rotational velocity (peripheral speed) increases linearly from the hub to the tip (V = ω × r).

q.t: Which of the stated relationships between lift and drag applies best for a flying helicopter (lift : drag)?
q.e: Modern rotor blades are highly efficient aerofoils, typically achieving a lift-to-drag ratio of approximately 45:1.

q.t: The reason for a stall at a given pitch angle can be...
o: constant peripheral speed and great vertical airflow through the rotor.
smaller vertical airflow through the rotor and constant peripheral speed.
smaller effective angle of attack and small peripheral speed.
smaller frontal resistance and turbulent airflow.
q.e: A reduction in vertical airflow (induced flow) at a constant pitch increases the effective angle of attack toward the stall point.

q.t: The neutral point is a point where...
o: the imaginary axes of a helicopter meet each other.
the entire helicopter mass can be assumed to attack.
the torque at the chord line remains constant for changing angles of attack.
q.e: The aerodynamic center (neutral point) is the point where the pitching moment remains constant regardless of changes in the angle of attack.

q.t: What shape of a rotor blade has a positive impact on the lift distribution?
o: Rectangular blade with a geometric setting of 1°
Double trapezoidal rotor blade with a radius at the blade tip
Trapezoidal blade without radius at the blade tip
Rectangular trapezoidal blade with no aerodynamic twist
q.e: Tapered or trapezoidal shapes reduce the chord at the tip, which helps equalize lift distribution and reduce tip vortices.

q.t: The rotor blade shape takes effect on the...
q.e: The planform (shape) and twist of a rotor blade are designed specifically to optimize how lift is distributed across the span.

q.t: The drive system of the autogyro's main rotor is based on...
o: an engine at the rotor blade tip.
q.e: Unlike a helicopter, an autogyro's rotor is not engine-driven; it is turned by the upward flow of air (autorotation) caused by forward flight.

q.t: The rotor RPM is kept constant by the engine RPM. It can be influenced by the...
q.e: In modern helicopters, the governor or FADEC automatically adjusts the throttle to maintain a constant rotor RPM.

q.t: The beam theory enables statements about the...
o: transition lift close to the ground.
q.e: Momentum (beam) theory is used to calculate the induced power and performance characteristics specifically during hovering.

q.t: During hover flight, the induced airflow velocity...
o: is equal above and below the rotor.
increases further having passed the rotor.
remains constant after having passed the rotor.
decreases after having passed the rotor.
q.e: According to momentum theory, air continues to accelerate after passing through the rotor disc, reaching maximum velocity in the vena contracta.

q.t: Why is a helicopter's climb initially accelerated after an increase of the pitch angle?
o: Large pitch causes compression until climb rate matches induced velocity
The inertia of the air increases the effective angle of attack temporarily
High initial airflow increases thrust until lower density reduces it
Conversion of energetic air into kinetic energy decreases with density
q.e: When pitch is increased, air inertia prevents an immediate change in flow, causing a temporary surge in AOA and thrust.

q.t: A helicopter hovers sideways to the right. At what azimuth is the pitch biggest?
q.e: To move right, the disc tilts right. Due to the 90° phase lag, the maximum pitch must be applied 90° prior, which is at the 0° (rear) position.

q.t: The airframe of an accelerating helicopter continues to bend until the...
o: horizontal thrust component equals the drag.
thrust passes in front of the centre of gravity.
vertical thrust component equals the drag.
thrust passes behind the centre of gravity.
q.e: Acceleration ceases and a steady speed is reached when the forward component of thrust is exactly balanced by the aircraft's drag.

q.t: What is the reason for retreating blade stall?
o: Large pitch angle and small effective airflow
Small pitch angle and large effective airflow
q.e: At high speeds, the retreating blade requires a very high pitch angle to compensate for the very low relative airflow, leading to a stall.

q.t: The induced airflow in level flight has the greatest value at the...
q.e: The downwash (induced flow) is not uniform; it is highest at the rear of the disc due to the accumulation of the wake.

q.t: Which option describes the term "asymmetric airflow"?
o: Advancing blade has more airflow than the retreating blade
Displacement of driving forces in autorotation
Performance difference in/out of ground effect
Greater lift in outer region of the rotor
q.e: Asymmetry occurs because the forward speed of the helicopter adds to the advancing blade's speed and subtracts from the retreating blade's speed.

q.t: The transitional lift can be noticed by...
q.e: As the helicopter transitions into forward flight, it moves out of its own turbulent wake, which typically causes characteristic vibrations.

q.t: Which statement about the rotor disc loading in a horizontal curve is correct?
o: It decreases with increasing bank angle
It increases with increasing bank angle
No change in relation to the cruise flight
Effects depend on the type of helicopter
q.e: In a turn, the rotor must produce more thrust to support both the aircraft's weight and the centrifugal force, increasing the disc loading.

q.t: What action is necessary during the transition to a horizontal turn?
o: Control column forward or raising collective
Control column backward or raising the collective
q.e: Since a portion of the lift is used for the turn, the pilot must increase total thrust or pull back to maintain altitude.

q.t: Why does a stall begin on the retreating rotor blade at high cruise speeds?
o: Small pitch and low speed cause small AOA
Large pitch angle and relatively low peripheral speed cause a large AOA
q.e: To balance lift across the disc, the retreating blade operates at a high pitch; combined with low relative speed, this results in a high AOA.

q.t: Without corrective moves, a helicopter hovering in ground effect will execute...
q.e: The ground effect "cushion" is inherently unstable, causing the helicopter to slightly "bob" or oscillate vertically.

q.t: The ground effect is noticeable by...
q.e: Ground effect reduces the induced flow and the angle of the resultant lift, thereby reducing the power required to hover.

q.t: What can be expected during hover in a forest glade?
o: Recirculation of air masses and an impairment of the ground effect
q.e: In confined areas like a glade, the rotor wash is forced back up and into the rotor (recirculation), which destroys the ground effect cushion.

q.t: Which landing site (no wind) prevents the impairment of the ground effect?
q.e: A flat, open surface (plain terrain) allows the rotor wake to flow outward smoothly, maximizing the ground effect.

q.t: What is the result of the vortex ring state?
q.e: In VRS, the helicopter sinks into its own downwash, causing a massive loss of lift and an uncontrollable increase in descent rate.

q.t: What is the correct way to counteract the vortex ring state?
o: Try to gain airspeed and enter autorotation
q.e: The primary recovery method is to gain forward airspeed to move the rotor horizontally out of the descending column of air.

q.t: What is the effect of vortex ring state?
o: High rate of descent and irregular motions
q.e: VRS is characterized by an extremely high sink rate accompanied by severe instability in pitch, roll, and yaw.

q.t: What is the risk in vertical autorotation with airspeed increase prior to landing?
q.e: Transitioning from a vertical descent to forward flight (to flare) requires precise timing to avoid hitting the ground.

q.t: What is the reason for the driving forces in an autorotation?
q.e: In autorotation, the air comes from below, tilting the resultant aerodynamic force vector forward, which provides the driving force.

q.t: During an autorotation the airspeed is limited by...
o: the drift of the driving forces on the returning blade.
q.e: Airspeed in autorotation is limited because the driving region shifts, potentially leading to a loss of rotor RPM control.

q.t: Which of the following has an effect on the autorotation characteristics?
q.e: The rate of descent and rotor energy in autorotation are primarily determined by the aircraft's weight and the air density.

q.t: In autorotation with forward speed, driving forces are located in the...
o: region of the retreating rotor blade.
region of the advancing rotor blade.
q.e: During forward autorotation, the driving (autorotative) region is asymmetric and primarily located on the retreating side.

q.t: During autorotation, a helicopter accelerates from 60 to 90 knots. The RPM will...
q.e: While acceleration typically increases RPM, in a stabilized autorotative state, the RPM is usually maintained within a narrow constant range.

q.t: What action has no effect on the rotor RPM in an autorotation?
q.e: The rotor friction brake is used only on the ground and has no aerodynamic or mechanical effect on flight RPM.

q.t: After entering an autorotation a large helicopter mass leads to...
o: a rapid build-up of the rotor RPM.
q.e: A heavier helicopter has more potential energy and requires more thrust to balance, leading to a faster rotor RPM build-up.

q.t: What shall be considered before terminating a turn in an autorotation?
q.e: Entering or exiting a turn changes the G-load; the resulting flapping and Coriolis effect will cause changes in rotor RPM.

q.t: Which energies maintain the rotor rpm in an autorotation?
q.e: The rotor's RPM is maintained by converting the helicopter's potential energy (altitude) and kinetic energy (airspeed) into rotor work.

q.t: The maximum range in an autorotation will be achieved by...
o: a relatively high effective angle of attack.
q.e: Maximum glide distance (range) is typically achieved at a lower airspeed which corresponds to a higher angle of attack.

q.t: Why does a flare during an autorotation generate higher rotor RPM?
o: Vertical airflow through the rotor disc increases
Ground effect leads to better performance
q.e: The flare tilts the rotor back, increasing the airflow from below, which increases the driving force and thus the RPM.

q.t: Which movement is caused by the Coriolis effect on the advancing rotor blade?
q.e: As the blade flaps up, it moves closer to the axis of rotation and, like a spinning ice skater, accelerates forward (lead).

q.t: Which factor affects the response time to initiate an autorotation after engine failure?
o: Inertia of the main rotor system
q.e: High rotor inertia stores more kinetic energy, providing the pilot with more time to react before the RPM decays dangerously.

q.t: Which statement about the force to change the pitch angle is correct?
o: Must be greater than disc loading
It must be greater than the tangential force
q.e: The control system (actuators or pilot) must exert enough force to overcome the aerodynamic tangential (drag) forces on the blade.

q.t: Why do semi-rigid rotor systems react slower than others?
o: The central flapping hinge does not transmit any moments
q.e: Because the flapping hinge is central (teetering), it cannot transmit hub moments to the airframe, relying only on thrust tilt.

q.t: The pitch angle of a tail rotor blade is changed...
q.e: Tail rotors do not have cyclic pitch; their blades change pitch together (collectively) to control yaw.

q.t: A delta-three hinge is used to allow...
o: decreased pitch angle at an upwards flapping blade.
q.e: Delta-3 coupling automatically reduces the blade's pitch as it flaps up, providing aerodynamic damping of flapping.

q.t: What needs to be observed regarding loss of tail rotor efficiency in hover?
o: Vortex ring stage of the tail rotor
q.e: A tail rotor can settle into its own wake (VRS), resulting in a sudden and severe loss of directional control.

q.t: What is caused by an increase of stability in a helicopter?
o: An increase of general flight safety
q.e: Higher stability reduces pilot workload and makes the aircraft more predictable, thereby increasing overall safety.

q.t: What is caused by an increase of stability in a helicopter?
o: A relief of the pilot in command
Enhance control under all load factors
q.e: Stable aircraft require fewer corrective inputs from the pilot, significantly reducing fatigue and mental workload.

q.t: Why are the stability criteria very important?
o: A lack of stability may lead to loss of control
q.e: An unstable helicopter can enter divergent oscillations that quickly exceed the pilot's ability to correct, leading to a crash.

q.t: The helicopter's stability is increased by...
q.e: Horizontal or vertical stabilizers provide aerodynamic damping and restorative moments, increasing the aircraft's stability.

q.t: What is the purpose of the vertical stabilizer?
q.e: The vertical fin acts like a weathercock, keeping the helicopter's nose pointed into the relative wind during forward flight.

q.t: An increase of stability in a helicopter causes...
q.e: In aircraft design, there is always a trade-off: the more stable an aircraft is, the less responsive (controllable) it becomes.

q.t: What behavior does a helicopter show after disturbances in hover without corrective action?
q.e: Most helicopters will tend to return to their original position (static stability) but the resulting oscillations will grow (dynamic instability).

q.t: What relieves the helicopter in a low G manoeuvre?
o: Increased vertical airflow through the rotor
q.e: In a low-G condition, the reduction in thrust is partially offset by an increase in vertical airflow (upwash) through the disc.

q.t: Vx is the speed...
o: for the best rate of climb.
for the best angle of climb.
q.e: Vx is the speed that provides the greatest gain in altitude over a given horizontal distance.

q.t: Vy is the speed...
o: for the best rate of climb.
for the best angle of climb.
q.e: Vy is the speed that provides the maximum gain in altitude over a specific period of time.

q.t: The term "flight time" is defined as...
o: The period from engine start for the purpose of taking off to engine shutdown.
The total time from the first take-off until the last landing.
The period from the start of the take-off run to the final touchdown.
The total time from the first aircraft movement until it finally comes to rest.
q.e: According to EASA/ICAO definitions, flight time is the total time from the moment an aircraft first moves for the purpose of taking off until it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight.

q.t: What should be considered regarding a scheduled flight over water, when land cannot be reached in case of an emergency landing?
o: The flight plan has to contain the exact waypoints.
Contact to the nearest ATC shall consist during the whole flight.
Transponder code 7600 has to be set during the whole flight.
For all passengers there must be life jackets or lifeboats present.
q.e: For extended flights over water where land is out of reach, safety regulations require adequate life-saving equipment (life jackets or rafts) for all occupants.

q.t: When should turns at low altitudes above villages be avoided with regard to noise abatement procedures?
q.e: Noise abatement procedures specifically recommend avoiding turns at low altitudes during the initial climb to minimize noise disturbance over populated areas.

q.t: Which kind of engine is susceptible to carburettor fire?
q.e: Piston engines use carburettors to mix fuel and air, making them susceptible to induction fires if backfiring or improper priming occurs.

q.t: Why is it dangerous to pump the throttle for engine start in cold weather?
o: It may cause a carburettor fire.
The engine might start with not enough power.
q.e: Rapidly pumping the throttle (accelerator pump) sprays raw fuel into the intake, which can ignite and cause a carburettor fire during cranking.

q.t: Which danger exists during engine start?
q.e: During the start sequence of a piston engine, one of the primary risks is an induction or carburettor fire caused by excess fuel.

q.t: May an engine, which previously was on fire, be restarted?
o: Yes, if the cause was a carburettor fire during start.
Yes, but only on the ground for taxiing.
No, the risk of a reignition of the fire would be too high.
Yes, if the aircraft is flying at a safe altitude.
q.e: Safety protocols strictly prohibit restarting an engine that has suffered a fire in flight due to the high risk of reignition and structural damage.

q.t: Which gas is most dangerous during an engine fire?
q.e: Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless, and highly toxic byproduct of combustion that can quickly incapacitate the crew if it enters the cabin.

q.t: Smoke enters the cockpit during an engine fire. Which actions have to be taken immediately?
o: Switching off the pitot and front window heating.
Switching off the master switch and the ignition.
Switching off the heating and the ventilating system.
Switching off the avionics and the cabin lighting.
q.e: Closing the heating and ventilation stops the intake of smoke and toxic gases from the engine compartment into the cockpit.

q.t: What should be the first action in case of a cable fire during a flight?
q.e: For an electrical fire (cable fire), isolating the power source by turning off the Master Switch is the immediate priority to stop the ignition source.

q.t: What extinguishing agent is the least suitable for an aircraft fire?
q.e: Water is unsuitable for aircraft fires because it can spread fuel fires and cause catastrophic short circuits in electrical systems.

q.t: In flight, a little smoke emerges from behind the instrument panel. An electrical fire is suspected. Which action should be taken?
q.e: If an electrical fire is suspected in the cockpit, the master switch must be turned off immediately to remove power from the faulty wiring.

q.t: In flight, a little smoke emerges from behind the instrument panel. An engine fire is suspected. Which action should be taken?
q.e: While shutting down the engine is a standard procedure for a fire, the provided material identifies turning off the master switch as the primary checklist action for this specific scenario.

q.t: A wind shear is...
o: A vertical or horizontal change of wind speed and wind direction.
A wind speed change of more than 15 kt.
A slow increase of wind speed above 13000 ft.
q.e: Wind shear is defined as a significant and sudden change in wind velocity (speed and/or direction) over a short distance.

q.t: Which weather phenomenon is typically associated with wind shear?
q.e: Thunderstorms create powerful downdrafts (microbursts) and gust fronts that are primary causes of violent low-level wind shear.

q.t: When do you expect wind shear?
o: During a summer day with calm winds.
In calm wind in cold weather.
q.e: Temperature inversions often decouple surface air from stronger winds aloft, creating a shear layer at the boundary of the inversion.

q.t: Approach experiences windshear with decreasing headwind. If no corrections are made, how do path and IAS change?
q.e: A loss of headwind results in a sudden drop in indicated airspeed and a loss of lift, causing the aircraft to sink below the intended path.

q.t: Approach experiences windshear with increasing headwind. If no corrections are made, how do path and IAS change?
q.e: An increasing headwind momentarily increases indicated airspeed and lift, causing the aircraft to balloon above the intended approach path.

q.t: Approach experiences windshear with decreasing tailwind. If no corrections are made, how do path and IAS change?
q.e: The provided source identifies that a decreasing tailwind results in a lower path and lower IAS, though physically it typically acts like an increasing headwind.

q.t: After take-off an aeroplane gets into a wind shear with decreasing headwind. As a result...
o: The aeroplane flies below the estimated climb path.
The aeroplane flies above the estimated climb path.
q.e: A loss of headwind during climb results in reduced airspeed and climb performance, causing the aircraft to fall below its projected path.

q.t: How may windshear be recognised in flight?
o: Baseless change of oil pressure and altitude.
Sudden change in altitude, airspeed, rate of climb or descent.
Sudden change in heading, turning rate, or engine speed.
Unexpected onset of drizzle and high stratus.
q.e: Rapid, unexplained fluctuations in the primary flight instruments (airspeed, VSI, altimeter) are classic indicators of a wind shear encounter.

q.t: How can a wind shear encounter in flight be avoided?
o: Avoid take-off and landing during heavy showers or thunderstorms.
Avoid take-offs and landings in mountainous terrain.
Avoid thermally active areas during summer.
Avoid areas of precipitation during winter.
q.e: Staying clear of thunderstorms and heavy rain is the most effective way to avoid the intense microbursts and gust fronts that cause shear.

q.t: After lift-off, a stronger than expected airspeed rise is experienced. What may be expected if entering a microburst?
o: A decreased climb rate and airspeed.
An increased climb rate and decreased airspeed.
A decreased climb rate and increased airspeed.
An increased climb rate and airspeed.
q.e: A microburst typically starts with an increasing headwind (initial lift), followed by a massive downdraft and a sharp loss of airspeed.

q.t: Wake turbulences develop during take-off just as the aeroplane...
o: Lifts off with the main gear.
Lifts off with the front gear.
q.e: Wake vortices are a byproduct of lift; they begin the moment the aircraft's weight is supported by the wings/rotors (at lift-off).

q.t: Wake turbulence is caused by...
o: Jet blast behind a turbine engine.
Turbulence at the downwind side of a mountain.
Wind shear at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
Pressure compensation at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
q.e: Wake turbulence consists of vortices formed by air flowing from the high-pressure lower surface to the low-pressure upper surface at the tips.

q.t: Wake turbulence is particularly strong...
q.e: The strength of wake vortices is highest when the aircraft is generating maximum lift at low speeds (high angle of attack).

q.t: Wake turbulence is particularly strong...
q.e: Vortex strength is directly proportional to the aircraft's weight; heavier aircraft must generate more lift and thus stronger vortices.

q.t: Two identical aircraft fly at different airspeeds. Which causes more severe wake turbulence?
o: The aircraft flying at lower altitude.
The aircraft flying at slower speed.
The aircraft flying at higher altitude.
The aircraft flying at higher speed.
q.e: For a given weight, an aircraft flying slower requires a higher angle of attack, which results in more powerful wake vortices.

q.t: Two identical aircraft fly with different speeds and altitude. Which aircraft will cause more wake turbulence?
o: The aircraft flying at a lower altitude.
The aircraft flying at a higher altitude.
The aircraft flying at lower speed.
The aircraft flying at higher speed.
q.e: Speed is the dominant factor here; lower speed corresponds to a higher coefficient of lift and stronger vortex production.

q.t: With only a slight crosswind, what is the danger at take-off after a heavy aeroplane?
o: Wake turbulence rotate faster and higher.
Wake turbulence twisting transverse to the runway.
Wake turbulence is amplified and distorted.
Wake turbulence on or near the runway.
q.e: A light crosswind can counteract the natural outward drift of a vortex, holding it stationary directly on the runway.

q.t: What should be observed when taxiing behind a commercial airliner?
o: Maintain a minimum distance of 200 m to avoid jet blast.
Maintain a minimum distance of 600 m to avoid jet blast.
Maintain a minimum distance of 300 m to avoid wake turbulence.
Maintain a minimum distance of 700 m to avoid wake turbulence.
q.e: Jet blast (exhaust velocity) from large aircraft can easily flip light aircraft; a minimum safety distance of 200m is required.

q.t: Which area is suitable for an off-field landing?
q.e: A harvested cornfield usually offers a relatively flat, firm surface with minimal obstructions compared to soft plowed fields or glades.

q.t: A landing conducted in response to circumstances forcing the aircraft to land is a / an...
q.e: An emergency landing is one forced by an immediate and critical situation, such as engine failure or fire.

q.t: A precautionary landing is a landing...
o: Conducted in response to circumstances forcing the landing.
Conducted in an attempt to sustain flight safety.
Conducted without power from the engine.
q.e: A precautionary landing is a voluntary landing made while the aircraft is still under control to avoid a developing hazard.

q.t: Which items should a passenger briefing in case of an imminent emergency landing include?
o: Blood type and first-aid kit location.
Nature of emergency, intentions, safety position, evacuation routes.
Radio usage and SAR telephone numbers.
Emergency checklist reading and home airport phone number.
q.e: In an emergency, passengers must be briefed on their brace position, how to exit, and what to do after landing.

q.t: In case of an emergency ditching, the life vests have to be inflated...
o: After disembarking at a safe distance of about 10 m.
q.e: Inflating life vests inside the aircraft can trap passengers if the cabin fills with water; they must be inflated after exiting.

q.t: What has to be considered when starting the engine in a strong wind condition?
o: The rotor brake should not be released before sufficient RPM.
The cyclic stick should be taken backwards and collective raised.
The mixture should be leaned and carburettor heat pulled.
The helicopter should be aligned with its longitudinal axis in the wind.
q.e: Starting into the wind provides the best cooling and prevents the wind from catching the rotor blades at low RPM.

q.t: What needs to be observed in conjunction with flying above mountainous terrain?
o: Unexpected changes in weather and turbulence.
Icing conditions over the predicted freezing level.
q.e: Mountainous terrain creates complex wind patterns, mechanical turbulence, and rapid, localized weather shifts.

q.t: What needs to be observed in particular when performing a slope landing?
o: Direction of rotation of the main rotor.
q.e: Landing on a slope carries a high risk of the helicopter sliding or rolling over due to the inclined terrain.

q.t: An autorotation in a mountainous area is performed:
q.e: Landing upslope allows for a quicker reduction of forward speed and safer touchdown in steep terrain.

q.t: When has the actual take-off time to be transmitted to ATC for a flight from an uncontrolled aerodrome?
o: At deviation from expected off-block time by more than 15 min.
q.e: For flights with a filed flight plan departing from uncontrolled aerodromes, the actual take-off time must be reported to FIS/ATC immediately after lift-off.

q.t: Landing is conducted at an airfield other than the destination in the flight plan. Who has to be contacted immediately?
