q.e: AIS must be informed of any diversion from the filed flight plan to ensure search and rescue (SAR) services are updated.

q.t: Exceeding the maximum allowed aircraft mass is...
o: only relevant if the excess is more than 10 %.
compensated by the pilot's control inputs.
q.e: Maximum mass limits are structural and performance boundaries; exceeding them compromises flight safety and airworthiness.

q.t: The center of gravity has to be located...
o: right of the lateral C. G. limit.
between the front and the rear C.G. limit.
in front of the front C.G. limit.
q.e: To ensure the aircraft remains stable and controllable, the CG must stay within the calculated forward and aft limits.

q.t: CG stays within approved limits to ensure...
o: both stability and controllability of the aircraft.
that the aircraft does not exceed Vne.
that the aircraft does not stall.
that the aircraft does not tip over on its tail.
q.e: Proper CG placement is critical because it dictates the aircraft's inherent stability and the effectiveness of the flight controls.

q.t: CG stays within approved limits (helicopter) to ensure...
o: that the helicopter does not stall.
that it does not exceed Vne.
that it does not tip over.
both stability and controllability of the helicopter.
q.e: In helicopters, keeping the CG within limits is vital for maintaining the necessary control margins in all axes of flight.

q.t: The result of a front C.G. position is:
q.e: A forward CG increases stability (1), but also increases fuel consumption (2) and stall speed (3) due to higher required lift/force to balance.

q.t: The basic empty mass of an aircraft includes...
o: total mass ready for operation including crew.
mass plus standard items, unusable fuel/fluids, lubricating oil, and fixed equipment.
mass ready for operation including fuel.
q.e: Basic Empty Mass consists of the airframe, engines, and all fixed equipment plus unusable fuel and full operating fluids.

q.t: The empty weight and the center of gravity (CG) are initially determined...
o: for one aircraft of a type only.
q.e: Every individual aircraft must be physically weighed to establish its specific empty weight and CG arm for legal operations.

q.t: The density of AVGAS 100LL at 15° C is...
q.e: For standard mass and balance calculations, the density of AVGAS 100LL is assumed to be 0.72 kg per liter.

q.t: The conversion factor from kilogram [kg] into pounds [lb] is...
q.e: To convert kilograms to pounds, multiply the mass in kg by 2.205.

q.t: Shift of the cargo may cause...
o: uncontrollable attitudes, structural damage, risk of injuries.
q.e: Unsecured cargo can shift during maneuvers, potentially moving the CG outside limits and creating an uncontrollable flight condition.

q.t: Loads must be adequately secured in order to...
o: avoid any centre of gravity (C.G.) movements.
q.e: Tie-downs and nets prevent cargo from moving, which maintains the calculated center of gravity during all flight phases.

q.t: The total weight of an aeroplane is acting vertically through the...
q.e: The center of gravity is defined as the single point through which the resultant force of gravity acts on the entire mass.

q.t: The term "center of gravity" is defined as...
o: point at which the total mass is considered to act.
half the distance to the datum.
q.e: Theoretically, the CG is the balance point where the aircraft would be level if suspended from that single spot.

q.t: The center of gravity (CG) defines...
o: point through which the force of gravity acts on a mass.
q.e: It is the specific point where the gravitational attraction of the Earth is concentrated for that object.

q.t: During an unaccelerated flight...
o: vertical thrust = gravity, horizontal thrust = drag.
q.e: In steady, level, unaccelerated flight, the forces are in equilibrium: Lift/Thrust-vertical equals Weight, and Thrust-horizontal equals Drag.

q.t: Compensation for a tail-heavy center of gravity in a helicopter?
o: Add fuel behind the rotor mast.
Add additional load in the front of the cabin.
q.e: To move the CG forward (countering a tail-heavy state), weight must be added to the forward part of the aircraft.

q.t: Helicopter rotates much more than expected during lift-off. This indicates...
o: CG is much more aft than expected.
centre of hub is overhead CG.
q.e: Excessive nose-up rotation during hover lift-off is a classic symptom of an aft (tail-heavy) center of gravity.

q.t: The term "datum" in mass and balance defines...
o: point on the longitudinal axis from which centers of gravity are referenced.
q.e: The datum is the fixed reference point (e.g., the nose or firewall) used as the "zero" for all arm and moment measurements.

q.t: The term "moment" in mass and balance is referred to as...
o: product of mass and balance arm.
q.e: Moment is the rotational force calculated by multiplying the weight of an item by its distance (arm) from the datum.

q.t: The term "balance arm" defines the...
o: distance from the datum to the center of gravity of a mass.
q.e: The arm is the horizontal distance from the reference datum to the location of a specific weight/item.

q.t: The distance between the center of gravity and the datum is called...
q.e: This distance is technically the arm of the center of gravity, used to find the aircraft's total moment.

q.t: The balance arm is the horizontal distance between...
o: the C.G. of a mass and the datum line.
the C.G. and the rear limit.
the front limit and the datum line.
q.e: Every component has its own arm, measured from the common zero point (the datum).

q.t: Data for mass and balance calculation can be found in the...
o: mass and balance section of the POH.
q.e: Section 6 of the Pilot’s Operating Handbook (POH) contains the specific weight and arm data for that particular aircraft.

q.t: When preparing for the weighing procedure, which is required?
q.e: Aircraft are weighed in a "Basic Empty" configuration, which requires draining all fuel that can be used by the engine.

q.t: Which section of the flight manual describes the basic empty mass?
q.e: Section 6 (Weight and Balance) provides the empty weight and CG as determined by the last physical weighing.

q.t: Which section describes the CG limitations of a helicopter?
q.e: The specific boundaries for safe operation (forward, aft, and lateral limits) are found in Section 2: Limitations.

q.t: Position of the center of gravity (See PFP-052e)?
q.e: Based on the table provided in PFP-052e, calculating the total moment divided by total mass results in 142 inches.

q.t: What mass equals 102 litres of Avgas 100LL?
q.e: 102 liters multiplied by the standard density of 0.72 kg/l equals approximately 74 kg.

q.t: CG after fuel burn (2300lb, CG 95.75, burn 170lb at 87.0)?
q.e: Calculating (Total Moment - Fuel Moment) / (Total Mass - Fuel Mass) results in a new CG of 96.57 inches.

q.t: CG after landing (746kg, CG 37.1, burn 30.5L at 45cm)?
q.e: Converting fuel volume to mass and recalculating the moment results in a landing CG of 36.9 cm.

q.t: CG after landing (1082kg, CG 0.254m, 55L at 0.40m)?
q.e: Calculating with mass/arms in meters and converting results in a landing CG of 24.8 cm.

q.t: Position of CG including fuel (See PFP-053e)?
q.e: Summing the masses and moments from the table in PFP-053e gives a total CG of 37.1 cm.

q.t: Cross marking CG (750kg, 625 mmkg) (See PFP-003)?
q.e: Intersection of 750 kg mass and 625 mmkg moment on the chart corresponds to point 1.

q.t: Cross marking CG (725kg, 650 mmkg) (See PFP-004)?
q.e: Intersection of 725 kg mass and 650 mmkg moment on the chart corresponds to point 1.

q.t: Cross marking CG (775kg, 700 mmkg) (See PFP-005)?
q.e: Intersection of 775 kg mass and 700 mmkg moment on the chart corresponds to point 1.

q.t: Most recently determined empty mass/CG (See PFP-006)?
q.e: The bottom row of the weight changes log in PFP-006 shows the latest values: 498 kg and 280.59 m.

q.t: "Maximum elevation figure" (MEF) is defined as...
o: highest elevation in 30'x30' area plus safety margin, rounded up to 100 ft.
q.e: MEF provides the highest terrain/obstacle clearance in a grid square, including a buffer and rounding up for safety.

q.t: Purpose of "interception lines" in visual navigation?
o: Recognizable guidance upon loss of orientation.
Help when visibility drops below VFR.
q.e: Linear features (rivers, tracks) help pilots regain their position if they become disoriented during visual flight.

q.t: The VFR semicircular rules are based on the...
q.e: Semicircular altitudes for VFR flights are determined by the magnetic course to ensure vertical separation between traffic.

q.t: Lowest VFR level (TC 181°, VAR 3°E)?
q.e: TC 181 - VAR 3E = MC 178. For MC 000-179, VFR levels are Odd + 500. Lowest above transition is FL055.

q.t: Upper limit of LO R 16 (See PFP-056)?
q.e: Restricted area LO R 16 is depicted on the chart with an upper limit of 1500 feet above Mean Sea Level.

q.t: Upper limit of LO R 4 (See PFP-030)?
q.e: According to the chart PFP-030, the restricted area LO R 4 extends up to 4500 feet MSL.

q.t: The term "FATO" is defined as...
o: final approach and take-off area for helicopters.
q.e: FATO is the specific area over which the final phase of the approach to a hover or landing is completed.

q.t: Taxi fuel to reduce mass (MRM 1150, Actual 1148, MTOM 1145)?
q.e: To reduce the actual mass (1148 kg) to the MTOM (1145 kg), 3 kg of fuel must be burned, which is ~4 liters.

q.t: What document contains information about the fuel consumption?
q.e: Engine fuel flow and consumption data for various power settings are found in the Performance section of the POH.

q.t: Required trip fuel (Start 5, Climb 12, Cruise 25, Descent 7, etc)?
q.e: Trip fuel covers only the phases from take-off to landing: 12 (climb) + 25 (cruise) + 7 (descent) = 44 Liters.

q.t: Message of the NOTAM (RWY 24L/06R CLOSED)?
o: closed Nov 21 2200 local to Nov 22 0500 local.
closed Nov 21 2200 UTC to Nov 22 0500 UTC.
q.e: NOTAM times are always given in UTC unless specifically stated otherwise.

q.t: Alternate aerodrome LOKH safe (Req 550m, LDA 500m)?
q.e: The NOTAM indicates the LDA is 500m due to a displaced threshold, which is less than the 550m required.

q.t: Overflight prohibited altitude (See PFP-024)?
q.e: Item G) in the NOTAM specifies the upper limit as 9500 FT AMSL (Above Mean Sea Level).

q.t: EOBT is specified in the flight plan as...
q.e: Estimated Off-Block Time must be provided in UTC to ensure clarity for international air traffic control.

q.t: Nature of the flight in flight plan (See PFP-051a)?
q.e: The route information and flight type code (G) in the plan indicate a local VFR traffic operation.

q.t: Specified speed in the flight plan (See PFP-051)?
q.e: The entry "N0100" in field 15 denotes a cruising speed of 100 knots.

q.t: What must be considered for cross-border flights?
q.e: Crossing national borders requires an ATS flight plan for identification and search and rescue purposes.

q.t: During a flight, a flight plan can be filed at the...
q.e: Pilots can file an airborne flight plan (AFIL) by communicating with a FIS frequency.

q.t: Actions if orientation is lost during helicopter flight?
o: Continue to next interception line and reorientate.
q.e: Heading toward a known linear landmark (interception line) is the standard procedure to regain orientation.

q.t: What needs to be observed on a hot day?
q.e: High temperatures increase density altitude, which significantly degrades engine and rotor performance.

q.t: Which factor has a positive effect on the power required?
q.e: Smooth, clean rotor blades maintain laminar flow and reduce drag, requiring less power for flight.

q.t: Max altitude hover IGE (2400 lbs, +20°C) (See PFP-045)?
q.e: Finding 2400 lbs on the bottom axis and following the +20°C line results in a ceiling of 8600 ft.

q.t: VNE at 4000 ft, +10°C, mass 2300 lbs (See PFP-046)?
q.e: Base VNE is 126; the note requires subtracting 10 KIAS for mass over 2200 lbs, resulting in 116 KIAS.

q.t: Section describing power required in a hover?
q.e: Performance charts for hovering, climb, and cruise are found in Section 5: Performance.

q.t: Power output of a piston engine is limited by...
q.e: Piston engines in helicopters are often "derated," with power limited by the torque capacity of the gearbox.

q.t: Power output of a turbine engine is limited by...
o: compressor RPM, turbine inlet temp, and gearbox.
q.e: Turbine performance is limited by its internal thermal limits (TIT) and mechanical limits (RPM/Torque).

q.t: How do manufacturers reduce power output for helicopters?
q.e: Power output is typically restricted by physically limiting the amount of fuel that can be delivered to the engine.

q.t: Point indicating speed for maximum endurance (See PFP-044)?
q.e: Point 3, the lowest point on the power demand curve, represents the speed where power usage is minimal.

q.t: Point indicating speed for maximum range (See PFP-044)?
q.e: Point 4, where a line from the origin is tangent to the curve, gives the best speed-to-power ratio.

q.t: What needs to be observed if carburettor heat is applied?
q.e: Carburetor heat introduces warm, less dense air into the engine, resulting in a measurable drop in power.

q.t: What factor is affected by headwind during a departure?
q.e: A headwind does not change the rate of climb, but it makes the flight path steeper relative to the ground.

q.t: Why does VNE decrease with increasing pressure altitude?
q.e: For a constant IAS, TAS increases at altitude, moving the blades closer to their high-speed stability limits.

q.t: variable properties affecting performance?
q.e: Performance is governed by air density, which is a function of temperature, pressure, and water vapor.

q.t: Regarding ice formation during flight?
q.e: Ice accumulation is dangerous because it simultaneously adds weight, increases drag, and spoils lift.

q.t: Increasing a helicopter's mass will...
q.e: Added weight requires more power to support; the remaining excess power for climbing is reduced.

q.t: Maximum endurance is achieved by flying at...
o: lower speed than max range and lowest altitude.
q.e: Minimum fuel flow occurs at the bottom of the power curve (low speed) and in high-density air (low altitude).

q.t: Helicopter approach is conducted into the wind because...
q.e: Landing into the wind reduces the ground speed at touchdown, significantly shortening the landing distance.

q.t: If TAS is significantly less than GS, you have...
q.e: Ground speed is the sum of TAS and the wind vector; if GS > TAS, a tailwind component is pushing you.

q.t: If the helicopter mass is increased...
q.e: Heavier aircraft require higher power settings to maintain flight, which uses fuel faster and reduces total range.

q.t: Max mass for departure (8000 ft, +20° C) (See PFP-045)?
q.e: Using the performance lines in PFP-045 for 8000 ft and +20°C limits the mass to 1950 lbs.

q.t: Max mass hover IGE (9000 ft, +10° C) (See PFP-045)?
q.e: Intersection of the 9000 ft altitude and +10°C temperature line indicates a limit of 2360 lbs.

q.t: Symbol for group of unlighted obstacles (See PFP-061)?
q.e: Based on ICAO chart standards in the provided annex, symbol B indicates unlighted obstacle groups.

q.t: Symbol for civil airport with paved runway (See PFP-062)?
q.e: According to ICAO symbology, a simple circle with internal runway markings (A) denotes a paved civil airport.

q.t: Symbol indicating general spot elevation (See PFP-063)?
q.e: A numerical value with a specific dot marker (C) is the standard ICAO symbol for a spot elevation.

q.t: What is the advantage of a gyrodyne compared to a helicopter?
q.e: Gyrodynes use a separate propulsion system for forward flight, allowing for higher cruise speeds than traditional helicopters.

q.t: How is referred to a tubular steel construction with a non self-supporting skin?
q.e: A tubular steel framework that relies on the internal structure rather than the skin for strength is called a grid or truss construction.

q.t: The sandwich structure consists of two...
o: thick layers and a light core material
thin layers and a light core material
thin layers and a heavy core material
thick layers and a heavy core material
q.e: Sandwich structures use two thin, strong outer layers bonded to a lightweight core to achieve high stiffness.

q.t: The load factor "n" describes the relationship between...
q.e: The load factor is the ratio of the lift generated by the rotors/wings to the actual weight of the aircraft.

q.t: Which are the advantages of sandwich structures?
o: Low weight, high stiffness, stability, and strength
Good formability and high temperature durability
High temperature durability and low weight
q.e: Sandwich panels provide an excellent strength-to-weight ratio and high structural rigidity.

q.t: Which of the stated materials shows the highest strength?
q.e: Carbon fiber reinforced plastics (CFRP) offer superior tensile strength and stiffness compared to the other listed materials.

q.t: What needs to be considered if permissible limitations were exceeded?
o: Helicopter must be inspected by a qualified engineer
Subjected to duplicate inspection by two engineers
Pilot inspection is sufficient if no defect found
q.e: Exceeding any operational limit requires a professional maintenance inspection before the aircraft is airworthy again.

q.t: What might be the reason for scratches on the tail stringer?
q.e: Tail stringer damage often occurs due to tail-low landings or strikes against the ground during maneuvers.

q.t: What kind of hydraulic oil is used in aeroplane systems today?
q.e: Modern aviation hydraulic systems primarily use fire-resistant synthetic phosphate ester fluids.

q.t: The hydraulic pump of the control system is driven by the...
q.e: To ensure control during autorotation (engine failure), the hydraulic pump is driven by the main rotor gearbox.

q.t: What reduces wearout on a skid-shoe landing gear?
q.e: Replaceable hardened steel shoes protect the main skid tubes from abrasion during landings on hard surfaces.

q.t: How can the pitch angle on a helicopter's rotor blade be controlled?
q.e: Mechanical control rods translate pilot inputs from the swashplate to the blade pitch horns.

q.t: What is caused by the movement of the cyclic stick?
o: Swash plate is inclined (periodic pitch change)
q.e: The cyclic stick tilts the swashplate, which changes blade pitch at specific points in the rotation (periodically).

q.t: What happens during cruise when the stick is moved forward without other corrections?
q.e: Forward cyclic tilts the rotor disk forward, increasing forward thrust (speed) but reducing the vertical lift component.

q.t: The control mixing assembly...
o: overlays periodic and collective control inputs
q.e: The mixing unit combines inputs from the cyclic and collective controls into a single output for the swashplate.

q.t: A spider control...
o: changes pitch via internal control rod
q.e: A "spider" system uses a central rod through the rotor mast to change blade pitch.

q.t: The trim is used to...
q.e: Trim systems relieve the pilot of the need to maintain constant pressure on the controls during flight.

q.t: The correlator (for pitch compensation)...
o: opens the throttle when collective is raised
q.e: A correlator is a mechanical link that automatically adds throttle as collective is increased to maintain RPM.

q.t: What has to be considered during refueling?
o: Turn on main switch and magnetos
No fires, smoking ban, apply ground cables
q.e: Safety protocols require grounding to prevent static sparks and strict fire prevention measures.

q.t: The primer is...
q.e: A primer injects fuel directly into the intake ports to help start a cold engine.

q.t: What is the purpose of the tank ventilation?
q.e: Ventilation allows air to replace the fuel being consumed, preventing a vacuum that would stop fuel flow.

q.t: An aeroplane's current supply is carried out by the:
q.e: The battery provides power for starting/emergencies, and the generator/alternator provides power during flight.

q.t: What is the unit for voltage?
q.e: Voltage (electrical potential difference) is measured in Volts.

q.t: What is the unit for electrical power?
q.e: Electrical power is the rate of energy consumption, measured in Watts.

q.t: What is the reason for static dischargers on aircraft?
q.e: These devices allow static electricity accumulated from friction with air to bleed off into the atmosphere.

q.t: What must be considered if the alternator fails in a helicopter?
o: No change if battery has power
q.e: If the alternator fails, the battery becomes the sole source of electricity until it is depleted.

q.t: When using direct current, electrically driven flight instruments are marked with...
q.e: DC stands for Direct Current, the standard electrical system type for light aircraft.

q.t: What devices can be affected by a failure of the electrical system?
q.e: Pitot-static instruments (airspeed/altimeter) are mechanical, but radios and electric gyros require power.

q.t: What cylinder arrangement is common in helicopters with piston engines?
q.e: Opposed-piston (Boxer) engines are common because they are flat, balanced, and easy to air-cool.

q.t: Which part of the cycle of a four-stroke Otto engine can be seen in figure AGK-007?
q.e: The figure shows the piston moving down with the intake valve open, indicating the induction stroke.

q.t: Which part of the cycle of a four-stroke Otto engine can be seen in figure AGK-008?
q.e: The figure shows the piston moving up with both valves closed, which is the compression stroke.

q.t: What is likely the cause if the engine runs unusually rough during magneto checks?
q.e: A fouled or defective spark plug will prevent proper combustion when that specific magneto is selected.

q.t: What needs to be checked regarding fuel after a cold night?
o: Fuel for water content and impurities
q.e: Cold nights cause moisture in empty tanks to condense into water; fuel must be drained and checked.

q.t: The highest absorbtion of humidity in fuel can be observed in which situation?
q.e: Empty tanks have more air space, allowing more moisture to condense from the air into the fuel.

q.t: Where does the condensation water converge in the tank?
o: It is mixed with the fuel
q.e: Water is denser than aviation fuel and will always sink to the lowest point of the tank.

q.t: What does the octane rating or fuel grade describe?
q.e: Octane rating measures a fuel's resistance to "knocking" or pre-ignition during combustion.

q.t: Which colour does Avgas 100 LL have?
q.e: 100 Low Lead (100LL) aviation gasoline is dyed blue for easy identification.

q.t: What is the major task of a carburettor?
q.e: The carburettor atomizes fuel and mixes it with air in the correct ratio for combustion.

q.t: How does the pilot compensate for power loss from using carburettor heat in a hover?
o: Adjust the height in a hover
q.e: Hot air is less dense; using carb heat makes the mixture richer, so pilot may need to adjust mixture.

q.t: When must carburettor heating be switched off even if icing is expected?
q.e: Carb heat reduces engine power and air density; full power is required for a safe take-off.

q.t: In which outside air temperature is icing most likely?
q.e: Carburettor icing can occur in warm temperatures (up to 20°C) if humidity is high due to the Venturi effect.

q.t: What is the task of cooling fins on air-cooled engine cylinders?
o: Quick heat transfer by expanding surface
q.e: Fins increase the surface area exposed to the air, allowing more heat to be dissipated.

q.t: Cylinder head temperature (CHT) indication relates to...
q.e: CHT is measured on the "hottest" or critical cylinder to ensure the entire engine is within limits.

q.t: What happens during oil filter clocking (clogging)?
q.e: To prevent engine seizure, a bypass valve allows dirty oil to continue circulating if the filter is blocked.

q.t: Which actions shall be taken if the engine oil pressure drops to zero?
o: Monitor temp and land at airfield
q.e: Zero oil pressure indicates imminent engine failure; an immediate landing is mandatory.

q.t: Piston engines of helicopters have...
q.e: Aviation engines use dual independent magnetos for redundancy and better combustion.

q.t: What is the most likely reason for the starter not turning when activated?
q.e: Many helicopters have a safety interlock that prevents the starter from engaging if the rotor brake is on.

q.t: How do you call fuel mixtures with a high amount of fuel?
q.e: A "rich" mixture has a higher ratio of fuel to air than the ideal (stoichiometric) ratio.

q.t: Why is leaning without an EGT indicator dangerous in helicopters?
q.e: Over-leaning can cause the engine to overheat or stumble/stop, which is critical in a helicopter.

q.t: With increasing altitude and unchanged mixture setting, the air/fuel mixture...
q.e: Air density decreases with altitude; if fuel flow isn't reduced, the ratio of fuel to air increases (richer).

q.t: With increasing altitude, the power of a carburettor engine...
q.e: Lower air density at high altitudes means less oxygen is available for combustion, reducing power.

q.t: What is the reason for a puddle of water below the helicopter in summer?
q.e: Air conditioning systems produce condensation (water) that drains out of the aircraft.

q.t: The droop stop...
o: prevents tail boom contact at low RPM
q.e: Droop stops limit the downward travel of blades when the rotor is slow or stopped to protect the airframe.

q.t: Which rotor blade material enables the construction of hingeless rotor heads?
q.e: Composite (plastic/fiberglass) materials provide the necessary flexibility to replace mechanical hinges.

q.t: What allows the removal of drag hinges in semi-rigid rotor systems?
q.e: Attaching the blades below the flapping hinge (underslung) reduces lead-lag forces (Coriolis effect).

q.t: What is the advantage of a hingeless rotor?
q.e: By using material flex instead of mechanical hinges, the system is simpler and lighter.

q.t: The advance angle is the angle between the...
q.e: It is a design angle in the control system to account for gyroscopic precession.

q.t: What kind of helicopter needs a tail rotor?
q.e: Shaft-driven single rotors produce torque that must be countered; blade-driven or twin rotors do not.

q.t: What is the advantage of a pushing tail rotor over a pulling tail rotor?
o: Less thrust loss by free outflow
q.e: A pusher rotor doesn't blow air against the tail boom, avoiding structural interference and thrust loss.

q.t: Why is the main rotor gearbox a limiting factor in most piston helicopters?
o: Gear wheels displace at high torque
q.e: High torque causes mechanical stress that can misalign gears and damage bearings.

q.t: The rotor brake should be engaged...
q.e: Engaging the brake during outside parking prevents wind from spinning and damaging the rotor system.

q.t: The connection between the main rotor mast and the head is...
q.e: Rotor heads are mechanically fastened (bolted/screwed) to the mast for strength and serviceability.

q.t: The mast bearing on the upper gearbox output acts against...
q.e: The mast bearing must support the weight of the helicopter (traction) and the forces from the rotor (bending).

q.t: What is the purpose of a belt clutch in the drive system?
q.e: A belt clutch allows the engine to start without the load of the rotor and then engage it slowly.

q.t: Why are all the connecting flanges of the main shaft designed flexible?
q.e: Flexibility prevents damage from vibration, thermal expansion, or slight misalignments.

q.t: How can the belts of a belt clutch be tightened?
q.e: Moving the pulleys further apart (increasing distance) applies the tension needed to transmit power.

q.t: Where does a geometrically twisted rotor blade have its largest pitch angle?
o: Next to the rotor blade roots
Next to the rotor blade tips
q.e: Blades are twisted to have more pitch at the root where speed is low, and less at the tip where speed is high.

q.t: A steel or lead rotor blade spar...
q.e: Heavy weights in the blade tips or spars increase rotational inertia, which is vital for autorotation.

q.t: Which components do rotor blades made of wood contain?
q.e: Traditional wooden blades used high-quality wood for the structure and a plastic/composite skin.

q.t: Which components do rotor blades made of metal contain?
q.e: Metal blades typically use a high-strength steel spar with lightweight aluminum ribs and skin.

q.t: Which components do rotor blades made of synthetic material contain?
q.e: Composite blades are mostly synthetic but use stainless steel (SS) on leading edges for erosion protection.

q.t: The rotor blades in a shrouded tail rotor can be arranged asymmetrically to...
q.e: Staggering the blades prevents them from all hitting the same frequency, significantly reducing noise.

q.t: Which gauges involve a measurement of temperature?
q.e: These gauges measure heat in the engine oil, coolant, cylinders, exhaust, and outside air.

q.t: European Certification Specifications CS 23 require that...
o: Calibrated to read "zero" at unusable fuel
q.e: Regulations require that "0" on the gauge must represent the point when no more usable fuel remains.

q.t: Which method of measurement is mostly used for the fuel supply on helicopters?
q.e: Capacitive sensors are preferred as they have no moving parts and measure the actual mass of the fuel.

q.t: Which actions shall be taken if the rotor RPM indicator fails during cruise flight?
q.e: Without knowing rotor RPM, you cannot safely manage the flight or perform an autorotation; land immediately.

q.t: Which value can the pilot derive from the tachometer?
q.e: A tachometer specifically measures the rotational speed of the engine and/or rotor system.

q.t: Which of the instruments listed obtain their readings through pressure?
o: Oil, fuel, manifold, altimeter, VSI, ASI
q.e: These instruments rely on measuring fluid pressure (oil/fuel) or atmospheric pressure (pitot-static).

q.t: The Pitot / static system is required to...
o: measure total and static air pressure
q.e: The system captures total pressure (Pitot) and ambient pressure (Static) to drive flight instruments.

q.t: Which pressure is sensed by the Pitot tube?
q.e: The Pitot tube faces the airflow and captures "Total" pressure (Static + Dynamic).

q.t: QFE is the...
o: barometric pressure at a reference datum
q.e: QFE is the local atmospheric pressure at the airfield level; with QFE set, the altimeter reads "0" on the ground.

q.t: QNE is the...
q.e: QNE is used at high altitudes; it is the altitude indicated when the subscale is set to standard 1013.25 hPa.

q.t: Which is the purpose of the altimeter subscale?
q.e: The subscale (Kollsman window) allows the pilot to set the reference pressure (QNH or QFE).

q.t: In which way may a subscale set to an incorrect QNH lead to an incorrect reading?
q.e: "High to Low, look out below" - if the set pressure is higher than actual, the plane is lower than indicated.

q.t: Lower-than-standard temperature may lead to...
q.e: In cold air, pressure levels are compressed; the altimeter will indicate a higher altitude than the aircraft's true height.

q.t: A flight level is a...
q.e: Flight Levels are based on the standard pressure setting (1013.25), which defines pressure altitude.

q.t: A true altitude is...
q.e: True altitude is the actual vertical distance above Mean Sea Level.

q.t: During a flight in colder-than-ISA air the indicated altitude is...
q.e: The instrument "over-reads" in cold temperatures.

q.t: In ISA mass with QNH set correctly, the indicated altitude is...
q.e: Under standard conditions and correct pressure settings, Indicated Altitude equals True Altitude.

q.t: Which instrument can be affected by the hysteresis error?
q.e: Hysteresis is a lag in the elastic response of the altimeter's capsules after a large/rapid altitude change.

q.t: The measurement of altitude is based on the change of the...
q.e: Atmospheric pressure decreases with height; the altimeter measures this static pressure drop.

q.t: Which states the working principle of a vertical speed indicator (VSI)?
q.e: The VSI compares instantaneous static pressure with static pressure trapped in a calibrated reservoir (bottle).

q.t: The VSI measures the difference of pressure between...
q.e: A VSI is a differential pressure gauge that measures the rate of change in static pressure.

q.t: Calibrated airspeed (CAS) equals...
q.e: CAS is Indicated Airspeed (IAS) adjusted for errors in the pitot system and the instrument itself.

q.t: A rough estimate of the TAS can be obtained by...
q.e: TAS increases roughly 2% for every 1000 ft of altitude over the CAS/IAS.

q.t: Heading 180°, TAS 100 kt, wind 180°/30 kt. Approximate ASI reading?
q.e: The Airspeed Indicator (ASI) measures speed through the air (TAS/IAS), which is independent of the wind.

q.t: Which factor could cause an erroneous airspeed indication?
q.e: Foils or dirt can disturb the airflow around the Pitot tube or static ports, causing errors.

q.t: What values are usually marked with a red line on instrument displays?
q.e: A red radial line indicates a maximum or minimum limit that must never be exceeded.

q.t: Which states the working principle of an airspeed indicator?
q.e: The ASI measures Dynamic pressure by subtracting Static pressure from Total pressure.

q.t: What is necessary for the determination of speed (IAS)?
q.e: IAS is derived from the difference between the Pitot pressure (total) and the Static pressure.

q.t: What is the meaning of the red range on the airspeed indicator?
q.e: The red line (or end of the yellow arc) is the "Never Exceed" speed for structural safety.

q.t: The compass error caused by the aircraft's magnetic field is...
q.e: Deviation is the error caused by local magnetic fields (engine, electronics) within the aircraft.

q.t: Why does a magnetic compass deviate from magnetic north?
q.e: Mechanical and magnetic factors cause the compass to be inaccurate during maneuvers or due to local fields.

q.t: Which cockpit instrument is connected to the pitot tube?
q.e: Only the Airspeed Indicator requires the ram-air (total) pressure from the Pitot tube.

q.t: Which cockpit instruments are connected to the static port?
q.e: All three primary pitot-static instruments require a reference to the ambient (static) air pressure.

q.t: Northern hemisphere turn 270° to 360°. Terminate at?
q.e: When turning toward North, the compass "leads" the turn; you must roll out early to account for this.

q.t: The term "static pressure" is defined as pressure...
q.e: Static pressure is the weight of the air above, measured in a location undisturbed by the plane's motion.

q.t: Northern hemisphere turn 360° to 270°. Terminate at?
q.e: When turning away from North, the compass "lags"; you must roll out before reaching the target heading.

q.t: Northern hemisphere turn 030° to 180°. Terminate at?
q.e: When turning toward South, the compass "lags"; you must roll out past the target heading on the dial.

q.t: What does the dynamic pressure depend directly on?
q.e: Dynamic pressure (q) formula is 1/2 ρ v², where ρis density and v is velocity.

q.t: What is a cause for the dip error on the direct-reading compass?
q.e: Magnetic flux lines point down into the earth near poles, pulling the compass needle with them.

q.t: What behaviour is shown by a rotating gyro in space?
q.e: Rigidity in space is a fundamental property of a gyroscope.

q.t: A gyro rotating in space responds to forces by...
q.e: This is "precession" - a force applied to a gyro manifests as a movement 90 degrees later in rotation.

q.t: The bank angle of a 2-minutes circle depends on the...
q.e: For a specific rate of turn, the required bank angle increases with the True Airspeed (TAS).

q.t: A turn and bank coordinator provides information regarding...
q.e: It shows how fast the aircraft is turning and if it is slipping or skidding (via the ball).

q.t: The airspeed indicator is unservicable.
q.e: The ASI is a mandatory flight instrument; the aircraft is grounded until it is repaired.

q.t: Which advises pilot to condition "corrective action may be required"?
q.e: Amber lights signify "Caution" - something needs attention soon but isn't an immediate emergency.

q.t: The Caution Area is marked on an airspeed indicator by?
q.e: The yellow arc on the ASI represents the caution range (operate only in smooth air).

q.t: An attitude director indicator (ADI) combines...
q.e: An ADI adds "command bars" (Flight Director) onto a standard artificial horizon.

q.t: What does the abbreviation HSI stand for?
q.e: The HSI is a combination of a directional gyro and a navigation display.

q.t: A horizontal situation indicator (HSI) combines...
q.e: The HSI shows the aircraft's heading and its position relative to a VOR or ILS path.

q.t: Altitude change if reference pressure changed 1000 to 1010 hPa?
q.e: 1 hPa is roughly 8 meters (27 ft). Increasing the setting increases the indicated altitude.

q.t: When is it necessary to adjust the pressure in an altimeter?
o: Before every flight and during cross country
q.e: Pilots must update the subscale to the current local QNH to ensure accurate altitude readings.

q.t: The altimeter's reference scale is set to airfield pressure (QFE).
q.e: Setting QFE makes the altimeter read height above the station (AAL - Above Aerodrome Level).

q.t: A vertical speed indicator measures the difference between...
q.e: It measures the change in static pressure over time.

q.t: The term "inclination" is defined as...
q.e: Inclination (dip) is the vertical angle of magnetic field lines relative to the earth's surface.

q.t: What does the slip indicator show?
q.e: The ball responds to gravity and centrifugal force, showing the "apparent" vertical direction.

q.t: Ball moved right during a right turn. How to center?
o: Reduce bank, increase rate of turn
Reduce rate of turn, reduce bank
Increase bank, increase rate of turn
q.e: "Step on the ball" - you must use rudder to increase the turn rate or decrease bank to balance forces.

q.t: What is the purpose of engine oil in piston engine?
q.e: Oil reduces friction, carries heat away from parts, and traps tiny metal particles for the filter.

q.t: The rotational axis of the Earth runs through the...
o: magnetic north pole and on the magnetic south pole.
geographic North Pole and on the geographic South Pole.
geographic North Pole and on the magnetic south pole.
magnetic north pole and on the geographic South Pole.
q.e: The Earth rotates around its geographic poles, which are distinct from the magnetic poles .

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the polar axis of the Earth?
o: crosses the geographic poles and is perpendicular to the equator.
crosses the magnetic poles and is at 66.5° to the equator.
crosses the geographic poles and is at 23.5° to the equator.
crosses the magnetic poles and is perpendicular to the equator.
q.e: The geographic poles are defined by the Earth's axis of rotation, which is perpendicular to the equatorial plane .

q.t: Which approximate geometrical form describes the shape of the Earth best for navigation systems?
q.e: Modern navigation systems like GPS use an ellipsoid model (e.g., WGS84) to account for the Earth's equatorial bulge .

q.t: Which statement about a rhumb line is correct?
o: It is a great circle intersecting the equator with 45° angle.
The center of a rhumb line is always the Earth's center.
A rhumb line cuts each meridian at the same angle.
The shortest track between two points follows a rhumb line.
q.e: A rhumb line (loxodrome) is a line that crosses all meridians of longitude at the same constant angle .

q.t: The shortest distance between two points on Earth is represented by a part of...
q.e: A great circle represents the shortest path between any two points on the surface of a sphere .

q.t: The circumference of the Earth at the equator is approximately...
q.e: The circumference is calculated as 360 degrees multiplied by 60 minutes of arc (1 NM per minute), equaling 21,600 NM .

q.t: What is the difference in latitude between A (12°53'30"N) and B (07°34'30"S)?
q.e: To find the difference between points in opposite hemispheres, add the latitudes: 12°53'30" + 07°34'30" = 20°28'00" .

q.t: Where are the two polar circles?
o: 23.5° north and south of the poles
23.5° north and south of the equator
q.e: The polar circles are at 66.5° latitude, which is exactly 23.5° (the Earth's tilt) away from the poles .

q.t: What is the distance between the parallels of latitude 48°N and 49°N along a meridian line?
q.e: One degree of latitude corresponds to exactly 60 nautical miles along a meridian .

q.t: What distance corresponds to one degree difference in latitude along any degree of longitude?
q.e: By definition, one minute of latitude is one nautical mile; thus, 60 minutes (one degree) is 60 NM .

q.t: Point A lies on 47°50'27"N. Which point is exactly 240 NM north of A?
q.e: 240 NM divided by 60 NM/degree equals 4 degrees. 47°50'27" + 4° = 51°50'27"N .

q.t: What is the distance between the meridians 150°E and 151°E along the equator?
q.e: At the equator, the distance between meridians is at its maximum, and one degree of longitude equals 60 NM .

q.t: Great circle distance between two points on the equator with 1° difference?
q.e: Since a great circle along the equator is identical to the equator itself, 1° longitude equals 60 NM .

q.t: Rhumb line distance between 010°E and 020°E on any parallel (not equator)?
q.e: Longitude distance decreases as one moves away from the equator; 10° is always less than 600 NM (its equatorial value) .

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 20° of longitude?
q.e: The sun moves at a rate of 15° per hour. 20° / 15° = 1.33 hours, or 1 hour and 20 minutes .

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 10° of longitude?
q.e: Since 15° equals 60 minutes, 1° equals 4 minutes. 10° * 4 minutes = 40 minutes .

q.t: The sun moves 10° of longitude. What is the difference in time? (decimal)
q.e: 40 minutes converted to decimal hours is 40/60 = 0.66, however the source indicates 0.4 h (likely meaning 40 mins) .

q.t: With CEST given as UTC+2, what UTC time corresponds to 1600 CEST?
q.e: To convert Summer Time (UTC+2) back to UTC, subtract 2 hours from the local time .

q.t: UTC is...
o: an obligatory time used in aviation.
a local time in Central Europe.
local mean time at a point on Earth.
q.e: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the global standard used in aviation to ensure synchronization across regions .

q.t: With CET given as UTC+1, what UTC time corresponds to 1700 CET?
q.e: To convert Central European Time (UTC+1) to UTC, subtract 1 hour from the local time .

q.t: Wien (016° 34'E) vs Salzburg (013° 00'E). Difference in sunrise/sunset?
q.e: Longitudinal difference is ~3.5°. 3.5° * 4 min/deg = 14 min. Solar events happen earlier in the East .

q.t: The term 'civil twilight' is defined as...
q.e: Civil twilight is the period when the center of the sun is between 0° and 6° below the true horizon .

q.t: Calculation: WCA -12°, TH 125°, MC 139°, DEV +2°E. Find TC, MH, CH.
q.e: TH = TC + WCA (125 = TC - 12 -> TC = 137). MH = TH + VAR (needs check) .

q.t: Calculation: TC 179°, WCA -12°, VAR +4°E, DEV +2°. Find MH and MC.
The angle between the true course and the true heading is called...
q.e: Wind Correction Angle (WCA) is the angle the aircraft must crab into the wind to stay on course .

q.t: The angle between the magnetic course and the true course is called...
q.e: Magnetic variation is the angular difference between geographic (true) north and magnetic north .

q.t: The term 'magnetic course' (MC) is defined as...
o: angle true north to course line.
angle magnetic north to course line.
q.e: Magnetic course is the direction of the intended path measured from magnetic north .

q.t: The term 'True Course' (TC) is defined as...
o: angle true north to course line.
angle magnetic north to course line.
q.e: True course is the direction of the intended path measured from geographic (true) north .

q.t: Calc: TC 183°, WCA +11°, MH 198°, CH 200°. Find TH and VAR.
Calc: TC 183°, WCA +11°, MH 198°, CH 200°. Find TH and DEV.
Calc: TC 183°, WCA +11°, MH 198°, CH 200°. Find VAR and DEV.
Where does the inclination reach its lowest value?
q.e: Magnetic inclination (dip) is 0° at the magnetic equator and increases to 90° at the magnetic poles .

q.t: The angle between compass north and magnetic north is called...
q.e: Deviation is the error in a compass reading caused by local magnetic fields within the aircraft .

q.t: Which direction corresponds to 'compass north' (CN)?
q.e: Compass North is the direction the needle actually points after both Earth and aircraft magnetic effects .

q.t: The term 'isogonal' connects all points with the same value of...
q.e: Isogonic lines connect locations on the Earth's surface that share the same magnetic variation .

q.t: The term 'agonic line' connects all points with the...
q.e: An agonic line is an isogonic line where the magnetic variation is exactly zero degrees .

q.t: Official basic units for horizontal distance in navigation?
q.e: Nautical Miles (NM) and Kilometers (km) are the standard units for horizontal distance in aviation .

q.t: 1000 ft equal...
q.e: Using the standard conversion (1 m ≈ 3.28 ft), 1000 feet is approximately 300 meters .

q.t: 5500 m equal...
q.e: 5500 meters converted to feet (multiplied by ~3.28) is approximately 18,000 feet .

q.t: Reason for changing runway indicators (e.g. from 06 to 07)?
q.e: Runway numbers are based on magnetic north; as variation shifts over decades, the numbers must be updated .

q.t: Electronic devices on board have influence on the...
q.e: Magnetic fields from electronic equipment can cause deviation errors in a direct-reading compass .

q.t: Which are the properties of a Mercator chart?
o: Scale constant, GC curved, Rhumb straight
Scale constant, GC straight, Rhumb curved
Scale increases with lat, GC curved, Rhumb straight
Scale increases with lat, GC straight, Rhumb curved
q.e: Mercator charts are conformal; rhumb lines are straight, but scale changes with latitude and great circles are curved .

q.t: Depiction of rhumb lines and great circles on a Mercator chart?
q.e: On a standard Mercator projection, lines of constant bearing (rhumb lines) are straight lines .

q.t: Which are the properties of a Lambert conformal chart?
o: Conformal and nearly true to scale
q.e: Lambert charts are widely used because they preserve angles and maintain a nearly uniform scale .

q.t: Which lines have to be used by the pilot to determine position?
q.e: True bearings (QTE) from ground stations are plotted on charts to determine an aircraft's position .

q.t: Radial from VOR Brünkendorf (BKD) to Pritzwalk (EDBU)?
q.e: Based on the chart (NAV-031), the radial from the BKD station toward EDBU is 024° .

q.t: Dist 220 NM, chart measures 40.7 cm. Scale?
VOR HAM R119, VOR BKD R320. Cross bearing position?
q.e: Plotting these radials on the provided chart (NAV-031) results in this coordinate .

q.t: Distance VOR Brünkendorf (BKD) to Pritzwalk (EDBU)?
q.e: Measured on the chart, the distance between these two points is 24 Nautical Miles .

q.t: 7.5 cm on chart represents 60.745 NM. Scale?
TC 245°, VAR 7° W. Find MC.
q.e: Using the rule "Variation West, Magnetic Best," you add the westerly variation: 245 + 7 = 252° .

q.t: IAS 150 kt at 8000 ft MSL. Rule of thumb TAS?
q.e: TAS increases by ~2% of IAS per 1000 ft: 150 + (150 * 0.02 * 8) = 174 kt .

q.t: Dist 210 NM, TAS 130 kt, Headwind 15 kt, ETD 0915 UTC. ETA?
TC 283°, Dist 75 NM, TAS 105 kt, Headwind 12 kt, ETD 1242 UTC. ETA?
TC 352°, Dist 100 NM, GS 107 kt, ETD 0933 UTC. ETA?
GS calc: 100 km in 56 minutes?
q.e: GS = (100 km / 56 min) * 60 min/h ≈ 107.1 km/h .

q.t: GS calc: 110 NM in 01:25?
q.e: GS = 110 NM / 1.416 h ≈ 77.6 kt, rounded to 78 kt .

q.t: Time for 236 NM at GS 134 kt?
Time for 185 NM at TAS 120 kt with 35 kt tailwind?
Distance flown: TAS 180 kt, headwind 25 kt, for 2h 25m?
CAS 155 kt, FL 80, OAT +15°C. True airspeed (TAS)?
q.e: At high density altitude (FL 80, warm OAT), the TAS is significantly higher than CAS (~180 kt) .

q.t: TC from Uelzen to Neustadt?
q.e: Measuring on the chart (NAV-031) gives a true course of 061° .

q.t: Pressure alt 7500, OAT -9°C, QNH alt 6500. True altitude?
q.e: Low OAT makes the air denser, meaning the aircraft is lower than indicated (6250 ft) .

q.t: Distance Neustadt to Uelzen?
q.e: Measured on the chart, the distance between these coordinates is 78 Nautical Miles .

q.t: Pressure alt 7000, OAT +11°C, QNH alt 6500. True altitude?
q.e: Warmer than standard temperatures mean the aircraft is higher than indicated (6750 ft) .

q.t: Pressure alt 7000, OAT +21°C, QNH alt 6500. True altitude?
q.e: Significant warm OAT (+21°) increases the true altitude to approximately 7000 ft .

q.t: TC 255°, TAS 100 kt, Wind 200°/10 kt. True heading?
q.e: The wind is from the left, requiring a corrective steer into the wind (left/smaller number) .

q.t: TC 165°, TAS 90 kt, Wind 130°/20 kt, Dist 153 NM. True heading?
q.e: A strong crosswind from 130° requires a correction to the left, resulting in TH 152° .

q.t: GS 160 kt, TC 177°, Wind 140°/20 kt. True heading (TH)?
q.e: To counter a wind from the left (140°), the pilot must head further left (169°) .

q.t: TC 220°, TAS 220 kt, Wind 270°/50 kt. Ground speed (GS)?
q.e: A quartering headwind from 270° reduces the ground speed to 185 kt .

q.t: TC 040°, TAS 180 kt, Wind 350°/30 kt. Groundspeed (GS)?
q.e: The headwind component from 350° reduces the ground speed to 159 kt .

q.t: TC 040°, TAS 180 kt, Wind 350°/30 kt. Wind correction angle (WCA)?
q.e: Wind from the left (350°) requires a negative (left) correction angle of 7 degrees .

q.t: TC 270°, TAS 100 kt, Wind 090°/25 kt, Dist 100 NM. GS?
q.e: Direct tailwind (090°) adds its full speed to the TAS: 100 + 25 = 125 kt .

q.t: TC 270°, TAS 100 kt, Wind 090°/25 kt, Dist 100 NM. Flight time?
q.e: GS = 125. Time = 100 / 125 = 0.8h = 48 minutes .

q.t: TC 040°, TAS 180 kt, Wind 350°/30 kt. WCA?
q.e: Wind from 350° is 50° to the left of the course, requiring a 7° left correction .

q.t: TC 120°, TAS 120 kt, Wind 150°/12 kt. WCA?
q.e: Wind is from the right (150°), requiring a 3° right correction steer .

q.t: Dist 120 NM. 7 NM off right at 55 NM. Course change to B?
q.e: Track Error (7.6°) + Closing Angle (6.4°) = 14° correction to the left .

q.t: Heading 090, 4.5 NM north of path at 45 NM. Heading to reach destination?
q.e: 6° TE + 6° CA = 12° total heading correction to the right .

q.t: What is the meaning of the 1:60 rule?
q.e: The rule states that a 1-degree track error results in a 1 NM offset after 60 NM flown .

q.t: A to B 220 NM, GS 120, depart 1200. 5 min ahead at 70 NM. Revised ETA?
q.e: Actual GS is higher than planned. Proportional calculation leads to ETA 13:35 .

q.t: Completes the flight plan: TH, MH, MC?
q.e: Based on the values in NAV-014, these are the correct calculations for the final row .

q.t: The approximate propagation speed of electromagnetic waves is...
q.e: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, approx. 300,000 kilometers per second .

q.t: Radio waves within the LF and MF range (e.g. NDB) travel as...
q.e: Low and Medium frequencies follow the Earth's surface and also reflect off the ionosphere .

q.t: Radio waves within the VHF range (e.g. VOR) travel as...
q.e: VHF signals are "line-of-sight" and do not follow the Earth's curvature .

q.t: Quasi-optical waves travel...
q.e: Space waves (quasi-optical) require a direct line of sight between the antenna and receiver .

q.t: A VHF direction finder (VDF) can determine...
q.e: VDF stations on the ground determine the magnetic bearing of the aircraft based on its radio signal .

q.t: Which equipment is needed on board to use a VHF direction finder (VDF)?
q.e: VDF is ground-based; the aircraft only needs a standard VHF radio to transmit .

q.t: QDM: 138°, VAR: 10° E. The QUJ equals...
q.e: QUJ (True Track to station) = QDM (Magnetic Track) + Variation (East): 138 + 10 = 148° .

q.t: QTE: 229°, VAR: 10° W. The QDM equals...
q.e: QDM = QTE + VAR - 180 (for reciprocal). 229 - 10 - 180 = 39 (incorrect in source?). Source states 059° .

q.t: QDR: 022°, VAR: 10° E. The QTE equals...
q.e: QTE (True Bearing from) = QDR (Magnetic Bearing from) + VAR (East): 22 + 10 = 32° .

q.t: QDM: 248°, VAR: 10° W. The QTE is...
q.e: QTE = QDM + VAR + 180 (to reverse). 248 - 10 - 180 = 58? Source indicates 078° .

q.t: QDR: 067°, VAR: 5° E. The QDM equals...
q.e: QDM is the magnetic bearing TO (reciprocal of QDR): 67 + 180 = 247° .

q.t: QDR 152, VAR 5W, DEV 5E. QUJ?
q.e: Reciprocal (332) - VAR (5W) = 327° .

q.t: QTE: 203°, VAR: 10° E. The QDR equals...
q.e: QDR = QTE - VAR (East). 203 - 10 = 193. Reciprocal = 13. Source indicates 023° .

q.t: QTE: 248°, VAR: 10° W. The QDR equals...
q.e: QDR = QTE - VAR (West/subtract). 248 - (-10) = 258° .

q.t: QDM: 134°, VAR: 5° W. The QTE equals...
q.e: QDM (134) + VAR (5W/subtract) = 129. Reciprocal = 309° .

q.t: Pilot receives QDR of 225°. Location relative to station?
q.e: QDR is the magnetic bearing FROM the station. 225° is Southwest .

q.t: The term QDR means...
q.e: QDR is the magnetic bearing from the ground station to the aircraft .

q.t: The term QTE means...
q.e: QTE is the true (geographic) bearing from the station to the aircraft .

q.t: Pilot receives QDR of 135°. Location relative to station?
q.e: A QDR of 135° indicates the aircraft is on the 135-degree magnetic radial (Southeast) .

q.t: Pilot receives QDR of 315°. Location relative to station?
q.e: A QDR of 315° indicates the aircraft is on the 315-degree magnetic radial (Northwest) .

q.t: The VDF range depends on...
q.e: VHF signals are line-of-sight; higher altitude increases the radio horizon .

q.t: Equipment to receive signals from a non-directional beacon (NDB)?
q.e: The ADF is the instrument used to track and navigate using NDB stations .

q.t: Non-directional beacons (NDBs) transmit within which frequency band?
q.e: NDBs operate in the Low and Medium Frequency bands, typically 190 to 535 kHz .

q.t: QDM approach logic with wind changes?
q.e: If RBI increases while MH is constant, crosswind has increased from left .

q.t: Proceed directly to beacon . Follow QDM of...
q.e: Based on the instrument display in the figure, the track to the station is 260° .

q.t: Difference between a locator beacon and an NDB?
q.e: Locators are low-powered NDBs used specifically for airfield approach guidance .

q.t: The range of NDBs (Medium Frequency) is greatest...
q.e: Ground waves travel further at night when D-layer absorption is gone, and sky waves reflect .

q.t: The shoreline effect is greatest...
q.e: Low altitude and small crossing angles maximize the refraction of waves at the land-sea boundary .

q.t: Fading in LF/MF frequency range occurs mainly...
q.e: Interference between ground waves and sky waves (fading) is most common at night .

q.t: Progress of electromagnetic oscillation described by...
q.e: The phase angle describes the specific point in the cycle of a periodic wave .

q.t: When transmitter and receiver move towards each other...
q.e: This is the Doppler Effect: perceived frequency increases as distance closes .

q.t: When transmitter and receiver move away from each other...
q.e: The Doppler Effect causes a drop in perceived frequency as the source and receiver separate .

q.t: VOR radials are defined based on the principle of...
q.e: VOR receivers calculate radials by comparing the phase of a reference and a variable signal .

q.t: A VOR radial corresponds to the...
q.e: A radial is the magnetic bearing FROM the station, which is defined as QDR .

q.t: Full deflection of the CDI means aircraft is located at least...
q.e: Standard VOR indicators show full deflection at 10 degrees off the selected course .

q.t: Location relative to VOR ?
q.e: According to the CDI display in the figure, the aircraft is to the Northeast .

q.t: The aircraft is on radial ?
q.e: Based on the OBS setting and CDI position in the figure, the aircraft is on radial 234° .

q.t: The range of a VOR is affected by...
q.e: VOR range is limited by line-of-sight, which is determined by altitude .

q.t: DME determines distance based on the principle of...
q.e: DME calculates distance by measuring the time delay of a pulse signal's round trip .

q.t: The DME reading is a...
q.e: DME measures the direct distance between aircraft and station, including altitude .

q.t: Slant range vs horizontal distance difference increases...
q.e: As an aircraft approaches the station, the vertical altitude component becomes dominant .

q.t: Primary radar direction determined by...
q.e: Primary radar "sees" the target's bearing based on the direction the dish is facing .

q.t: Instantaneous info from ground radar?
q.e: Primary radar provides the 2D position (distance and bearing) of a target .

q.t: The on-board equipment of the secondary surveillance radar (SSR) is a...
q.e: The transponder receives the radar's query and transmits a coded reply .

q.t: Difference between primary and secondary radar?
q.e: Primary radar reflects pulses; secondary radar uses transponder responses .

q.t: The transponder code in case of hi-jacking is...
q.e: Squawk 7500 is the international emergency code for unlawful interference .

q.t: The transponder code in case of a radio communication failure is...
q.e: Squawk 7600 informs ATC that the pilot cannot communicate via radio .

q.t: Which altitude is transmitted by the transponder in mode C?
q.e: Mode C transponders transmit altitude relative to the 1013.25 hPa datum .

q.t: Satellites for precise 3D position determination?
q.e: Four satellites are required to resolve X, Y, Z coordinates and time errors .

q.t: GPS deviation interpretation?
q.e: Full deflection in NM depends on the mode (Enroute, Terminal, Approach) .

q.t: What is meant by the term "terrestrial navigation"?
q.e: Terrestrial navigation (pilotage) involves comparing the ground to a chart .

q.t: Ground features for orientation during visual flight?
q.e: Distinct, linear features are easiest to recognize and follow from the air .
